en: The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One.
[In the Danben (Dunhuang manuscript), the two characters "Small Version" (Xiǎopǐn) appear above "Mahā.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
1. The First Chapter, Chapter One. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, like well-trained elephant kings; they had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, were liberated through right gnosis, and had attained mastery over their minds—with the sole exception of Ānanda.
At that time, the Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Since you delight in eloquence, explain for the sake of the bodhisattvas the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that they should accomplish.
Śāriputra then had this thought:
"Does Subhūti speak this by his own power,
or does he do so by receiving the Buddha's spiritual power?
Subhūti, knowing what Śāriputra was thinking, said to Śāriputra:
"Whatever the disciples of the Buddha dare to say, it is all by the power of the Buddha.

Why is this? Regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, those who train therein are able to realize the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Having realized them, whatever they say does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena, precisely because of the power of those characteristics."
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha has commanded me to explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that they should accomplish.”
"Bhagavān!
Regarding that which is called 'bodhisattva, bodhisattva,' what dharma or meaning constitutes a bodhisattva?
I do not perceive any dharma that can be named 'bodhisattva.'"
"Bhagavān!
I do not see a bodhisattva, nor do I apprehend a bodhisattva; I also do not see or apprehend the prajñāpāramitā. Toward what kind of bodhisattva should I teach the prajñāpāramitā?"

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, but practices according to what has been taught, this is called the instruction in the Prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should train in this way: they should not give rise to the thought, "This is the bodhisattva-mind. Why is that?
"This mind is no-mind, because the characteristic of mind is fundamentally pure.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"Does this 'no-mind' exist?"
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Can a mind that is not [a mind] be apprehended as either existing or non-existing?
Śāriputra replied:
"No," Subhūti said to Śāriputra,
"if neither mind nor non-mind can be apprehended as existing or non-existing, should one say that there is mind or that there is no mind?"
Śāriputra asked,
“What dharma is not mind?
Subhūti replied:

"Without being impaired or making conceptual distinctions, when a bodhisattva hears this teaching, they are not startled, not terrified, do not sink, and do not retreat; one should know that this bodhisattva does not depart from the practice of the prajñāpāramitā."

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to train in the stage of the śrāvaka, they should hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to its teaching.
One who wishes to study the stage of a pratyekabuddha should hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to its teaching.
One who wishes to study the stage of a bodhisattva should likewise hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to its teaching.
"Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the dharmas that a bodhisattva should study are explained in detail.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bhagavān! Since I do not see a bodhisattva, what bodhisattva should I instruct in the perfection of wisdom?
Bhagavān!”
"I do not see any coming or going of the bodhisattva-dharmas, yet you apply the designation 'bodhisattva' to one; therefore, I have doubts and regrets.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, the designation 'bodhisattva' is neither fixed nor has it any place of abiding."
Why is this so? Because these words have no existence;
that which has no existence is neither fixed nor localized.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing these matters, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, one should know that this bodhisattva ultimately dwells in the stage of non-retrogression, dwelling in non-dwelling.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide in form; they should not abide in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."
Why is this? If one dwells within form, one performs the activity of form;
if one dwells within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one performs the activity of consciousness.
If one practices with conceptual construction, one cannot receive the *prajñāpāramitā* and cannot cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*;
lacking the fulfillment of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one cannot achieve *sarvajñatā*.
Why is this? Form is without sensation or perception; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without sensation or perception.
If form is without sensation, it is not form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—when there is no grasping at them, they are not consciousness.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without grasping.

A bodhisattva should train in the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way; this is called the bodhisattva’s samādhi of non-grasping at all dharmas—vast, immeasurable, and undetermined, which cannot be destroyed by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Why is this? This samādhi cannot be attained through signs.
If this samādhi could be attained through signs, the brahmin Śreṇika would not have been able to give rise to faith in the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The Brahmin Śreṇika entered into this Dharma with finite knowledge; having entered, he did not grasp at form, nor did he grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

This Brahmin did not perceive this knowledge by means of hearing or seeing it through internal form, nor did he perceive it through external form, nor did he perceive it through both internal and external form, nor did he perceive it apart from internal and external form.

He did not perceive this knowledge by means of internal feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor did he perceive it through external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor did he perceive it through both internal and external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor did he perceive it apart from internal and external feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
The Brahmin Śreṇika had faith and understanding in the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*); because he realized the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), he attained liberation.
Having attained liberation, he neither grasped nor rejected anything among all phenomena, even regarding nirvāṇa he neither grasped nor rejected.
"World-Honored One!
This is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) which does not grasp form, and does not grasp feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.

Although they do not grasp form, nor grasp feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, as long as they have not yet fulfilled the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities, they will never enter parinirvāṇa midway."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should reflect in this way:
'What is this perfection of wisdom?'"
"Whose is this prajñāpāramitā?
Is it prajñāpāramitā because no dharma can be apprehended?

When a bodhisattva reflects and contemplates in this way, if they are not startled, not terrified, and not afraid; if they do not sink down and do not retreat, one should know that this bodhisattva is not separated from the practice of prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If form is separate from the nature of form, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are separate from the nature of consciousness, and if the *prajñāpāramitā* is separate from the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*, for what reason do you say that a bodhisattva does not depart from the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Subhūti said: "It is so, Śāriputra!

Form is detached from the nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are detached from the nature of consciousness; the *prajñāpāramitā* is detached from the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*. All these dharmas are detached from their own-nature (*svabhāva*), and even their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are detached."
Śāriputra asked:
"If a bodhisattva trains in this, can they accomplish sarvajñatā?
Subhūti replied:
"In this way, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva who trains thus is able to accomplish sarvajñā. Why is that?
"Because all dharmas are without arising and without accomplishment,
if a bodhisattva practices in this way, they will draw near to sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
At that time, Subhūti said to Śāriputra:

“If a bodhisattva practices with the activity of form as a mental sign, or with the arising of form as a mental sign, or with the cessation of form as a mental sign, or with the destruction of form as a mental sign, or with the emptiness of form as a mental sign.”
I practice this practice, which is itself a mode of practice.

If one practices the practice of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, that is a mode of practice; if one practices the arising of consciousness, that is a mode of practice; if one practices the cessation of consciousness, that is a mode of practice; if one practices the destruction of consciousness, that is a mode of practice; if one practices the emptiness of consciousness, that is a mode of practice.
"My practicing this practice is itself a conceptualization of the practice. If one thinks,
'One who can practice in this way is practicing the Prajñāpāramitā,' that too is a conceptualization of the practice."
"You should know that this bodhisattva has not yet become well-versed in skillful means.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti, "How, then,
must a bodhisattva now practice to be said to be practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Subhūti said:

"If a bodhisattva does not practice with regard to form, does not practice with regard to the arising of form, does not practice with regard to the cessation of form, does not practice with regard to the destruction of form, and does not practice with regard to the emptiness of form; and if they do not practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor with regard to the arising of consciousness, nor with regard to the cessation of consciousness, nor with regard to the destruction of consciousness, nor with regard to the emptiness of consciousness—this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom."

Not to think of practicing the perfection of wisdom, not to think of not practicing, not to think of both practicing and not practicing, and also not to think of neither practicing nor not practicing—this is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are without grasping.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s samādhi of the non-grasping of all dharmas; it is vast, immeasurable, and indeterminate, and cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
“A bodhisattva who practices this samādhi will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, spoke these words:
“If a bodhisattva practices this samādhi, they do not think or discriminate:”
"If I shall enter this samādhi," "I am now entering this samādhi," or "I have entered [this samādhi]"—
if there is no such discrimination, one should know that this bodhisattva has already received from the Buddhas the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
“The samādhis practiced by a bodhisattva enable them to receive from the Buddhas the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
"Can this samādhi be demonstrated?
Subhūti replied, "No, Śāriputra."
Why is this? Son of good family!
One does not discriminate within this samādhi.
"Why is this? Because the nature of samādhi is non-existent.
The Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
I declare that among those who dwell in the samādhi of non-contention, you are the foremost.
As I have taught, a bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.”
"If one trains in this manner, this is called training in the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva trains in this way, what dharma is he training in?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva trains in this way, he trains in no dharma at all.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
these dharmas are not as they are grasped by ordinary worldlings.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that they exist now?”
The Buddha said:
"As it is non-existent, so it exists.
Because all these phenomena are thus non-existent, they are called ignorance."

Ordinary persons, through the discrimination of ignorance and their craving attachment to ignorance, fall into the two extremes; they neither know nor see, and within phenomena that do not exist, they engage in recollective conceptualization and discrimination, craving and clinging to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Because of their greedy attachment, they neither know nor see that all phenomena are non-existent; they do not transcend them, do not believe in them, and do not abide in them. For this reason, they fall into the category of ordinary beings who are greedily attached.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva trains in this manner, they do not train in omniscience (sarvajñatā) either.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they do not train in omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Training in this way is called training in omniscience and accomplishing omniscience.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If someone were to ask:”
“Would a phantom person who trains in omniscience (sarvajñatā) actually achieve omniscience?
“World-Honored One!
How should I answer this?”
“Subhūti! I shall question you in return; answer as you please.
What do you think?”
“Is illusion different from form, or is form different from illusion? Is illusion different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
Subhūti replied, “Illusion is not different from form, and form is not different from illusion.”
Illusion is itself form, and form is itself illusion.
Illusion is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; consciousness is not different from illusion.
Illusion is itself consciousness, and consciousness is itself illusion.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Are the five aggregates of clinging called ‘bodhisattva’?”
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva training in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should train like an illusory person."
Why is this? One should know that the five aggregates are themselves an illusory person. Why is that so?

"It is said that form is like an illusion; it is said that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like illusions—consciousness being the six sense faculties and the five aggregates.
"World-Honored One, will bodhisattvas who have newly resolved not be startled, terrified, or fall back upon hearing this teaching?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved follows evil associates, they will become terrified, fall back, and sink into despondency.
However, if they follow virtuous associates and hear this teaching, they will have no fear, nor will they sink or fall back."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
what constitutes a bodhisattva’s bad friend?”
The Buddha said:
"They instruct them to distance themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*, causing them not to delight in bodhi.

Furthermore, they instruct them to study the discrimination of signs and the adornment of prose and verse; they instruct them to study the various sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and they provide them with the causes and conditions for performing the works of Māra."
"These are called the evil friends of a bodhisattva.
"World-Honored One,
who are the good friends of a bodhisattva?"
"If they are instructed to study the Prajñāpāramitā, one should explain the works of Māra and the faults and evils of Māra;
having caused them to recognize the works of Māra and the faults and evils of Māra, one should instruct them to remain far removed from them."
“Subhūti! These are called the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has set out with the mind of the Great Vehicle and is adorned with the great adornment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called a ‘bodhisattva,’ what is the meaning of ‘bodhisattva’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"To study all dharmas without obstruction and to know all dharmas as they truly are—this is the meaning of 'bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If one knows that all phenomena are called 'Bodhisattva,' by what further meaning are they called 'Mahāsattva'?
The Buddha said:
"One who shall act as the leader for the great assembly is the meaning of 'Mahāsattva.'"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, too, would like to explain the meaning of why one is called a mahāsattva.”
The Buddha said,
"Speak as you wish.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

A bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for the sake of severing the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a person, as well as views of existence and non-existence, views of annihilation and permanence, and so forth; this is what is meant by the term ‘Mahāsattva.’”
"Therefore, having no attachment within this mind is also called the meaning of 'Mahāsattva'.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason is there no attachment within this mind?"
Subhūti said: "Because there is no mind, within this state of mind there is nothing to which one is attached.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Because a bodhisattva has set out in great adornment and mounts the Great Vehicle, this is the meaning of ‘mahāsattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘a bodhisattva’s donning of the great armor,’ what is meant by ‘donning the great armor’?
The Buddha said:
“The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
‘I should deliver immeasurable, incalculable sentient beings.
Having delivered these sentient beings, there are no sentient beings who have been brought to parinirvāṇa.’”
Why is this? Because such is the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
It is, for example, like a skilled illusionist who, at a crossroads, conjures up a great multitude of people and then severs the heads of all those illusory beings.
"What do you think?
Would there be any injury or death [to them]? Subhūti said:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"The Bodhisattva is also like this; having delivered immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, there is not a single sentient being who has been brought to extinction."
“If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this matter, is neither startled nor terrified, you should know that this bodhisattva has set out in great armor.
Subhūti said, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should know that this bodhisattva has set out in great armor and has thus armored themselves.”
Why is this? All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is a dharma that is uncreated and unarisen, yet for the sake of sentient beings, one dons the great armor.
These sentient beings, too, are dharmas that are uncreated and unarisen.
"Why is this? Because form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated.
Pūrṇa said to Subhūti:
“Is it that form is neither bound nor liberated, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also neither bound nor liberated?
Subhūti replied, “Form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also neither bound nor liberated.”
Pūrṇa asked: "What is form that is neither bound nor liberated?
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are neither bound nor liberated?"
Subhūti said: “The form of an illusory person is neither bound nor liberated; the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness of an illusory person are neither bound nor liberated.”
Because there is nothing that exists, there is neither bondage nor liberation;
because of detachment, there is neither bondage nor liberation;
because there is no arising, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
"This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the great armor to adorn themselves.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
What is the Great Vehicle?
What is it for a bodhisattva to set out upon the Great Vehicle?
Where does this vehicle abide?
"From where does this vehicle emerge?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The Great Vehicle is without measure and without numerical division."
As for where this vehicle departs from and where it abides: this vehicle departs from the triple world and abides in *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
There is no departure from this vehicle by means of a vehicle.
"Why is this? Since both the phenomenon that emerges and the one who emerges are both non-existent, what phenomenon could possibly emerge?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That which is called the Mahāyāna, the Mahāyāna, surpasses all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
World-Honored One!”
The Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Just as space accommodates immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings,
so too does the Mahāyāna accommodate immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.
This Mahāyāna is like space: it has no place from which it comes, no place to which it goes, and no place where it abides;
the Mahāyāna is likewise: its prior limit cannot be apprehended, its middle limit cannot be apprehended, and its posterior limit cannot be apprehended.
"This vehicle is equal throughout the three periods of time; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“The Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should be as you have described it.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“The Buddha has sent Subhūti to speak of the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet he speaks of the Mahāyāna?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is what I have said not perhaps departing from the *prajñāpāramitā*? "No, Subhūti!
What you have said accords with the *prajñāpāramitā*."
“World-Honored One!
I do not apprehend a bodhisattva of the past, nor do I apprehend a bodhisattva of the future or the present.
Because form is limitless, the bodhisattva is also limitless;”
"World-Honored One, because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are boundless, the bodhisattva is also boundless. Since, in this way,
a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended in any place, at any time, or in any manner, what bodhisattva should one instruct in the perfection of wisdom?"
"I must see the Bodhisattva; what dharma should I teach him so that he may enter the Prajñāpāramitā?
World-Honored One!
That which is called 'Bodhisattva,' 'Bodhisattva,' is merely a name."
Just as it has been taught regarding the self— that the nature of the self is ultimately unarisen—
World-Honored One,
the nature of all phenomena is likewise so.
In this context, what is form that is unattached and unarisen?
What are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that are unattached and unarisen?
Form is unapprehendable as a bodhisattva; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable as a bodhisattva; even that which is unapprehendable is itself unapprehendable.
"Bhagavān!
Since a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended in any place, at any time, or in any manner, what dharma should one teach them to enter the prajñāpāramitā?"
"Bhagavān!
A bodhisattva exists as a mere name.
Just as I am ultimately unarisen, so too is the nature of all phenomena."
In this context, what is form that is unattached and unarisen?
What are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are unattached and unarisen?
The nature of all phenomena is thus; this nature is also unarisen, and even non-arising is itself unarisen.
"Bhagavān!
Should I now teach that non-arising dharmas enter into the prajñāpāramitā?
For what reason?"
Apart from dharmas that do not arise, one cannot find a bodhisattva practicing for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, is neither startled nor terrified, it should be known that this bodhisattva is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Bhagavān!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate in this way: 'All dharmas do not receive form. Why is that?"
The non-arising of form is itself not form; the non-ceasing of form is itself not form.
Without arising and without ceasing, there is neither duality nor distinction.
To speak of this as "form" is precisely the teaching of non-dual dharmas.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not grasp at feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Because consciousness that is unborn is not consciousness; consciousness that is unceasing is not consciousness.
"Without arising and without ceasing, without duality and without distinction.
If one speaks of consciousness, it is precisely this non-dual dharma.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"As I understand the meaning of what Subhūti has said, a bodhisattva is non-arising.
If a bodhisattva is non-arising, for what reason are there difficult practices, such as undergoing suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings?"
Subhūti said: “I do not wish to cause the bodhisattva to undergo difficult practices. Why is that?
If one conceives the notion that [bodhisattva practice] is difficult to perform and the notion that it is suffering, one will be unable to benefit immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings.

If, toward sentient beings, one conceives the notion that they are easy to deal with, the notion that they are sources of joy, the notion of them as parents, the notion of them as children, and the notion of them as "mine," then one will be able to benefit immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings.
Just as my Dharma cannot be apprehended in any place, at any time,
or in any manner, so too should a bodhisattva conceive such a thought regarding internal and external phenomena.
If a bodhisattva practices with such a mind, it is also called "difficult practice.
As Śāriputra has said:
"Bodhisattvas are non-arising."
"In this way, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva is truly without birth.
Śāriputra said:
"But is it that the Bodhisattva is unarisen, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is also unarisen?
Subhūti replied, "Omniscience is also unarisen."
Śāriputra asked:
"If omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is unarisen, are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) also unarisen?
Subhūti replied:
"Ordinary beings are also non-arisen.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If bodhisattvas are non-arisen, then the dharmas of a bodhisattva are also non-arisen;..."
All-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) is unborn, and the dharmas of all-knowledge are also unborn;
ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are unborn, and the dharmas of ordinary beings are also unborn.
Now, by means of the unborn attaining the unborn, a bodhisattva should attain all-knowledge.
Subhūti said: "I do not wish for non-arising dharmas to be apprehended. Why is this? Because..."
"Because the dharma of non-arising cannot be apprehended.
Śāriputra said: "The arising of arising is the non-arising of arising."
"Regarding what you have said—that which is 'eloquent speech' (prapañca)—is it born or is it unborn?
Subhūti replied, "All dharmas are unborn;
that which is spoken is unborn, and eloquent speech is also unborn—it is thus that one speaks with eloquence."
Śāriputra said: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
Among those who preach the Dharma, you are the foremost.
Why is this? Subhūti!
"Because they are able to answer whatever is asked. Subhūti said,
"The nature of dharmas must be thus."
The disciples of the Buddhas are able to answer whatever is asked regarding the dharma that is without dependence. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are without fixed nature.
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent!
By the power of which pāramitā is this?"
Subhūti said: "This is the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*, Śāriputra!"

If, when hearing such teachings and such discourses, a bodhisattva does not doubt, does not regret, and does not find them difficult, it should be known that this is the practice of that bodhisattva; this practice is never apart from this mindfulness.
Śāriputra said:

"If a bodhisattva does not depart from these practices and does not depart from these thoughts, and all sentient beings likewise do not depart from these practices and do not depart from these thoughts, then all sentient beings should also be bodhisattvas."
"Why is this? Because all sentient beings do not depart from this thought. Subhūti said:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
You wish to depart from me in order to establish my own meaning.”
Why is this? Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that mindfulness also lacks intrinsic nature;
because sentient beings are detached, mindfulness is also detached.
Because sentient beings cannot be apprehended, mindfulness also cannot be apprehended. Śāriputra,
I desire that bodhisattvas practice the perfection of wisdom by means of this mindfulness.
Chapter Two: Śakra-devānām-indra. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra was present in the assembly together with forty thousand devaputras;
the Four Great Kings were present in the assembly together with twenty thousand devaputras;
and Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, was present in the assembly together with ten thousand Brahmā devas.
Even the hosts of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, numbering in the thousands, were all present in the assembly.
However, because of the light of the Buddha’s body and his supernormal power, the karmic retribution lights of these celestial hosts no longer appeared at all.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"These countless hosts of devas have all assembled together, desiring to hear Subhūti explain the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā."
“How does a bodhisattva dwell in the perfection of wisdom?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the assembly of devas: “Kauśika!
I shall now, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, discourse on the Prajñāpāramitā.
If there are any sons of the gods who have not yet resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should now do so.
If a person has already entered the stage of certainty (samyaktva-niyāma), they are incapable of generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Why is this? Because they have already established an insurmountable barrier between themselves and saṃsāra.
If such a person should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall likewise rejoice in it and will never sever their merit. Why is this?
"A superior person should seek the supreme Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"You are able to thus exhort and gladden all bodhisattvas. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
I shall repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Just as the Buddhas of the past and their disciples taught, so too does the Tathāgata, dwelling within the dharma of emptiness, teach the various pāramitās.
The Tathāgata studied this Dharma and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
I shall now likewise protect and mindfully care for all bodhisattvas.
"By reason of my protective mindfulness, all bodhisattvas shall swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!"
Listen attentively: the bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of wisdom. Kausika!
The bodhisattva, having donned the great armor and mounted the Great Vehicle, dwells in the perfection of wisdom by means of the dharma of emptiness.
One should not dwell on form; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One should not dwell on form as permanent or impermanent; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as permanent or impermanent.
One should not dwell on form as suffering or pleasure; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as suffering or pleasure.
One should not dwell on form as pure or impure; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as pure or impure.
One should not dwell on form as self or non-self; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as self or non-self.
One should not dwell on form as empty or non-empty; one should not dwell on feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as empty or non-empty.

One should not dwell on the fruit of a stream-enterer; one should not dwell on the fruit of a once-returner; one should not dwell on the fruit of a non-returner; one should not dwell on the fruit of an arhat; one should not dwell on the path of a pratyekabuddha; and one should not dwell on the Buddha-dharma.

One should not dwell on the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry; one should not dwell on the stream-enterer as a field of merit; one should not dwell on the stream-enterer’s state of wandering through birth and death for up to seven more times.

One should not dwell on the unconditioned fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin; one should not dwell on the field of merit of a sakṛdāgāmin; nor should one dwell on the thought that a sakṛdāgāmin will return once more to this world to bring an end to suffering.

One should not dwell on the unconditioned fruit of an Anāgāmin; one should not dwell on the field of merit of an Anāgāmin; one should not dwell on the parinirvāṇa attained by an Anāgāmin in that realm.

One should not dwell on the unconditioned fruit of arhatship; one should not dwell on the field of merit that is the arhat; one should not dwell on the arhat entering nirvana without remainder in this very life.

One should not dwell in the unconditioned fruit of the Pratyekabuddha path; one should not dwell in the field of merit of a Pratyekabuddha; nor should one dwell in the parinirvāṇa of a Pratyekabuddha who, having transcended the stage of the Śrāvaka but not yet reached the stage of a Buddha, passes into extinction.
"One should not dwell on the thought: 'I shall benefit immeasurable sentient beings through the Buddha-dharma; I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"In what manner, then, should a bodhisattva dwell?"
Subhūti, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, said to him:
"What do you think?
In what place does the Tathāgata abide?"
Śāriputra said:
“The Tathāgata has no abiding; that mind which does not abide is called the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata does not abide in the nature of the conditioned, nor does he abide in the nature of the unconditioned.”
“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should also abide in this manner: just as the Tathāgata abides, he neither abides nor does not abide in any phenomena.”
At that time, there were among the assembly certain sons of gods who thought to themselves:
"The speech and phrases of the various yakṣas can still have their meanings understood, but what Subhūti speaks and discusses is difficult to comprehend."
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"In this there is no speaking, no showing, and no hearing.
The sons of the gods then had this thought:
“Subhūti wishes to make this meaning easy to understand, yet it becomes even more profound and subtle.
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
“If a practitioner wishes to realize the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or wishes to abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, they must not depart from this patience (kṣānti).”

Those who wish to realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, or the fruit of an Arhat; those who wish to realize the path of a Pratyekabuddha, or wish to realize the Buddha-dharma—they too do not depart from this patience.
At that time, the sons of the gods had this thought:
"What kind of person is able to listen in accordance with what Subhūti has said?
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the sons of the gods, spoke to them, saying:
"A phantom person can comply with and listen to what I say, yet there is neither listening nor realization.
The sons of the gods then thought:
"Is it that only the listener is like a phantom, or are sentient beings also like phantoms?"
"Is the fruit of the stream-enterer, up to and including the path of the pratyekabuddha, also like an illusion?
Subhūti, knowing what the devaputras were thinking, said to them:

"I have taught that sentient beings are like illusions and like dreams; the fruit of the stream-enterer is also like an illusion and like a dream; the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, the fruit of the arhat, and the path of the pratyekabuddha are also like illusions and like dreams."
The devaputras asked,
"Does Subhūti also say that the Buddha-dharma is like an illusion and like a dream?
Subhūti replied:
"I say that even the Buddha-dharma is like an illusion and like a dream; I say that even nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream.
The devaputras asked, "Venerable Subhūti, do you also say that nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream?"
Subhūti said: "O sons of the gods!
Even if there were a dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, I would likewise say it is like an illusion and like a dream."
"O sons of the gods!
Illusion and dreams, and nirvana, are non-dual and without distinction.
At that time, Śāriputra, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, and Mahākātyāyana asked Subhūti:
"When the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* is explained in this way, who is able to receive it?
At that time, Ānanda said:

"When the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* is explained in this way, those who are bodhisattvas of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), those who possess right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and Arhats whose vows are fulfilled—these are the ones who can receive it."
Subhūti said: "When the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* is explained in this way, there is no one who can receive it. Why is that?
"In this Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can be spoken, nor any dharma that can be shown.
For this reason, there is no one who can receive it.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:
"The Elder Subhūti is raining down the rain of Dharma.
I should rather manifest transformed flowers and scatter them over Subhūti.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately manifested transformed flowers and scattered them over Subhūti.
Subhūti had this thought:
"The flowers now scattered by Śakra Devānām Indra are such as I have never seen before in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
These flowers emerge from the wish-fulfilling tree; they do not grow from an ordinary tree."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing what was in Subhūti’s mind, said to Subhūti:
“These flowers are not born; nor are these flowers produced from a tree of the mind.”
Subhūti said to Śakra, the Devānām-indra:
"Kauśika! As for what you have said—that these flowers are not produced, and that the flowers likewise do not grow from a mind-tree—[it is so]."
"If it were not a produced phenomenon, it could not be called a flower.
Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:
"The Venerable Subhūti possesses profound wisdom; he explains the ultimate meaning without destroying conventional designations."
Having reflected thus, he said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is! Subhūti!"
As Subhūti has said, a bodhisattva should train in this way.
A bodhisattva who trains in this way does not train for the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha.
If one does not study this stage, it is called studying the Buddha-dharma and studying sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
If one studies the Buddha-dharma and studies sarvajñā, then one studies immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.

If one studies the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, one does not study for the sake of increasing or decreasing form; one does not study for the sake of increasing or decreasing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness;
nor does one study for the sake of grasping form, nor for the sake of grasping feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
"This person trains because there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be extinguished regarding the Dharma.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"The practitioner does not train for the sake of grasping omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), nor does he train for the sake of extinguishing omniscience."
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!”
The bodhisattva trains in everything up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) because it is neither grasped nor extinguished.
When observing in this way, one is able to train in omniscience and is able to accomplish omniscience.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:
"Where should one seek the Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Śāriputra replied:
“The *prajñāpāramitā* should be sought within the turning [of the wheel] by Subhūti.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, said to Subhūti:
“By whose spiritual power is this?”
Subhūti said: "This is the Buddha’s spiritual power, Kauśika!"
Regarding your question as to where one should seek the *prajñāpāramitā*:
one should not seek the *prajñāpāramitā* within form (*rūpa*), nor within feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*);
yet one should not seek it apart from form, nor apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? Form is not the perfection of wisdom, and apart from form there is no perfection of wisdom;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the perfection of wisdom, and apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness there is no perfection of wisdom.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“The Great Perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā; the Immeasurable Perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā; the Boundless Perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā.”
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is, Kauśika!”
The Great Perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā; the immeasurable perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā; the boundless perfection is this Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! Because form is immeasurable, the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable, the Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable.
Because conditions are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless;
because sentient beings are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless. Kausika!
Why is it that because conditions are boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless?
All dharmas have no beginning, no middle, and no end; therefore, because conditions are boundless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is boundless.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

All dharmas are boundless; their prior limit cannot be apprehended, nor can their middle limit or subsequent limit be apprehended. Therefore, because conditions are boundless, the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Venerable Subhūti!
In what way are sentient beings infinite and the prajñāpāramitā infinite?"
“Kauśika! Sentient beings are immeasurable; they cannot be grasped by calculation.
Therefore, sentient beings are boundless, and the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless.”
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Venerable Subhūti, in what sense do you speak of 'sentient beings'?"
Subhūti said: “The meaning of ‘sentient beings’ is itself the meaning of ‘dharmas.
What do you think?”
"What is the meaning of 'sentient beings,' when you speak of sentient beings?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "Sentient beings do not have the nature of dharmas, nor do they have the nature of non-dharmas; they exist only as provisional designations."
"These names have no fundamental basis and no cause; they are established by force, and thus we speak of 'sentient beings.
Subhūti said: "What do you think?"
"In this regard, is there any truly existent sentient being that can be described or pointed out?
"No, indeed! Subhūti said:
“Kauśika! If sentient beings are ineffable and cannot be pointed out, how can you say:
‘Sentient beings are boundless, and the Prajñāpāramitā is boundless’?”
"Kauśika! Suppose the Tathāgata were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and say:
'Sentient beings, sentient beings. "
"Is there, in reality, any sentient being who undergoes birth and death?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied, "No!"
Why is this? Because sentient beings have been eternally pure from the very beginning. "Kauśika!
"Therefore, you should know that sentient beings are limitless, and the Prajñāpāramitā is limitless.
*The Minor Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll One;
*The Minor Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Stūpas (The "Treasure Stūpa" Chapter according to the Danben).

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-deva-rāja, Maheśvara-deva-rāja, the Lord of Sentient Beings, and the various celestial maidens were all filled with great joy and simultaneously proclaimed three times:
"How wonderful, how wonderful!
Because the Buddha has appeared in the world, Subhūti is now able to expound this Dharma.
At that time, the great assembly of devas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva is able not to depart from the practice of the prajñāpāramitā, one should regard such a person as a Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the devaputras:
"So it is, so it is! In the past, when I was in the city of Puṣpā, in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I did not depart from the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā.

At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara prophesied for me: 'In a future age, after incalculable kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.'"
The devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is able to encompass all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).”
The Buddha, on account of Śakra Devānām Indra, addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, as well as the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—saying: "Kauśika!

If there are good sons or good daughters who can receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā and practice according to what is taught, then Māras, or the gods of Māra, humans, or non-humans shall find no opportunity to harm them, and they shall never die an untimely death.
Because good sons and good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite the *Prajñāpāramitā*,

the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who have resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* but have not yet received, upheld, read, or recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* come to where they are.
Furthermore, Kauśika,

when a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, whether they are in an empty house, on a road, or have lost their way, they shall have no fear.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If good sons and good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, and practice according to what is taught, we shall all provide them with protection and mindfulness."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If good sons or good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, and practice according to what is taught therein, I shall protect and mindfully attend to them.”
The Brahma King and all the Brahma devas addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If good sons or good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, and practice according to what is taught, we shall likewise protect and keep them in mind.”
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
That good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā obtain such present-life merits as these.”
“World-Honored One!
If one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, then one upholds all the pāramitās.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Kauśika!
One who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā thereby upholds all the pāramitās."
Furthermore, Kauśika!
Listen well now, for I shall explain to you the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said to Kauśika:

"If there should be anyone who wishes to destroy, disturb, or oppose this Dharma of mine, though they harbor such an intention, it will gradually perish of its own accord and shall never be fulfilled."
Why is this? Kausika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, then whatever various acts of destruction, confusion, or opposition may arise, they shall by the nature of the Dharma all be extinguished; therefore, such a person will ultimately not fail to fulfill their aspirations.
Kauśika! Sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā shall obtain such merits in this present life.

It is like a medicine named Mahi; suppose there is a hungry snake wandering in search of food that sees a small insect and wishes to eat it, but when the insect rushes toward the place where the medicine is, the snake, smelling the scent of the medicine, immediately turns back and departs.
Why is this? Because the power of the medicine is able to neutralize the snake's venom. Kausika!

Good sons and good daughters are also like this: if they receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, and various kinds of destructive, disruptive, or contrary events arise, by the power of the Prajñāpāramitā, these will immediately be extinguished of themselves.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If one upholds, recites, and studies the Prajñāpāramitā, the four world-protecting Heavenly Kings shall all provide protection and mindfulness.
Furthermore, Kauśika!"

Such a person never speaks words that are unbeneficial; whatever they say is trusted and accepted by others. They have little anger and never harbor resentment. They are not shrouded by pride nor driven by ill will.
Good sons and good daughters, when they are overcome by anger, should be able to form this thought:
"If I become angry, my faculties will be impaired and my complexion will change."
"I desire to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; how could I follow a mind of anger?
Thinking thus, he immediately attained right mindfulness.
Kauśika! Good sons and good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā shall likewise obtain these merits in the present life.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
For the sake of dedication, the Prajñāpāramitā does not give rise to arrogance.”
The Buddha told Kauśika:

"If a son or daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, should they enter an army formation, whether they are reciting the Prajñāpāramitā while stationed there or departing from it, there is no possibility that they will lose their life or be harmed;
even if blades and arrows are directed at them, they shall ultimately be unable to cause injury."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is a great mantra, an unsurpassed mantra.

Sons and daughters of good family who study this mantra will not conceive evil thoughts toward themselves, will not conceive evil thoughts toward others, and will not conceive evil thoughts toward both; they will harbor no malice.
By studying these incantations, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, acquires the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), and is able to observe the minds of all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Wherever a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra resides, or wherever it is read and recited, neither humans nor non-humans shall find an opportunity to cause harm;
this applies except for those who must experience the results of their own karmic actions."
Kauśika! It is like the precincts of a bodhimaṇḍa: whether humans or animals, none are able to cause them distress. Why is this?
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present attain the Way within this; they have attained it, are now attaining it, and will attain it.
In this place, all sentient beings are without fear or dread, and none can cause them harm or affliction.
"Kauśika! Because of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), this place is auspicious; it is where people offer respect, offerings, and prostrations.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write out the Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold its scrolls, and make offerings to it with reverence, respect, honor, and praise—using fine flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, burning incense, powdered incense, blended incense, silk canopies, banners, and pennants—to make such offerings to it.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who makes offerings to, reveres, honors, and praises the relics of the Tathāgata, using excellent flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, burning incense, powdered incense, blended incenses, silk canopies, banners, and streamers as their offerings.
"In what way is that merit great?
"Kauśika! I shall question you in return; answer as you see fit."
What do you think?
By practicing which path did the Tathāgata attain the body that is the basis for *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and thereby realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment)?
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is because the Tathāgata has studied the Prajñāpāramitā that he has attained this body and realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Kauśika! It is not because of the body that a Buddha is called a Tathāgata;
it is because he has attained sarvajñā (all-knowledge) that he is called a Tathāgata.”
Kauśika! The *sarvajñā* of all Buddhas arises from the *prajñāpāramitā*, because this body is that upon which the wisdom of *sarvajñā* relies.

It is by means of this body that the Tathāgata attains the wisdom of *sarvajñā* and achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; because this body is the support for *sarvajñā*, my *śarīra* (relics) receive offerings after my parinirvāṇa.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes down the Prajñāpāramitā, receives, upholds, reads, and recites it, and makes offerings to it with reverence, respect, honor, and praise—using fine flowers, incense, garlands, ointments, burning incense, powdered incense, blended incenses, silk canopies, banners, and streamers—then that son or daughter of good family is, in fact, making an offering to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Therefore, if a person writes out the Prajñāpāramitā, makes offerings to it, honors it, respects it, and praises it, one should know that this person attains great merit.
"Why is this? Because it is an offering to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do the people of Jambudvīpa not know that such great benefits can be obtained, that they do not offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said,
"Kauśika, what do you think?"
"How many people in Jambudvīpa have attained indestructible faith in the Buddha?
How many people have attained indestructible faith in the Dharma and in the Saṅgha?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Few are those who have attained indestructible faith in the Buddha, and few are those who have attained indestructible faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
World-Honored One!
In Jambudvīpa, there are very few people who attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.”
"Those who attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha become even fewer;
those who are able to practice the path of a Bodhisattva likewise become even fewer. "So it is, so it is!"

Kauśika! In Jambudvīpa, there are few people who have attained indestructible faith in the Buddha; even fewer are those who are able to resolve their minds on anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practice the bodhisattva path.

Kauśika! Among the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, perhaps only one or two abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Therefore, you should know that good sons and good daughters who resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who are even able to receive, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because these people think:
"The Buddhas of the past, when they were practicing the bodhisattva path, learned from this; we, too, should learn from this."
"The Prajñāpāramitā is my great teacher.
"Kauśika! Whether I am present in the world or have passed into parinirvāṇa, a bodhisattva should always rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā."
If good sons or good daughters, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgata, erect stupas made of the seven treasures;
and throughout their entire lives, they make offerings to these stupas with excellent flowers, incense, unguents, powdered incense, robes, banners, and streamers.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would that son of good family or daughter of good family obtain much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

If a son or daughter of good family makes offerings to a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, honoring, respecting, and praising it with fine flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, and streamers, their merit will be exceedingly great.

“Kauśika! Setting aside this single stūpa, suppose there were stūpas made of the seven treasures filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa; and suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for as long as their life lasts, were to make offerings to these stūpas with excellent flowers, incense, and even music.
"What do you think?
By reason of this cause and condition, would that person obtain much merit?
Śakra Devānām-indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Kauśika:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family makes offerings to a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, honoring, respecting, and praising it with fine flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, and streamers, their merit will be exceedingly great.”

“Kauśika! Setting aside these stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill Jambudvīpa, or those stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill the four continents—if someone were to offer flowers, incense, and even music as an offering throughout their entire life;”
Furthermore, Kausika, if there were someone who made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, their merit would be far greater.

Setting aside these stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill the four continents under heaven, or even those stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill a Cūḍika small thousand-world system— if someone were to spend their entire life making offerings of exquisite flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers, [the merit of the former would still be surpassed].
Furthermore, Kausika, if there were someone who made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, their merit would be far greater.

Setting aside these stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill a Cūḷikā-sāhasra-lokadhātu, suppose there were stūpas made of the seven treasures filling a Dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu; if a person were to offer flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers to them for as long as they live, [their merit would still be surpassed by that of one who honors the Prajñāpāramitā].
Furthermore, Kausika, if there were someone who made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, their merit would be exceedingly great.

Setting aside this system of two thousand middle-worlds, suppose there were stūpas made of the seven precious jewels filling a trichiliocosm; and suppose a son or daughter of good family, for as long as their life lasts, were to make offerings of flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers to them.
Kauśika! What do you think?
By reason of these causes and conditions, would that person obtain much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
“Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Kauśika:

"If there should be another person who makes offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scroll, honoring, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers, their merit will be exceedingly great."

“Kauśika! Setting aside these stūpas made of the seven treasures that fill a trichiliocosm, suppose all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were simultaneously to obtain human bodies, and each individual were to erect a stūpa made of the seven treasures and, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to those stūpas with every kind of exquisite flower, famous incense, banners, pennants, music, song, and dance.”
Kauśika! What do you think?
By reason of these causes and conditions, would that person acquire much merit?
“Very much, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Kauśika:

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family makes offerings to a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, honoring, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers, their merit will be very great.”
Śakra Devānām Indra said: “So it is, so it is!
World-Honored One!”
If a person makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are making offerings to and honoring the omniscience (sarvajñatā) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
“World-Honored One!

Setting aside this trichiliocosm, suppose every single sentient being were to erect a stupa made of the seven treasures; and suppose all the sentient beings filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions were to attain human bodies, and each one were to erect a stupa made of the seven treasures, and for an entire kalpa—or even slightly less than a kalpa—were to make offerings to these stupas with fine flowers, incense, and even music.”

Furthermore, if there is a person who makes offerings to a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, honoring, respecting, and praising it with flowers, incense, and even music, their merit will be exceedingly great.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Kausika!"
Because these sons and daughters of good family have made this offering of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra scroll, their merit is exceedingly great—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable.
Why is this? Kausika!
The sarvajñā-jñāna (all-knowing wisdom) of all Buddhas is born from the prajñāpāramitā.

Kauśika! For this reason, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family makes offerings to a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra—honoring, respecting, and praising it with offerings of flowers, incense, and even music—the former merit cannot equal even one hundredth part of this; it cannot equal one thousandth, ten-thousandth, or even one hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

Chapter 4: The Chapter on Mantras. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Four: The Chapter on Mantras. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, together with forty thousand devaputras who were present in the assembly, said to Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!...”
"You should uphold, recite, and chant the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!"
When you uphold, maintain, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, if the asuras should give rise to the thought,
"I wish to fight with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," at that time you should recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā.
"For this reason, the evil mind of the asuras was immediately extinguished.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is the great vidyā-mantra; the Prajñāpāramitā is the unsurpassed mantra; the Prajñāpāramitā is the unequaled mantra.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Kauśika!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is the great mantra of illumination; the Prajñāpāramitā is the unsurpassed mantra; the Prajñāpāramitā is the mantra unequaled by any other.
For what reason? Kausika!
The Buddhas of the past attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of this vidyā-mantra.
The Buddhas of the future shall also, by means of this mantra, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions likewise, by means of this mantra, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Kauśika! It is because of this vidyā-mantra that the ten paths of wholesome action appear in the world; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers appear in the world.”

Because of the Bodhisattvas, the ten paths of wholesome action appear in the world; the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers appear in the world.

If the Buddhas did not appear in the world, it would be solely because of the Bodhisattvas that the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers would appear in the world.
For example, Kausika, when the moon does not appear, the light of the stars illuminates the world. In the same way,
when there is no Buddha in the world, all virtuous conduct and right practice arise from the Bodhisattva.
The skillful means of bodhisattvas all arise from the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika,

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family makes offerings to a copy of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, honoring, respecting, and praising it, they will obtain these merits in the present life.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of merit and blessings are obtained in the present life?”
“Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family cannot be harmed by poison, cannot be burned by fire, and shall never meet with an untimely death.”

Furthermore, if a son or daughter of good family should encounter legal proceedings, by reciting and keeping the Prajñāpāramitā in mind, those legal matters will immediately be extinguished, and those who seek to find fault with them shall gain no advantage.
Why is this? Because they are protected by the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Good sons and good daughters who recite and keep the Prajñāpāramitā in mind, whether they go before a king, a prince, or a high minister, shall all be received with joy and greeted; they will converse with them.
Why is this? Kauśika!
The Prajñāpāramitā emerges for the sake of compassion for all sentient beings.
"Therefore, Kauśika!
Those who seek faults shall find no opportunity.
At that time, one hundred renunciants of non-Buddhist sects, wishing to find fault with the Buddha, approached the place where the Buddha was.
Śakra Devānām-indra had this thought:
"These one hundred non-Buddhist renunciants have come to where the Buddha is, wishing to find fault with him.
I shall now recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā that I received from the Buddha."
"These non-Buddhists have come to where the Buddha is; they might be able to interrupt the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Having thought thus, he immediately recited and contemplated the *prajñāpāramitā* that he had received from the Buddha.
At that time, the various non-Buddhists circumambulated the Buddha from afar and departed by way of their original path.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"For what reason and by what cause have these non-Buddhists circumambulated the Buddha and departed?"
The Buddha, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, addressed him:
“This Śakra Devānām Indra is reciting and contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā.

Among these non-Buddhists, not a single one possesses a virtuous mind; they have all come with malicious intent to seek out the Buddha’s faults. For this reason, the non-Buddhists have each returned by way of their respective paths.”
At that time, Māra the Evil One thought to himself:

"Now these four assemblies, as well as the devaputras of the desire and form realms, are seated before the Buddha; among them there must be bodhisattvas who have received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and I shall corrupt and disturb them."
He immediately manifested the fourfold army and proceeded toward the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"Māra has arrayed his fourfold army and come to the place where the Buddha is."
These four types of military formations were not possessed by King Bimbisāra of Magadha, nor by King Prasenajit of Kośala, nor by the Śākyas, nor by the Licchavis.
"This present military conflict must surely be the work of an evil Māra.
This Māra has long sought to find fault with the Buddha and to harass and disturb sentient beings; I shall now recite and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā."
Śakra Devānām Indra then silently recited the Prajñāpāramitā; as he recited it, the evil Māra gradually retraced his path and departed.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven manifested celestial flowers, which they scattered from mid-air over the Buddha, thinking:
"May the Prajñāpāramitā long abide in Jambudvīpa, so that the people of Jambudvīpa may study and recite it."
At that time, the devas again scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who practice the prajñāpāramitā and cultivate the prajñāpāramitā, Māra or the devas of Māra shall find no opportunity against them.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are people who hear this Prajñāpāramitā, they must have already drawn near to various Buddhas in the past; they have not come from meager merit.”
How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, training as it has been taught and practicing as it has been taught. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
“O Bhagavat, the sarvajñā of all bodhisattvas should be sought within the prajñāpāramitā.
Bhagavat, it is just as,
for example, great treasures should be sought within the great ocean.”
“World-Honored One!
The great treasure of the *sarvajñā* of all Buddhas should be sought within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Kauśika! All the sarvajñā of the Buddhas are born from within the prajñāpāramitā."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Why is it that the World-Honored One does not praise the name of the *dānapāramitā*, nor praise the names of the *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, or *dhyānapāramitā*, but praises only the name of the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom guides the five perfections.”
"What do you think?
If one practices giving without dedicating it toward omniscience (sarvajñatā), does it constitute the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā)?
Ānanda replied:
"No, World-Honored One! If one practices morality,
patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, but does not dedicate them toward sarvajñā (all-knowledge), do they constitute the perfection of prajñā?"
Ānanda said: “No, World-Honored One!”
“Ānanda! For this reason, the perfection of wisdom is the guide for the five perfections. Ānanda!”
For example, when seeds are sown within the great earth, they grow through the convergence of causes and conditions; yet they will never grow if they do not rely upon this earth. Ānanda!
In this way, these five pāramitās abide within the prajñāpāramitā and attain growth; because they are protected by the prajñāpāramitā, they proceed toward sarvajñatā.
"Therefore, Ānanda,
the perfection of wisdom acts as the guide for the five perfections.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If these good sons and good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, and practice according to what is taught, the merit they obtain is such that even the Tathāgata could not fully describe it.”
The Buddha told Kauśika:
"I have not merely spoken of the merit of this person who upholds, recites, and studies the Prajñāpāramitā, and who practices according to what is taught."

Kauśika! If there are good sons or good daughters who make offerings to a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, honoring, respecting, and praising it with fine flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers—I shall also describe the merit they obtain.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I, too, shall protect and keep in mind those sons and daughters of good family who make offerings to this scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, honoring, respecting, praising, and extolling it with fine flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers.”
The Buddha said:
"Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā."
Hundreds of thousands of assemblies of devas came to his location in order to hear the Dharma.
When this Dharma master preached the Dharma for the devas, non-human beings augmented his physical strength and vigor.
If the Dharma-preacher becomes exhausted and no longer delights in preaching the Dharma, because the devas revere the Dharma, they will cause him to delight in preaching it.
Kauśika! This is also a present-life merit obtained by these good men and good women.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
when these sons and daughters of good family teach the Prajñāpāramitā among the fourfold assembly, their minds will not fear anyone who comes to challenge, question, or reprimand them."

Why is this? Because these people are protected and sustained by the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not perceive anyone who can find fault with the Prajñāpāramitā, nor is there any fault to be found in the Prajñāpāramitā itself.
Because such a person is thus protected and sustained by the Prajñāpāramitā, they have no fear of anyone coming to challenge, question, or reproach them. Kauśika!
This, too, is a merit of the good man or good woman in the present life.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Because these sons and daughters of good family read and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, they are loved by their parents; they are respected by their kinsmen, friends, śramaṇas, and brahmins; and they are able to resolve, in accordance with the Dharma, any decline, affliction, strife, or litigation."
Kauśika! This, too, is the merit of good men and good women in the present life.
Furthermore, Kauśika!

In whatever place this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra resides, the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings who have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi will all come to that place where the Prajñāpāramitā is located; there they shall receive, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and pay homage to it before departing.

The devas from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi all come to where the Prajñāpāramitā is, receive, uphold, read, and recite it; they make offerings, pay homage, and then depart.

The gods of the Brahmā realm—the Brahmapārisadya, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahmā, the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, the Ābhāsvara, the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Anabhraka, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, the Avṛha, the Atapa, the Sudṛśa, the Sudarśana, and the Akaniṣṭha—heavenly beings who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all come to where the Prajñāpāramitā is, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, make offerings, and pay homage before departing.
Kauśika, do not think that only the minor devas have come for the sake of making offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

All the devas of the desire realm and the form realm within the trichiliocosm who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* have all come to where the *prajñāpāramitā* is, to receive, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and pay homage to it, before departing.
Good sons and good daughters should form this thought:

"In the immeasurable, incalculable lands of the ten directions, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who come to where the Prajñāpāramitā is located to receive, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and pay homage to it—at that time, I shall give the gift of the Dharma through the Prajñāpāramitā."

"Good sons and good daughters, wherever a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra resides—whether in a hall or a chamber—nothing can destroy it, except for the effects of past karma that must necessarily be experienced."
“Kauśika! This is also the merit of good men and good women in the present life.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How do these good sons and good daughters know that the devas have come to receive, uphold, read, recite, make offerings to, and pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family sees a great radiance, they should know for certain that devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others have come to their place.”
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family perceives an extraordinary fragrance, they should know for certain that the devas have arrived at their location."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Wherever a son or daughter of good family dwells, they should ensure that place is clean and pure.
Because it is clean and pure, non-human beings will all rejoice greatly and come to that place."
The minor spirits who previously resided therein were unable to endure the majestic power and virtue of the mighty devas, and thus all fled;
as the mighty devas came repeatedly, the hearts of those [spirits] gradually turned toward delighting in the Great Dharma.
