Therefore, in the place where they dwell, one should not allow any foul odors, filth, or impurities to exist on the four sides.
"Furthermore, Kauśika, these sons and daughters of good family will experience no physical exhaustion; their rising and reclining will be peaceful and secure, and they shall see no evil dreams."

If, during their dreams, they see only the Buddhas, the stupas and temples of the Buddhas, the assembly of Arhats, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, practicing the six pāramitās, training in sarvajñā (all-knowledge), and purifying Buddha-fields.

Furthermore, one hears the names of Buddhas: "In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, the Buddha [Name] is surrounded by several hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of followers, who respectfully attend him as he preaches the Dharma."
Kauśika! When good men and good women see such things in their dreams, upon waking they are peaceful and happy, their vigor is fully restored, and their bodies are light and agile.
These good sons and good daughters do not crave food and drink.
They are like a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna who, having arisen from samādhi, does not crave food and drink because he has trained in meditation.
Why is this? Kauśika!
It is because non-human beings augment their physical strength and vigor.
Good sons and good daughters who wish to attain such worldly merits as these should receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, and practice according to what is taught therein.

Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is unable to receive, uphold, read, and recite the *prajñāpāramitā* and practice according to what is taught, they should write out the scriptural volume and provide it with offerings, reverence, respect, and praise, using fine flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, blended incenses, robes, banners, streamers, and musical instruments.
5. The Chapter on Relics (Śarīra-varga). The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Five: The Chapter on Relics. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śakra-devānām-indra, saying: “Kauśika!
Suppose there were one portion consisting of the relics filling the entire Jambudvīpa, and another portion consisting of a single scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Between these two portions, which would you take?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I shall take up the Prajñāpāramitā.”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
It is not that I lack reverence for the śarīra; rather, it is because the śarīra is born from the *prajñāpāramitā* and is permeated by the *prajñāpāramitā* that it receives such offerings.
World-Honored One!
In the Sudharmā Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, I have a seat there because the various sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven come to make offerings to me.
If I am not on my seat, the sons of the gods pay homage with reverence to my place, circumambulate it, and depart, thinking:
"Śakra Devānām-indra sat here and preached the Dharma for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven."
"The relics of all Buddhas are likewise: born from the *prajñāpāramitā* and being that upon which *sarvajñā* relies, they receive offerings.
For this reason, World-Honored One!"
"Of these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!

Setting aside the śarīra that fills Jambudvīpa, suppose there were one portion consisting of the śarīra filling a trichiliocosm, and another portion consisting of the scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra."
Of these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā. Why?
Because the śarīras of all Buddhas arise from the Prajñāpāramitā; it is for this reason that they receive offerings.
“World-Honored One!
It is like a debtor who constantly fears his creditor; yet because he has gained the opportunity to draw near to and serve a king, the creditor instead comes to revere and fear him.”
For what reason?
Because they rely upon and take refuge in the king, whose power is great.
World-Honored One!
The śarīra relics are also like this; because they rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā, they receive offerings.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is like a king, and the śarīra relics are like those who attend upon the king.
The relics of the Tathāgata receive offerings because they rely upon all-encompassing wisdom.
World-Honored One,
since the all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas also arises from the Prajñāpāramitā, I choose the Prajñāpāramitā over the other two portions.
“World-Honored One!
It is like a priceless jewel that possesses such meritorious qualities:
wherever it dwells, non-human beings cannot find an opportunity to cause harm.”
Whether it be a man or a woman, whether old or young, if they are possessed by non-human spirits, the presence of this precious jewel at their location will cause those non-humans to depart.
If there is a feverish illness, the jewel can eliminate it.
If one has a wind disorder, by placing the bead upon the body, the affliction of wind is immediately eliminated.
If one has a cold disorder, by placing the bead upon the body, the affliction of cold is likewise eliminated.
Wherever this jewel resides, it can provide illumination during the night, coolness when it is hot, and warmth when it is cold.
Wherever the jewel dwells, the venom of snakes cannot enter.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whether old or young, if they are stung by a venomous insect, by showing them this bead, the poison will be immediately eliminated.
If there are various ailments of the eyes, by placing the bead upon the eyes, the eye ailment will be immediately cured.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if this precious jewel is placed in water, it takes on the same color as the water;
if it is wrapped in white silk and placed in water, the color of the water immediately becomes white.

If one wraps various colored silks—blue, yellow, purple, red, and so forth—and places them in water, the water immediately takes on each of those colors, and if the water was turbid, it becomes clear.
"This jewel accomplishes such meritorious qualities.
At that time, Ānanda asked Śakra-devānām-indra,
"Is this a treasure of Jambudvīpa?"
"Is this a treasure from the heavens?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"This is a treasure from the heavens."
The people of Jambudvīpa also possess such jewels, but they have little merit and are heavy.
The precious pearls of the heavens have great merit and are light.
When human jewels are compared to celestial jewels, they cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
“World-Honored One!
If this jewel is within a casket, even though the jewel has been taken away, because of the merit of the jewel, that casket remains precious.
World-Honored One!”
By virtue of the merit of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*), the relics (*śarīra*) receive offerings after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;
for these relics of the Tathāgata are the locus where that wisdom of omniscience resides.
Between these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
World-Honored One!

Setting aside these śarīras that fill a trichiliocosm, suppose there were one portion consisting of the śarīras filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and another portion consisting of the written scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Between these two, I would still choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
Between these two portions, I would choose the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why? Because the *sarvajñatā*-wisdom of all the Tathāgatas arises from the Prajñāpāramitā; it is because they are permeated by *sarvajñatā* that the śarīras receive offerings.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If good sons or good daughters wish to see, as it truly is, the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya Buddhas of the ten directions, they should practice the Prajñāpāramitā; they should cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is! Kausika!”
All Buddhas of the past attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
all Buddhas of the future will also attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and all Buddhas currently residing in the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds of the ten directions likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Great Pāramitā is the Prajñāpāramitā; it is by means of this Prajñāpāramitā that the Buddha knows the minds and the mental activities of all sentient beings.”
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika, it is because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have practiced the perfection of wisdom for a long night.”
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva practice only the prajñāpāramitā and not the other pāramitās?”
The Buddha said:
"Kauśika! All bodhisattvas practice the six pāramitās."
When practicing generosity, the perfection of wisdom is the foremost;
when observing ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or contemplating all phenomena, the perfection of wisdom is the foremost.

For example, in Jambudvīpa there are various kinds of trees with various shapes, various colors, various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits; yet their shadows are all one and the same, without any distinction.
"The five perfections are also like this; when they enter into the perfection of wisdom, there is no distinction between them.
"World-Honored One!
This perfection of wisdom possesses great merit; it possesses immeasurable and boundless merit; it possesses merit that is equal to the unequaled."
Bhagavān!
If there is someone who copies a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and makes offerings to it with reverence, respect, honor, and praise, using fine flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers;
or if there is another person who copies a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to others.
"Between these two merits, which is greater?
The Buddha said, "Kauśika!"
I shall question you further; answer me as you see fit.
What do you think?
Suppose there were someone who obtained the relics of a Buddha and made offerings to them alone.
If there is another person who obtains the Buddha’s relics and makes offerings to them themselves,
and also causes others to make offerings to them— of these two merits, which is greater?
Śakra Devānām-indra said:
“World-Honored One!
If a person obtains the relics of the Buddha and makes offerings to them themselves, and also causes others to make offerings to them, their merit is exceedingly great.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Kausika!"

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to copy a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and provide it with offerings, respect, honor, and praise—using fine flowers, incense, and even banners and streamers—it would not be as meritorious as if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to copy a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, personally making offerings to it, and also giving it to others so that they may make offerings to it; the latter’s merit is far greater.
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, wherever they may be, explains the Prajñāpāramitā to others, their merit will be exceedingly great.”
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll II;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll III.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Six: On Assisting.
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: “Kauśika!
If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the people of Jambudvīpa to practice the ten paths of wholesome action,
what do you think?
Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, obtain much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
“Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to give a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to another person so that they may write it out, read it, and recite it; the merit of the latter is far greater.”

“Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa, suppose there were someone who taught the sentient beings of the four continents, causing them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.”

Setting aside these four continents, or the Cāturmahādvīpaka small thousandfold world-system, or the dvisāhasra medium thousandfold world-system, or the trisāhasramahāsāhasra great thousandfold world-system of sentient beings—let alone teaching the sentient beings of worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person obtain much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

It is not as meritorious as when a son or daughter of good family provides a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to another person, enabling them to copy, read, and recite it; the latter's merit is far greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, causing them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers."
“By these causes and conditions, would that person obtain much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
“Very much, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to give a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to another person so that they may transcribe, read, and recite it; their merit is far greater.”

“Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa and even those of the trichiliocosm, let alone teaching the sentient beings of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, and causing them to practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person gain much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

It is not as meritorious as when a son or daughter of good family provides a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to another person, enabling them to copy, read, and recite it; the latter's merit is far greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who give a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to others so that they may transcribe, read, and recite it;
this does not equal the merit of a son or daughter of good family who reads and recites it for others themselves—the latter's merit is far greater."
Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family recites the Prajñāpāramitā for themselves or others, it is not as meritorious as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family explains its meaning for themselves or others; the latter's merit is far greater.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what kind of persons should the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā be explained?”
The Buddha said,
“Kauśika! If there are sons or daughters of good family who, because they do not understand the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, should have its meaning explained to them.”
Why is this? Kausika!
In future ages, there will be a semblance of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Good sons and good daughters who, within this context, desire to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, will fall into error upon hearing this counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"World-Honored One,
what is this counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?"
“Kauśika! In future ages there will be bhikṣus who, wishing to expound the Prajñāpāramitā, will instead expound a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā.”
“World-Honored One!
How do the bhikṣus preach a counterfeit prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
The bhikṣus said: "Form is impermanent;
if one seeks it in this way, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; if one seeks them in this way, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
"Kauśika! This is called the teaching of a counterfeit Prajñāpāramitā. Kauśika!"
Because one does not destroy form, one contemplates the impermanence of form;
because one does not destroy feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, one contemplates the impermanence of consciousness.
One who does not practice contemplation in this manner is said to be practicing a semblance of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika! For these reasons, the merit of a bodhisattva who explains the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly great.
Furthermore, Kauśika!
If there were a son or daughter of good family who taught the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, causing them to attain the fruit of a srotāpanna—
what do you think?
Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
“Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Kauśika! It is not as good as a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, gives it to another person so that they may copy, read, and recite it, saying:
‘You shall obtain these merits corresponding to the Prajñāpāramitā.’”
The merit thereof is exceedingly great. Why is this?
Because the fruit of srotāpanna arises from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

“Kauśika! Setting aside this Jambudvīpa, and even this trichiliocosm, let alone teaching the sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and causing them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna.”
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person’s merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
It is not as good as if a son or daughter of good family were to take a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and give it to another person so that they may copy, read, and recite it, saying:
"You shall obtain these merits corresponding to the Prajñāpāramitā."
The merit thereof is exceedingly great. Why is this?
Because the fruit of srotāpanna emerges from the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, causing them to attain the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an Anāgāmin, the fruit of an Arhat, or the path of a Pratyekabuddha."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person’s merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
It is not as good as a son or daughter of good family who, with a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, gives it to another person so that they may copy, read, and recite it, saying:
"You shall obtain these merits corresponding to the Prajñāpāramitā."
The merit thereof is exceedingly great. Why is this?
By following and studying this Dharma, you shall attain the dharma of sarvajñā (omniscience).

In accordance with the attainment of the dharma of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), one shall accordingly attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha.

“Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa and even those of the trichiliocosm, let alone teaching the sentient beings of as many worlds in the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, and causing them to attain the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of Anāgāmin, the fruit of Arhat, or the path of Pratyekabuddha.
"What do you think?
Based on these causes and conditions, would the merit of this person be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
It is not as meritorious as when a son or daughter of good family takes a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and gives it to another person so that they may copy, read, and recite it, saying:
"You shall thereby obtain the merits corresponding to this Prajñāpāramitā."
The merit thereof is exceedingly great. Why is this?
By following and studying this Dharma, you shall attain the dharma of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

In accordance with the attainment of the dharma of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), one shall accordingly attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, and the path of a pratyekabuddha.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all the sentient beings filling Jambudvīpa were to each resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to provide them with a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, enabling them to copy, read, and recite it."
"By reason of this, would that person's merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"Kauśika! It is not as good as a son of good family or a daughter of good family giving a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to a single bodhisattva who is irreversible (avaivartika), while forming this thought:"
"If this bodhisattva trains in this, they shall be able to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
For this reason, the perfection of wisdom will increase and spread widely; their merit will be greater than that [of the former].

“Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa and even those of the trichiliocosm, let us consider all the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, who have all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, gave it to someone so that they might transcribe,
read, and recite it— what do you think?
"By these causes and conditions, would that person's merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
"It is not as good as a son or daughter of good family who, with a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, gives it to a single avaivartika bodhisattva, thinking:
'This bodhisattva shall study within this [sūtra] and will be able to cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.'"
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā will increase, spread, and circulate, and the merit [of the former] will be far greater than that.
"Furthermore, Kausika!
Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to each resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who gave them a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and explained its meaning for them,
what do you think?
"By these causes and conditions, would that person's merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!

It is not as meritorious as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to a single avaivartika bodhisattva and explains its meaning for them; their merit is far greater than that.”

“Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa and even those of the trichiliocosm, suppose one were to teach the sentient beings in as many worlds throughout the ten directions as there are sands in the Ganges River, causing them all to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If there were a good man or a good woman who gave them a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and explained its meaning for them,
what do you think?
"By reason of this, would that person's merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, World-Honored One!"

The Buddha said, "It is not as meritorious as when a son or daughter of good family gives a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra to a single non-regressive bodhisattva and explains its meaning for them; the latter's merit is greater than that."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were irreversible bodhisattvas.
If a good man or a good woman were to teach them the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, [the merit would be even greater]."
"What do you think?
By reason of this, would that person’s merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!
Among them, there may be a bodhisattva who quickly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
yet if someone were to teach this person the meaning of the prajñāpāramitā, their merit would be greater than that.

“Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa and even those of the trichiliocosm, let alone all the sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—suppose they were all irreversible bodhisattvas.”
If there were a son or daughter of good family who taught them the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā,
what do you think?
By reason of this, would their merit be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! Suppose there were a bodhisattva among them who would swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If someone were to teach this person the meaning of the prajñāpāramitā, their merit would be greater than that.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is, so it is!
World-Honored One!”

As the Bodhisattva draws closer to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should increasingly instruct him in the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā* and should also increasingly provide him with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine; the merit of this is exceedingly great.
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
Such is the nature of dharmas: the closer one approaches *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the more merit one gains.
At that time, Subhūti praised Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!”
"You are a noble disciple; it is the duty of the Dharma that you assist all bodhisattvas by comforting and protecting them with regard to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

If, when the Buddha first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddhas of the past and their disciples had not comforted and assisted him with the six *pāramitās*, he would not have been able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Kauśika! When the Buddha first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because the Buddhas of the past and their disciples had comforted and assisted him by means of the six *pāramitās*.
Chapter Seven: Dedication (*Pariṇāmanā*) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Seven: Dedication. At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

"The merit of rejoicing (*anumodanā*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is the greatest, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among the merits of other sentient beings' generosity, observance of precepts, and cultivation of dhyāna."
At that time, Subhūti asked Maitreya Bodhisattva: "If a bodhisattva,
regarding the immeasurable, incalculable Buddhas of the past who have attained parinirvāṇa in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions—
[considering] those Buddhas from their first production of the thought of awakening until they attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
From the attainment of unsurpassed *samyak-saṃbodhi* and entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, until the time when the Dharma is about to perish— in this interval—
all the roots of goodness and merit corresponding to the six *pāramitās*, as well as the merit from the giving, observance of precepts,
and cultivation of meditation by all the *śrāvaka* disciples, including all those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*) who are free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Merit, as well as the Buddhas’ aggregate of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
their great kindness and great compassion; their benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings;
the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas and that which they have taught—within these dharmas, sentient beings receive and train.
All the merit possessed by these sentient beings, as well as the merit planted by sentient beings after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas— having gathered and weighed all this merit—
one rejoices with a mind that is greatest, most excellent, supreme, and most wondrous.
Having rejoiced, they dedicate [the merit] toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
making this reflection:
"By means of this merit of mine, may I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If a bodhisattva thinks:
"I dedicate this mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," are those objects and those things,
which are the focal points of that mind, capable of being apprehended?
Maitreya said:
"These various conditions and phenomena cannot be apprehended, just as the mind grasps at signs. Subhūti said:
"If these various conditions and phenomena were not thus, this person would be without inversion of perception, inversion of view, and inversion of mind.

[Yet they] take the impermanent to be permanent, suffering to be pleasure, the impure to be pure, and the non-self to be self, thereby giving rise to inversion of perception, inversion of view, and inversion of mind."
If all conditions and all phenomena are as they truly are, then awakening is likewise, and the mind is likewise.
If all conditions and phenomena, awakening, and the mind are not different, what is this mind of sympathetic joy that is dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Maitreya said:
“Subhūti! This method of dedication should not be explained before bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.”
Why is this? Subhūti, all the faith, joy, reverence, and pure mind that such a person possesses shall utterly perish. Subhūti!
This method of dedication should be explained before an avaivartika bodhisattva.

If it is explained to one who associates with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), such a person, upon hearing this, will not be startled, will not be terrified, will not sink into despondency, and will not retreat.
When a bodhisattva rejoices in merit, they should dedicate it toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Yet, the mind used for this dedication is itself exhausted and extinguished.
What mind, then, is there that dedicates [the merit] toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)?
"If one uses the mind to dedicate the mind, these two minds do not coexist; furthermore, the nature of the mind cannot be found to be dedicated.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti, "Will newly resolved bodhisattvas not be terrified upon hearing this?"
“How, then, does a bodhisattva now truly dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy?
At that time, Subhūti, on account of Maitreya Bodhisattva, spoke these words:

“Regarding the Buddhas of the past—whose path has been severed, whose formations have ceased, whose conceptual proliferation is exhausted, who have destroyed the thorns, laid down the heavy burden, achieved their own welfare, exhausted the fetters of existence, liberated through right knowledge, and attained mastery of mind—the bodhisattva collects and weighs all the roots of goodness and the power of the merit of those Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, as well as the roots of goodness planted by their disciples in the presence of those Buddhas.”
These various merits are rejoiced in with a mind that is greatest, most excellent, supreme, and most wondrous.
Having rejoiced, they are dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
How, then, should this bodhisattva now avoid falling into the inversion of perception, the inversion of view, and the inversion of mind?

If this bodhisattva, using this mind, dedicates it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet does not give rise to the notion of "mind" within that very mind, then it is truly a dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a bodhisattva gives rise to mental characteristics within this mind, they fall into the inversion of perception, the inversion of view, and the inversion of mind.

When a bodhisattva rejoices, this mind is of the nature of total cessation; if they know, as it truly is, the nature of total cessation and the phenomena that are of the nature of total cessation, then there can be no dedication.
The mind of dedication is likewise of such a nature, and the phenomena to which they are dedicated are likewise of such a nature.
If one can dedicate in this manner, it is called right dedication.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy in this manner:

"Whatever merit has been produced by the Buddhas of the past, together with their disciples and ordinary persons—even down to animals—who have planted roots of goodness upon hearing the Dharma; and whatever merit has been produced by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who, having heard the Dharma, have generated the mind directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); all of this, taken together and weighed."
These various merits, one rejoices in with a mind that is greatest, most excellent, supreme, and most wondrous.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a bodhisattva reflects thus:
"All these dharmas are utterly extinguished,
and the destination to which they are dedicated is also utterly extinguished," this is called the correct dedication of the merit of sympathetic joy toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva knows thus—that there is no dharma capable of dedicating itself to any dharma—this is called the correct dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
If a bodhisattva dedicates in this manner, they will not fall into perversion of perception, perversion of view, or perversion of mind. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva does not cling to the dedication; therefore, it is called the unsurpassed dedication.
If a bodhisattva, regarding merit, gives rise to conceptualization by grasping at signs, they will be unable to dedicate that merit. Why is this?
These dharmas that arise through volitional effort are all devoid of marks;
the merit of sympathetic joy is likewise devoid of marks.
If a bodhisattva knows that the dharmas arising from their thoughts are all devoid of marks, it should be known that this constitutes the practice of the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, the roots of goodness and merit of all Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa are likewise dedicated;
the nature and characteristics of the method used for dedication are also likewise."
If one can know in this way, it is called the correct dedication toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas do not permit dedication that grasps at signs.
If a phenomenon has passed away and been extinguished, that phenomenon is without marks and cannot be apprehended by means of marks.
If one discriminates even in this way, it is called grasping at marks;
if one does not discriminate even in this way, it is called right dedication.
How can one dedicate [merit] without grasping at signs or making conceptual distinctions?
For this reason, a bodhisattva should train in the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one does not hear and obtain the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, then one cannot enter into this matter.
If one does not hear and obtain the skillful means of the Prajñāpāramitā, it is impossible for them to be able to correctly dedicate all their merits. Why is this?

This person regards the bodies of the Buddhas of the past and their various merits as having already entered parinirvāṇa; yet, grasping at signs and making conceptual distinctions, they claim to have obtained these merits and wish to dedicate them.
Dedicating in this manner is not permitted by the Buddhas, nor do they rejoice in it.
Why is this? Because in all such cases, there is still the apprehension of phenomena as having intrinsic existence.

To take up signs and engage in conceptual discrimination regarding the Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa in the past, and to perform dedication with a sense of attainment, is itself great attachment.
The Buddhas do not say that there is any great benefit for one who performs dedication with such a mind of attainment.
Why is this? This dedication is called "mixed with poison" and leads to decline and affliction.
It is like fine food that contains poison; although it possesses an excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, because it contains poison, it must not be eaten.
If a foolish and ignorant person eats this food, although it is fragrant, delicious, and pleasing at first, there is a great retribution of suffering when the food begins to digest.

In the same way, there are people who do not correctly receive, read, or recite [the teachings], nor do they understand their meaning, yet they instruct their disciples with words of dedication, saying:
"Good sons!..."

Come! Just as the Buddhas of the past, future, and present possess the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—along with the roots of goodness planted by their śrāvaka disciples and ordinary persons; and the roots of goodness planted by those pratyekabuddhas who have been prophesied by the Buddhas to become pratyekabuddhas; and the roots of goodness planted by those bodhisattvas who have been prophesied to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—collect and weigh them all together.
"One rejoices in all these merits; having rejoiced, one dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a person dedicates in this manner, because that dedication involves grasping at signs and conceptual discrimination, it is called 'mixed with poison.'"
It is like food mixed with poison; for one who has a grasping at attainment, there is no dedication. Why?
Because all such grasping at attainment is mixed with poison.
For this reason, a bodhisattva should reflect in this way:

"Regarding the roots of goodness and merit of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, how should they be dedicated so that it is called a 'right dedication' leading to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
“If a bodhisattva wishes not to slander the Buddhas, they should dedicate in this way:

‘In whatever manner, with whatever characteristics, whatever nature, whatever essence, and whatever reality the merits known by the Buddhas exist, I likewise rejoice in them. By means of this rejoicing, I dedicate [the merit] toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.’”
When a bodhisattva dedicates merit in this way, there is no fault, and they do not slander the Buddhas.
Such dedication is untainted by poison and is called following the teachings of all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should dedicate the merit of sympathetic joy in this manner:

Just as the categories of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are not bound to the realm of desire, not bound to the realm of form, and not bound to the formless realm;
they are neither past, nor future, nor present."
Because it is unattached, this dedication of merit is also unattached; the dharma of dedication is unattached, and the object of dedication is also unattached.
If one can dedicate in this way, then it is not mixed with poison.
If one does not dedicate in this manner, it is called wrong dedication.

As for the bodhisattva’s method of dedication: dedicating in the same way as all Buddhas of the three periods of time know how to dedicate, and dedicating likewise toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is called right dedication.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"You are able to perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Subhūti!

If all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers, it would not equal the merit of this bodhisattva’s dedication; that [dedication] is the greatest, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there were sentient beings in a trichiliocosm, all of whom had resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Each one of these bodhisattvas, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were to provide with a mind of grasping all manner of requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and every article of comfort—to as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges worlds.

In this way, each and every bodhisattva, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, with a mind that perceives objects, makes offerings to these sentient beings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all articles of pleasure.
"What do you think?
By this causal condition, would these bodhisattvas obtain much merit? Subhūti said:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
It is beyond analogy.
If this merit were to have a physical form, even worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not be able to contain it.”
The Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva, being protected by the perfection of wisdom, is able to dedicate these merits, then compared to the merit of giving with a mind of grasping as previously described, it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousand-millionth part, nor even any part reachable by calculation or analogy.
At that time, twenty thousand devaputras from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings joined their palms, paid homage to the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
This dedication of the bodhisattva is called the ‘Great Dedication.’”
By means of skillful means, this surpasses the merit of the giving of a bodhisattva who perceives something as obtainable. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva’s dedication is protected by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

At that time, one hundred thousand devaputras from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven made offerings to the Buddha with celestial flowers, perfumes, ointments, powdered incense, celestial robes, banners, and various celestial musical instruments, all saying these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
This dedication of the bodhisattva is called the "Great Dedication.
By means of skillful means, it surpasses the merit of the giving of a bodhisattva who perceives things as having intrinsic existence. Why is this?
"This dedication of the bodhisattva is protected by the perfection of wisdom.

Then, one hundred thousand devaputras from the Yāma Heaven, one hundred thousand devaputras from the Tuṣita Heaven, one hundred thousand devaputras from the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and one hundred thousand devaputras from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven all made offerings to the Buddha with celestial flowers, celestial incense, and even celestial music, saying these words:
"World-Honored One!
This dedication of the bodhisattva is called the "Great Dedication.
Because it employs skillful means, it surpasses the merit of the giving of a bodhisattva who perceives things as having objective existence. Why is this?
"This dedication of the bodhisattva is protected by the perfection of wisdom.
The sons of the gods from the Brahma world cried out in a great voice:
"This dedication of the bodhisattva is called the Great Dedication."
By means of skillful means, this surpasses the merit of the giving of a bodhisattva who perceives something to be attained. Why is this?
Because this bodhisattva’s dedication is protected by the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

The devaputras of the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, Ābhāsvara, Śubha, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha heavens joined their palms, paid homage to the Buddha, and all spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!...”

These sons and daughters of good family who seek the Buddha-way are most rare; because they are protected by the Prajñāpāramitā, they are able to surpass the merit of the giving of bodhisattvas who grasp at attainments.
"Why is this? It is because this dedication of the bodhisattva is protected by the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens:

"Setting aside these sentient beings of the trichiliocosm, suppose all the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions were to each resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Suppose each of these bodhisattvas, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, were to provide sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions with offerings—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and every kind of article of pleasure—while still maintaining a mind that perceives objects."

In this manner, each and every bodhisattva, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, should provide these sentient beings with offerings—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all articles of pleasure—while maintaining a mind that grasps at objective existence.

If there is a bodhisattva who, regarding all the categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the roots of goodness planted by their śrāvaka disciples and ordinary persons, collects and weighs them together.
These merits, one rejoices in with a mind that is greatest, most excellent, supreme, and most wondrous.
Having rejoiced, one dedicates them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; the merit thereof is exceedingly great.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, regarding these various merits, having gathered and weighed them together, one rejoices with a mind that is greatest, most excellent, supreme, and most wondrous.”
Having rejoiced, one dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One,
what is called the greatest, most excellent, highest, and most wondrous rejoicing?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva, regarding all dharmas of the past, future, and present, neither grasps nor rejects them, does not dwell upon them, and does not apprehend them—within this there is no dharma that has already arisen and ceased, that is now arising and ceasing, or that will arise and cease.”
Just as one rejoices in accordance with the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), so too should one dedicate [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, this is called the greatest, most excellent, highest, and most wondrous rejoicing and dedication of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva wishes to rejoice in the generosity,

ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they should rejoice in this manner."
As it is with liberation, so it is with the precepts;
as it is with liberation, so it is with concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
as it is with liberation, so it is with faith and understanding.
As it is with liberation, so it is with sympathetic joy;
as it is with liberation, so it is with future dharmas that have not yet arisen;
as it is with liberation, so it is with the Buddhas and their disciples of the past, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds.
As it is with liberation, so it is now with the Buddhas and their disciples in the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the ten directions;
as it is with liberation, so it will be with the Buddhas and their disciples in the immeasurable, incalculable worlds of the future.

These characteristics of all phenomena are neither bound nor fettered, neither liberated nor released; dedicating [merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by virtue of their being neither born nor extinguished.
Subhūti! This is called the greatest, most supreme, highest, and most wonderful rejoicing and dedication of a bodhisattva.
By means of this dedication, it surpasses those of worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

If all bodhisattvas, with a mind of grasping, were for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges to provide sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all articles of pleasure—and were to practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration with a mind of grasping—the merit of rejoicing in and dedicating [the roots of goodness] of this [present practice] would surpass it such that the former would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one part in a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor even what can be reached by calculation or analogy.
Chapter 8: On the Hells (Niraya-varga). At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"This is the perfection of wisdom; the Buddha says this is the perfection of wisdom.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is able to provide illumination."
Bhagavan,
the Prajñāpāramitā is worthy of veneration. Bhagavan!
The perfection of wisdom can bestow light.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom eliminates all darkness.
"Bhagavān,
the Prajñāpāramitā is unstained.
Bhagavān!"
"Blessed One, the Prajñāpāramitā brings benefit;
Blessed One,
the Prajñāpāramitā brings peace."
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can provide eyes to the blind.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can cause those who practice erroneously to enter the right path.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is itself sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One!
"Bhagavān, the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither a dharma that arises nor a dharma that ceases. Bhagavān,
the *prajñāpāramitā* fully possesses the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects."
Bhagavan!
The Prajñāpāramitā is able to provide protection for those who are destitute and solitary.
Bhagavan!
The Prajñāpāramitā can extinguish birth and death.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā can reveal the nature of all dharmas.
“World-Honored One,
how should one venerate and regard the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha said:
"One should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā as one reverently beholds the Buddha; one should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā as one pays homage to the Buddha.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
Having thought, "For what reason and by what causes does Śāriputra ask this? he questioned Śāriputra:
"For what reason and by what causes do you ask this?"
Śāriputra said:

“Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the perfection of wisdom, rejoices in merit and dedicates it toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), their merit is the most supreme among all the giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and so forth of the aforementioned bodhisattvas; for this reason, I asked this question.”
Kauśika! It is like a multitude of hundreds of thousands of blind people who, lacking a guide, are unable to proceed toward a city or a village.
Kauśika! The five pāramitās, when separated from the prajñāpāramitā, are like blind people without a guide; they cannot cultivate the path to reach sarvajñā.
If the five perfections are protected by the perfection of wisdom, they then possess eyes.
It is through the power of the perfection of wisdom that the five perfections receive the name "perfection."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) produced?”
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva does not give rise to form, then they give rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If they do not give rise to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, then they give rise to the perfection of wisdom."
“Thus arising, what dharma does this prajñāpāramitā accomplish? “Śāriputra,
thus arising, this prajñāpāramitā accomplishes nothing among dharmas.”
"If there is nothing accomplished, that is called Prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Does the perfection of wisdom also not accomplish all-knowledge (sarvajñatā)?
“Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom does accomplish all-knowledge; it is simply that it does not accomplish it by way of arising as a dharma through names and signs.”
“World-Honored One!
How should it be accomplished?
The Buddha said:
"As it is not accomplished, so it is accomplished.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"
“Is it because the Prajñāpāramitā does not bring about arising nor bring about cessation that it exists?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
If a bodhisattva likewise discriminates in this way, they lose the prajñāpāramitā and distance themselves from the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“For this reason, if a bodhisattva thinks that the prajñāpāramitā is empty and non-existent, they lose the prajñāpāramitā and distance themselves from the prajñāpāramitā.”
“Subhūti! This is called the Prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!”
"What dharma does the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* reveal? "Subhūti, the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* does not reveal form;

it does not reveal feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It does not reveal the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha. It does not reveal the Buddha-dharma."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
This great pāramitā is the prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said:
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
"For what reason, then, is the Mahāpāramitā the Prajñāpāramitā?
Subhūti replied, "The Prajñāpāramitā does not make form (rūpa) great, nor does it make it small; it does not join it together, nor does it disperse it."
Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one does not make them great, nor does one make them small; one does not make them conjoined, nor does one make them dispersed.
World-Honored One, the Prajñāpāramitā does not make the ten powers of a Buddha strong, nor does it make them weak.
From the four fearlessnesses up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*), one neither forms them into a combination nor disperses them.
World-Honored One,
if a bodhisattva discriminates in this manner, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā possesses no such characteristic as:
"I shall deliver so many sentient beings."
This is precisely because the Bodhisattva conceives of there being something to be attained.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are unarisen, the Prajñāpāramitā is unarisen.
Because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, the Prajñāpāramitā lacks intrinsic nature.
Because sentient beings are free from marks, the Prajñāpāramitā is free from marks.
Because sentient beings do not cease, the Prajñāpāramitā does not cease.
Because sentient beings are inconceivable, the Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.
Because sentient beings are unknowable, the Prajñāpāramitā is unknowable.
"Because the power of sentient beings is gathered, the power of the Tathāgata is also gathered.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva can believe in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, without doubt, regret, or hesitation, and understands its meaning in accordance with it—
from where did such a person pass away to be reborn here?
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! This bodhisattva has passed away from a buddha-field in another direction and has been reborn here.”
Śāriputra! Those bodhisattvas who have come from other buddha-fields have previously drawn near to and made offerings to various Buddhas, inquiring about their profound meanings.
Now, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, they immediately give rise to joy, as if hearing it directly from a Buddha.
"If one sees the Prajñāpāramitā, it is as if seeing the Buddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Can the Prajñāpāramitā be heard or seen?
The Buddha said: “No.”
“World-Honored One!
For how long has this bodhisattva been able to practice the prajñāpāramitā since first generating the mind of awakening? “Subhūti!
This matter should be analyzed.
There are bodhisattvas who encounter hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of buddhas, and under those buddhas, they practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya).
Yet there are those who, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in the midst of the great assembly, lack a heart of reverence and immediately depart.

Subhūti! You should know that such persons, because they abandoned the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* when it was preached by the Buddhas of the past, likewise abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* upon hearing it now; their body and mind are in discord, and they give rise to the karma of ignorance.
Because they have accumulated the causes and conditions of ignorant karma, they slander and reject the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti, those who slander and reject the profound Prajñāpāramitā are, in fact, slandering and rejecting sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Those who slander and reject omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are, in fact, slandering and rejecting the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Subhūti!

Because these deluded people give rise to such grave karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, they shall suffer the punishments of the great hells for many hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, passing from one great hell to another.

While undergoing retribution by moving from one great hell to another great hell, if the fire calamity arises, they fall into a great hell in another direction, where they likewise move from one great hell to another great hell.
While undergoing retribution by passing from one great hell to another great hell, if that fire calamity arises, they fall again into a great hell in another direction.
Having fallen into a great hell in another direction, they once more pass from one great hell to another great hell.
While undergoing retribution by moving from one great hell to another great hell, if that fire calamity arises, they return and fall back into this very great hell.
There, these people again move from one great hell to another great hell, experiencing various intense sufferings.
Thus they pass through successive cycles until the fire kalpa arises once more, undergoing these immeasurable karmic retributions of suffering and affliction.
Why is this? Because they have given rise to the karma of harsh speech.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Such karma resembles the five heinous crimes."
“Śāriputra! Do not think that the offense of destroying the Dharma is comparable to the five heinous crimes. Why is this?
When such a person hears the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they slander and reject it, thinking:
"One should not study this Dharma; this Dharma was not spoken by the Buddha."
“Because of these causes and conditions, their transgressions increase further, and they also cause others to depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
“Such a person ruins their own body and also ruins the bodies of others;”
They drink poison themselves and cause others to drink poison;
they bring ruin upon themselves and cause others to suffer ruin;
not knowing and not understanding the Prajñāpāramitā themselves, they likewise teach others not to know or understand it.
Śāriputra! I would not even permit such a person to leave the household life, let alone accept offerings within my Dharma. Why is this?
One should know that such a person is a defiler of the Dharma;
one should know that such a person is like dregs, their nature being turbid and dark.
If there are sentient beings who believe and accept their words, they too shall undergo this same intense suffering and grave retribution.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
if one destroys the *prajñāpāramitā* or defiles the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that such a person is a destroyer of the Dharma and a defiler of the Dharma.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
do you not speak of the size of the bodies received by these people?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Set aside the question of the size of this person's body; there is no need to speak of it.
If this person were to hear the description of its dimensions, hot blood would issue from their mouth, and they would either die or be near death."

If one were to hear the description of the dimensions of that body and recognize these transgressions for oneself, one would fall into deep sorrow and the body would wither away; therefore, there is no need to describe the size of the body one receives.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We only pray that the Buddha will describe the dimensions of this person’s body, so that people of future generations may take this as a clear warning and know that it is because of such karmic offenses that one receives such a massive body.”

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to believe in and understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that this bodhisattva is like one who is non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*)."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
If a person, in past lives, did not practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for long, they will be unable to believe and understand it.
"Bhagavān!
If there are those who revile and reject the Prajñāpāramitā, one should know that such persons have for a long time already reviled and rejected the Prajñāpāramitā."
Why is this? Because such a person lacks faith in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, lacks a pure mind, and does not inquire about their doubts with the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddhas.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra said to Śāriputra:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is profound.
It is not surprising that those who have not long practiced the bodhisattva path are unable to believe and understand it."
"If a person pays homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are paying homage to the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).
Śāriputra said, "So it is, so it is!"
Kauśika! If a person pays homage to the Prajñāpāramitā, they are paying homage to the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).
From the Prajñāpāramitā arises the omniscient wisdom of all Buddhas, and from that omniscient wisdom, in turn, arises the Prajñāpāramitā.
“A bodhisattva should dwell in the perfection of wisdom in this way; they should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How does a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) come to be said to 'dwell' in the perfection of wisdom, and to be said to 'cultivate' the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Kauśika! You are able to ask the Buddha about this matter.
That which you have asked is entirely through the power of the Buddha.
Kauśika! If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell in form.
If they do not dwell in form, that is precisely the cultivation of form; they likewise do not dwell in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
If one does not dwell in consciousness, that is the cultivation of consciousness.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a bodhisattva does not cultivate form, and if they do not cultivate form, they do not dwell in form; they do not cultivate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
If one does not practice with consciousness, then one does not abide in consciousness.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
This is called a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom and abiding in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep, immeasurable, and bottomless.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell in the profundity of form, this is practicing the profundity of form;
if they do not dwell in the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the profundity of consciousness.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice the profundity of form, this is called not abiding in the profundity of form;
if they do not practice the profundity of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is called not abiding in the profundity of consciousness.
“World-Honored One!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* should be taught before irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattvas; when such persons hear it, they will have neither doubt nor regret.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Śāriputra:
"If one were to speak before a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment], what fault would there be? "Kauśika!

If a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that this bodhisattva has long since resolved upon the Great Vehicle; he is close to receiving a prediction and will certainly receive it before long.
"If they pass beyond one Buddha or two Buddhas, they shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction hears this profound prajñāpāramitā, you should know that this bodhisattva has long since set forth the mind of the Great Vehicle.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I shall now speak a parable."
The Buddha said,
“Speak as you wish.
[He replied,] “World-Honored One!”
For example, if one seeking the bodhisattva path dreams of sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), one should know that this bodhisattva is close to attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If one who seeks the bodhisattva path hears this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that this bodhisattva has long since resolved upon the Great Vehicle, has perfected their roots of goodness, and is close to receiving a prediction of enlightenment; before long, they will certainly receive that prediction.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!"
“Relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, you should further explain this.
“World-Honored One!

It is like a person who wishes to traverse a perilous road—whether it be one hundred yojanas, or two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred yojanas—and when they wish to emerge from that difficulty, they first see various signs.”
If one sees someone tending cattle or sheep, or sees boundary markers, or sees groves and gardens—
because of seeing such signs, one should know that there must be a city or a village within this area.
Having seen these signs, he thinks:
"According to the signs I have seen, cities and villages are not far from here.
His mind becomes peaceful and secure, and he no longer fears enemies or the harm of bandits.
World-Honored One!
It is the same for a bodhisattva.

If they hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that this bodhisattva is close to receiving the prediction of enlightenment; before long, they will certainly receive the prediction, and at that time, they will not fear falling into the stages of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have attained these primary signs, namely, they have attained the vision of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and have attained the hearing of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person who wished to see the great ocean and proceeded forward step by step; if they saw trees or the signs of trees, or mountains or the signs of mountains, they should know that the ocean was still far away.

If one does not see trees and has no perception of trees, and does not see mountains and has no perception of mountains, one should know that the great ocean is not far from this place; because the great ocean is deep, it contains neither mountains nor trees. Although this person does not see the sea, they know they must be near it.
World-Honored One!

It is the same for a bodhisattva: having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, although they have not yet received a prediction in the presence of the Buddhas of the present, they know for themselves that they are certainly close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For what reason?
Because I have obtained the opportunity to see, hear, and make offerings to the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
"World-Honored One!..."
For example, when in spring the leaves of a tree fall away, one should know that this tree will soon produce flowers, leaves, and fruit.
Why is this? Because its primary signs have appeared.
When the people of Jambudvīpa saw the signs at the base of the tree, they were all filled with joy and thought:
"This tree will soon produce flowers, leaves, and fruit."
"World-Honored One!
It is the same for a bodhisattva.

If they are able to see or hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that this bodhisattva has accomplished roots of goodness; it is because of the causes and conditions of roots of goodness from past lives that they now obtain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
In that assembly, there were those who had previously seen the Buddha; all the devas were filled with great joy and thought to themselves:
"The former bodhisattvas also had such primary signs when they received their predictions; this bodhisattva shall before long receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“World-Honored One! It is like a woman who is pregnant;

as her pregnancy progresses, she becomes increasingly uncomfortable, her body is utterly exhausted, she finds no pleasure in worldly affairs, and she sleeps uneasily. Her intake of food and drink diminishes, suffering manifests in her body, and she has no desire for speech. She grows weary of what she was formerly accustomed to and no longer recalls past pleasures. Because these signs have appeared, one should know that this woman will give birth before long.”
The accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s roots of goodness is likewise so.
If one should see, hear, or contemplate the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, it should be known that this bodhisattva will, before long, receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”
"Whatever you delight in expounding is all through the Buddha's spiritual power.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata has well explained the affairs of all bodhisattvas. “Subhūti!

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have, throughout the long night, brought great benefit, great peace, and great happiness; out of compassion for the world, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and expound the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully cultivate and practice the perfection of wisdom?”
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and does not perceive an increase in form, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if they do not perceive an increase in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is practicing the perfection of wisdom.”
Not perceiving the diminution of form is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
not perceiving the diminution of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, not perceiving any phenomenon, nor perceiving what is non-phenomenal—this is called practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, it is inconceivable."
“Subhūti! Form is inconceivable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable.
If a bodhisattva does not discriminate form as being inconceivable, [he is practicing rightly].”
"Not discriminating between feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is inconceivable;
this is what constitutes practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"World-Honored One!"
“Such is the perfection of wisdom; who is able to believe and understand it?
“Subhūti, those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva come to be called one who has practiced for a long time? “Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom and does not differentiate the ten powers of a buddha or the four fearlessnesses, up to and including not differentiating omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), this is called "long-term practice."
Why is this? The ten powers of the Buddha are inconceivable; the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities are inconceivable; even up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*), they are inconceivable.
Form is inconceivable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inconceivable; all dharmas are likewise inconceivable.
When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it is called practicing without a locus while practicing the prajñāpāramitā; for this reason, it is called "practicing for a long time."
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; the Prajñāpāramitā is a treasury of rare jewels, as pure and marvelous as space.”
“World-Honored One!
Since obstacles may arise regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, if one wishes to transcribe it, one should complete the transcription as quickly as possible, even if it takes up to a year.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to copy, read, recite, and practice the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught, even for a single year, they should do so with great diligence."
“Subhūti! The Dharma of rare jewels has many enemies and robbers.
“World-Honored One!”
“Māra, the Evil One, constantly seeks to find an opportunity to interrupt the perfection of wisdom. “Subhūti!
Although Māra seeks to find an opportunity to interrupt it, he shall not succeed.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By whose spiritual power is it that evil Māra is unable to create obstacles for the Prajñāpāramitā?"
“Śāriputra! By the spiritual power of the Buddha, evil Māras are unable to create obstacles. Śāriputra!”

Furthermore, by the spiritual power of all the Buddhas currently residing in the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, evil Māras are unable to create obstacles; and because all Buddhas together protect and mind this Bodhisattva, evil Māras cannot find an opportunity to prevail.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
for a bodhisattva who is protected by all the Buddhas, there should be no obstacles to the Dharma.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

if anyone writes down, recites, or explains the Prajñāpāramitā, the present Buddhas of the ten directions— immeasurable and incalculable in number— are by the nature of the Dharma destined to protect and mindfully sustain them.
"If there are those who recite the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that these bodhisattvas are able to recite it with fluency because they are protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
"World-Honored One!
You should know that those sons and daughters of good family who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā are seen by the Buddha’s eye."

“Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and even transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that such a person is seen by the Buddha-eye.”
Śāriputra! If good sons and good daughters seeking the Buddha-way accept, uphold, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā, they will be close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Even to the extent of writing it oneself or having others write it,
and having written it, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it—
for these causes and conditions, the merit is exceedingly great.
Śāriputra! After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Prajñāpāramitā shall circulate in the south; from the south it shall circulate to the west, and from the west it shall circulate to the north.
Śāriputra! When my Dharma flourishes, there is no sign of its extinction.

If in the northern direction there are those who even transcribe, uphold, and make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, such persons are likewise seen by the Buddha-eye, known by him, and kept in his mind.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
During the final five hundred years, will the Prajñāpāramitā be widely disseminated in the northern region?”
“Śāriputra! In the final five hundred years, it shall be widely disseminated in the north.

Any sons of good family or daughters of good family therein who hear this Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice it, should be known as having long since set their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“World-Honored One!
How many bodhisattvas will there be in the northern direction who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā? “Śāriputra!”
Although there are many bodhisattvas in the north who can read, hear, and receive the Prajñāpāramitā, few are able to recite it fluently or practice it.
When such a person hears it, they will neither be startled nor terrified.
This person has previously seen the Buddha and has posed questions and inquiries.
It should be known that this person is able to fully practice the bodhisattva path; for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they are able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

Why is this? Śāriputra, for the sake of these good men and good women, I have taught the dharmas that correspond to sarvajñatā; when these persons change their bodies, they likewise delight in expounding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
With single-minded harmony, they reach the point where even Māra cannot destroy their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Upon hearing the *prajñāpāramitā*, these people experience great joy in their hearts and attain purity of mind; they cause many sentient beings to plant the roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These good sons and good daughters shall speak these words before me:

"We who practice the bodhisattva path shall always, by means of the Dharma, instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings, causing them to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Śāriputra! Observing their minds, I give rise to sympathetic joy; these people practice the bodhisattva path and shall, by means of the Dharma, instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings, causing them to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

In this way, sons and daughters of good family who delight their hearts in the Mahāyāna and aspire to be born before the Buddhas currently teaching the Dharma in other directions will there continue to hear extensively the preaching of the Prajñāpāramitā.

In that buddha-field, he likewise uses the Dharma to instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings, causing them to abide in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
