Regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata does not know, and no dharma that he does not recognize."
Regarding the bodhisattvas of future ages who, with great desire and great diligence, zealously seek the prajñāpāramitā—
the Tathāgata fully knows those sons and daughters of good family who obtain it through seeking, as well as those who obtain it without seeking.
“Śāriputra! There are many sons and daughters of good family who, because they are diligent and untiring, obtain the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) without seeking it.”
“World-Honored One!
Will these sons and daughters of good family also obtain, without seeking, those other sūtras that correspond to the six pāramitās?”
“Śāriputra! If there are other profound sūtras corresponding to the various pāramitās, these good sons and good daughters shall also obtain them without seeking.”
For what reason?
Śāriputra, such is the nature of dharmas.

If there is a bodhisattva who, for the sake of all sentient beings, instructs, exhorts, benefits, and gladdens them regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and also trains therein himself, then when this person changes bodies, he will encounter the profound sūtras on the *pāramitās* and obtain them even without seeking.
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: On the Deeds of Māra.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The merits of good sons and good daughters have already been explained; how, then, do obstacles arise?
"Subhūti! If a teacher of the Dharma does not immediately delight in speaking,"
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
there may be a teacher of the Dharma who delights in speaking without ceasing.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, the one who preaches the Dharma does not preach it to its ultimate conclusion.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, when the Prajñāpāramitā is being written, read, recited, or explained, one becomes arrogant and conceited.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, when the Prajñāpāramitā is being written, read, recited, or explained, they mock and deride one another.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, when the Prajñāpāramitā is being written, read, recited, or explained, they treat one another with contempt.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, when the Prajñāpāramitā is being written, read, recited, or explained, their minds become distracted.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, when the Prajñāpāramitā is being written, read, recited, or explained, the mind is not one-pointed.
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti! A practitioner may have this thought:
"I find no flavor in the Prajñāpāramitā," he says,
and departs from his seat.
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti! A practitioner should form this thought:
"Within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no prediction of enlightenment for me."
"With his mind unpurified, he leaves his seat.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
The practitioner thinks:
"In the Prajñāpāramitā, my name is not mentioned.
Thus, their mind is not pure.
Bodhisattvas should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti! A practitioner might have this thought:
"In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is not taught where I was born—whether in a city, a town, or a village.

For this reason, they take no pleasure in hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā* preached; they then abandon it and depart. According to the thoughts that arise within them, they retrogress for a certain number of kalpas before they can once again return to cultivate the bodhisattva path.
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti,

if there are various sūtras that cannot lead to *sarvajñatā*, and a bodhisattva abandons the *prajñāpāramitā* to read and recite them, that bodhisattva is abandoning the root to grasp the branches and leaves.

Why is this? It is because by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), these bodhisattvas are able to accomplish mundane and supramundane dharmas; by studying the perfection of wisdom, they are able to study mundane and supramundane dharmas. The bodhisattva should know that if they abandon the perfection of wisdom, this constitutes the work of Māra.
Subhūti! It is like a dog that abandons the portion of food given by its master and instead seeks it from the laborers.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
In future ages, there may be bodhisattvas who abandon the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and instead take up other sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
“Subhūti! It is as if a person who has found an elephant does not examine it, but instead seeks its tracks.
What do you think? Is this person wise?”
“No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva.”
Having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abandon it and instead seek *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) within the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What do you think: is such a person wise?
"No, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra. "Subhūti!"
It is, for example, like a person who wishes to see the great ocean;
having seen it, they instead seek out water from a cow's footprint and say:
"Can the water of the great ocean be so much?"
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti!"
In future ages, bodhisattvas will be just like this:
having attained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will abandon it and instead recite and study the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"What do you think? Is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."

“Subhūti! Suppose, for example, there were a craftsman who, wishing to construct a palace as magnificent as that of Śakra, instead went about calculating the dimensions of the palaces of the sun and the moon.
What do you think? Would this person be considered wise?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it shall be the same for bodhisattvas in future ages."
Having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abandon it and instead seek *sarvajñatā* within the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What do you think: is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra. "Subhūti!"
It is, for example, like a person who wishes to see a wheel-turning monarch; having seen him, they do not recognize him and think:
"What are the physical features and majestic power of a wheel-turning monarch?
Upon seeing various minor kings, they take note of their appearances and say: [This is how he is].
“Is the physical appearance and majestic virtue of a Wheel-Turning King such as these marks?
“What do you think? Is this person wise?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! In future ages, bodhisattvas will also be like this.
Having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will abandon it and instead seek *sarvajñatā* within the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
"What do you think? Is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
“Subhūti! Suppose there were a hungry person who, having set aside food of a hundred flavors, instead ate rice that had been kept for sixty days.
What do you think? Would this person be considered wise?”
"No, World-Honored One!
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva."
Having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they abandon it and instead seek *sarvajñatā* within the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What do you think: is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra. "Subhūti!"
“Suppose, for example, a person were to obtain a priceless jewel and compare it to a crystal.
What do you think—would this person be wise?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti! In future ages, bodhisattvas will also be like this:
having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will instead compare it to the sūtras of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, seeking *sarvajñatā* therein.”
"What do you think? Is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when one is writing, reading, reciting,
or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā, if one speaks much of other matters, it will obstruct and cause the neglect of the Prajñāpāramitā."
"A Bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
“Can the Prajñāpāramitā be written down, read, recited, or explained?
“No, Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes down the words and forms this thought:”
"‘I am writing the Prajñāpāramitā’—
this, Subhūti, is the work of Māra."
At that time, you should instruct these sons and daughters of good family: "Do not think that by merely writing down the words, you can form the thought:
'I am copying the Prajñāpāramitā.'"
"O sons of good family, it is by means of these words that the meaning of the Prajñāpāramitā is revealed; therefore, you must not become attached to the words.
If you become attached to the words, a bodhisattva should know that this is the work of Māra."
If one does not become greedily attached, one abandons the works of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when writing, reading, reciting, or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā, one might recall various regions, kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages; one might recall kings, enemies, and bandits, or matters of warfare; one might recall one's father, mother, brothers, and sisters."
Māra causes such thoughts as these to arise, obstructing and causing the abandonment of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
A bodhisattva should recognize them all. Subhūti!
You should know that this, too, is the work of Māra. Furthermore, Subhūti,

when one is copying, reading, reciting, or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā, if matters of worldly service arise— such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities of life— they will obstruct and cause the abandonment of the Prajñāpāramitā.
Bodhisattvas should recognize all such instances. Subhūti,
you should know that these, likewise, are the works of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
Māra creates the conditions that cause a bodhisattva to obtain various profound sūtras;
yet a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means does not give rise to greedy attachment toward these profound sūtras."
“Subhūti, a bodhisattva who lacks skillful means abandons the perfection of wisdom and takes up these profound sūtras.

Within the perfection of wisdom, I have extensively explained skillful means; one should seek them therein, yet instead they seek skillful means within other profound sūtras concerning the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
"What do you think? Is this person wise?
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti!"
Know that this, too, is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there may be one who wishes to hear the Prajñāpāramitā; yet the listener desires to hear it, [while the speaker does not].
If the teacher of the Dharma becomes weary and is not inclined to preach it, Subhūti,
such a lack of harmony is also the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the teacher of the Dharma does not become physically exhausted and delights in preaching the Prajñāpāramitā;
yet the listener of the Dharma wishes to go to another country and is unable to write down, read, recite, or explain the Prajñāpāramitā."
Such lack of harmony is also the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the listener possesses mindfulness and wisdom, and desires to hear, receive, read, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā; yet [the teacher] does not."
If the teacher of the Dharma wishes to go to another country and cannot write out, read, recite, or explain the Prajñāpāramitā,
such a lack of harmony is also the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Suppose the teacher of the Dharma prizes material wealth, clothing, food, and drink, while the listener of the Dharma is stingy and does not give them to him;
then he will be unable to write down, read, recite, or explain the Prajñāpāramitā."
Such lack of harmony is also a work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
it may be that the listener has a mind of faith and joy and wishes to make offerings to the teacher of the Dharma, yet the teacher of the Dharma is not proficient in recitation and study."
If those who listen to the Dharma do not delight in hearing and receiving it, and thus fail to write, read, recite, or explain the *prajñāpāramitā*,
such lack of harmony is also the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
it may be that the teacher of the Dharma delights in expounding it,
while the listener does not delight in hearing and receiving it; thus they shall not be able to write, read, recite, or explain the Prajñāpāramitā."
Such lack of harmony is also the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
the teacher of the Dharma may have a body that is heavy and utterly exhausted, overcome by sleep, and take no pleasure in speaking."
If those who listen to the Dharma desire to hear, receive, read, and recite it,
yet they do not act in harmony in this way, this too is the work of Māra.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
If, while one is writing, reading, reciting, or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā, someone comes and speaks of the sufferings of the three evil realms, saying:
"In the hells there are such sufferings; in the animal and hungry ghost realms there are such sufferings."
"It would be better to attain parinirvāṇa by exhausting all suffering within this very body; what use is there in being born again to undergo these various sufferings!
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should know that this too is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when one is writing, reading, reciting, or explaining the Prajñāpāramitā, if someone should come and praise the happiness of the heavens, saying:

'In the desire realm (kāmadhātu) there is the exquisite happiness of the five sensory pleasures; in the form realm (rūpadhātu) there is the happiness of meditative concentration (dhyāna); and in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) there is the bliss of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).'"
These pleasures of the three realms are all impermanent, suffering, and empty, characterized by decay and ruin.

Within this very body, you may attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat, so that you need not undergo further rebirths.
"A bodhisattva should know that this, too, is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the teacher of the Dharma may delight in having a large following and say: "
"If you can follow me, I shall give you the Prajñāpāramitā;
if you do not follow me, I will not give it to you.
For this reason, many people followed him.
At that time, the Dharma-preacher, wishing to pass through a place of perilous difficulty where lives were at risk, said to the people:
"Good sons! Do you know?"
"What use is it for you to follow me through these perils and hardships? Deliberate well for yourself; do not let there be regret later.
And he spoke these words:
"For what reason have you come here into the midst of this famine and hostile bandits?"
The teacher of the Dharma, on account of such subtle and minute causes and conditions, abandons those people.
The listener of the Dharma thinks to themselves:
"This is a sign of abandonment; it is not the mark of the *prajñāpāramitā*. One must not write, read, recite, or explain the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"In this way, such disharmony should be known by the bodhisattva as also being the work of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If the Dharma-preacher intends to travel through places infested with evil beasts such as tigers, wolves, and lions, or through regions plagued by enemies, poison, and harm, where there is no water, the Dharma-preacher says to the people:
"Do you know this?"
‘Wherever I go, I must pass through places infested with fierce beasts, hostile bandits, poisonous harms, and a lack of water; how could you possibly endure such suffering?
By means of such subtle and minute reasons, the Dharma-preacher abandons them.
The people no longer followed him, thinking to themselves:
"This is the mark of renunciation; it is not the mark of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thereupon, they immediately turned back.
"Subhūti! Such difficulties as these, a bodhisattva should know, are also the works of Māra.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Dharma-preacher values the donor; for this reason, he frequently travels back and forth.
Because of these matters, he says to those who listen to the Dharma:
"O sons of good family!..."
"I have a donor whom I ought to go visit and inquire after.
The people thought to themselves: "This is not in accord with our Prajñāpāramitā."
"Immediately abandoning [the teachings], they are unable to study, write, read, recite, or explain them.
Such disharmony, a Bodhisattva should know, is also the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
Māra exerts himself with skillful means, desiring that no one should read, recite, or practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does Māra diligently employ skillful means to prevent people from reading, reciting, and practicing the Prajñāpāramitā? “Subhūti!”
The Māra deceives people by saying:
"This is not the true Prajñāpāramitā.
The sūtras that I possess are the true Prajñāpāramitā."
"Subhūti! Māra the evil one thus deceives the multitude with such guile; those who have not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment] shall give rise to doubt regarding the Prajñāpāramitā."
"Because of doubt regarding causes and conditions, one is unable to read, recite, or practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should know that this, too, is the work of Māra."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, there is yet another demonic obstacle:
if a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā were to realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and thereby attain the fruit of a śrāvaka."
"In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should know that this too is the work of Māra.
Chapter Twelve: The Small Simile, from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“The Prajñāpāramitā has such obstacles as these.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “So it is, so it is!”
"Bhagavān!
There are many obstacles to the Prajñāpāramitā.
Just as precious jewels have many enemies and bandits, so it is with the Prajñāpāramitā."

If a person does not receive, uphold, read, recite, or practice the Prajñāpāramitā, one should know that this person has newly resolved to attain the Way; they possess little wisdom and little faith, do not delight in the Great Dharma, and are possessed by Māra.
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti!

If a person does not receive, uphold, read, recite, or practice the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that this person has newly resolved upon the path; they have little wisdom and little faith, do not delight in the Great Dharma, and are possessed by Māra."

Subhūti! Although there are many such demonic activities and obstacles regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, if good sons and good daughters are able to receive, uphold, write, read, recite, and explain it, you should know that all these instances are due to the power of the Buddha.
Why is this? Although Māra, the Evil One, diligently employs skillful means in an attempt to extinguish the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddhas likewise diligently employ skillful means to protect it.
Subhūti! It is like a woman who has many sons—perhaps ten, or a hundred, or even up to a hundred thousand.
If that mother falls ill, each of her sons diligently seeks a remedy for her treatment, and they all make this vow:

"We must ensure that our mother lives long, her body remains peaceful and secure, free from all suffering and affliction, and unharmed by wind, rain, cold, heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, or venomous stings."
One should, by means of various medicinal causes and conditions, bring peace and security to one's mother. Why is this?
For she gave birth to us, bestowed life upon us, and revealed the ways of the world; her kindness is exceedingly heavy.
"Subhūti! All the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions constantly keep the Prajñāpāramitā in mind and all speak thus:
'The Prajñāpāramitā can give birth to all Buddhas and can reveal sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).'"
Why is this? Because the sarvajñā (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas is born from the prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti!
All Buddhas who have attained, are now attaining, or will attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment do so entirely because of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
“Subhūti! The Prajñāpāramitā thus reveals the sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and it also reveals the world.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals all Buddhas to the world.
World-Honored One!”
"What is the world?
The Buddha said,
"The five aggregates are the world."
“World-Honored One!
How does the prajñāpāramitā demonstrate the five aggregates?
The Buddha said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the five aggregates have the characteristic of being indestructible.
Why is this? Subhūti!...”
Emptiness is the mark of indestructibility; signlessness and wishlessness are marks of indestructibility.
Thus does the Prajñāpāramitā reveal the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
Because the Buddha accords with the infinite and boundless natures of sentient beings, he knows their minds as they truly are. Thus, Subhūti,
the Prajñāpāramitā reveals the world to all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
As for the distracted minds and concentrated minds of sentient beings, the Buddha knows those distracted and concentrated minds as they truly are. Subhūti!"
How does the Tathāgata know the distracted minds and concentrated minds of all sentient beings?
Subhūti, he knows them by means of the characteristics of dharmas.
By means of the characteristics of phenomena, one knows that the mind is not distracted; in this way, one knows the distracted mind.
How does the Tathāgata know the concentrated mind? Subhūti!
The Tathāgata knows the characteristic of the exhaustion of the mind; he knows the characteristic of exhaustion as it truly is, and thus knows the gathering of the mind.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when sentient beings have a defiled mind, the Tathāgata knows that defiled mind as it truly is."
With a mind of anger, he knows a mind of anger as it truly is; with a mind of delusion, he knows a mind of delusion as it truly is.
How does the Tathāgata know a defiled mind as it truly is, know a mind of anger as it truly is, and know a mind of delusion as it truly is?
Subhūti! The true mark of a defiled mind is that it is not a defiled mind;
the true mark of a hateful mind or a deluded mind is that it is not a hateful mind or a deluded mind.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
From the *prajñāpāramitā*, all Buddhas give birth to the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*). How so? The Tathāgata, with a mind free from passion, knows as it truly is a mind free from passion;
with a mind free from malice, he knows as it truly is a mind free from malice.
A mind free from delusion knows, as it truly is, that it is a mind free from delusion.

Subhūti, within a mind free from passion there is no characteristic of a mind free from passion; within a mind free from hatred there is no characteristic of a mind free from hatred; within a mind free from delusion there is no characteristic of a mind free from delusion.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The perfection of wisdom reveals the world to all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the expansive mind of sentient beings as it truly is—an expansive mind.
How does the Tathāgata know the expansive mind of sentient beings as it truly is—an expansive mind?
Subhūti! These minds of sentient beings neither increase nor expand, because they do not depart from the characteristic of departure.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata knows the expansive mind of sentient beings as it truly is—an expansive mind.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata knows the great mind of sentient beings as it truly is—a great mind."
How does the Tathāgata truly know the great mind of sentient beings as a great mind?
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows that this mind neither comes nor goes, and has no abiding.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata knows the great minds of sentient beings as they truly are, as great minds.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as they truly are—immeasurable minds.
How does the Tathāgata know the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as they truly are—immeasurable minds?

Subhūti! The Tathāgata knows that this mind does not abide, but abides in quiescence, having no point of reliance, and is immeasurable like space; he knows that the characteristics of the mind are likewise so.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata knows the immeasurable minds of sentient beings as they truly are—immeasurable minds.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
By means of the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the invisible mind of sentient beings.
How does the Tathāgata know, as it truly is, the invisible mind of sentient beings?
Because of the meaning of signlessness, the Tathāgata knows the invisible mind as it truly is. Thus, Subhūti,
by means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the invisible minds of sentient beings as invisible minds, knowing them as they truly are.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by means of the prajñāpāramitā,
the Tathāgata knows, in accordance with reality, the non-manifesting minds of sentient beings as non-manifesting minds."
How is it that the Tathāgata, regarding the non-manifesting mind of sentient beings, knows that non-manifesting mind as it truly is—a mind that cannot be seen by the five eyes?
It is thus, Subhūti!
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, in accordance with reality, that the minds of sentient beings do not manifest, and that those minds do not manifest.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the arising and ceasing of sentient beings.
How does he know their arising and ceasing?
The arising and ceasing that occur for sentient beings all depend on form for their birth; they depend on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness for their birth.
What are these various appearances and disappearances?
They are as follows: the view that "the self and the world are eternal" relies upon form, and relies upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The view that "the self and the world are impermanent," "both eternal and impermanent," or "neither eternal nor impermanent" likewise relies upon form, and relies upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

"The world is finite," "the world is infinite," "it is both finite and infinite," or "it is neither finite nor infinite"—these views depend upon form, and they depend upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

"The view that 'the self exists after death,' 'the self does not exist after death,' 'the self both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'the self neither exists nor does not exist after death'—these views depend upon form, and they depend upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
"The body is identical to the self"—this view relies upon form, and relies upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"The body is one thing and the self is another"—this view relies upon form, and relies upon feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
By means of the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows the various appearances and disappearances of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, knows the characteristics of form (*rūpa*).
How does he know the characteristics of form?
He knows them as suchness (*tathatā*).
Subhūti! The Tathāgata knows the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
How does he know the characteristic of consciousness?
One knows suchness.
Subhūti, the suchness of the five aggregates is precisely the suchness of appearance and disappearance spoken of by the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of the world; the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of all dharmas.
The suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, and the suchness of the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The suchness of the path of the pratyekabuddha is the very suchness of the Tathāgata.
All these suchnesses are a single suchness; they are without duality or distinction, inexhaustible, and immeasurable.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
It is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Tathāgata attains this mark of suchness (*tathatā*).

Thus it is, Subhūti! The *prajñāpāramitā* reveals the world to all Buddhas and is able to give birth to all Buddhas. Because the Buddhas know the suchness of the world and attain this suchness as it truly is, they are called Tathāgatas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This *tathatā* (suchness) is profoundly deep; the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas arises from this *tathatā*.”
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has attained this profound Dharma and is able to explain this suchness (tathatā) for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding such a state of suchness, who would be able to believe it?
“Only irreversible bodhisattvas, those who possess right view, and arhats whose vows are fulfilled are able to believe this, Subhūti!”
"This Suchness is inexhaustible; the Buddha has spoken of it as truly inexhaustible.

Chapter Thirteen: On Characteristics and the Absence of Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇālakṣaṇa-parivarta*) At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, together with ten thousand sons of the gods from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and twenty thousand sons of the gods from the Brahma world (*brahmaloka*), all went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This Dharma is extremely profound. Within this Dharma, how should one form mental signs?"
The Buddha told the devaputras:
"All dharmas have emptiness as their characteristic; they have non-characteristic, non-activity, non-arising, non-birth, non-extinction, and non-reliance as their characteristics."
The devaputras said:
“The Tathāgata has taught that these marks are like space, having no basis.
Such marks cannot be destroyed by any in the world—whether gods, humans, or asuras.”
Why is this? Because all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—are themselves that very characteristic.
World-Honored One!

These marks are not something that can be produced; these marks do not fall within the category of form, nor do they fall within the categories of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
These marks were not created by a person, nor were they created by a non-person.
The Buddha addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms:
"If someone were to ask:
'By whom was space created?'"
“Would this person be asking correctly?
“No, World-Honored One!
Space has no creator.”
Why is this? Because space is unconditioned.
"O sons of the gods!

These marks are also like this: whether a Buddha exists or not, they abide eternally without change. Because these marks abide eternally, once the Tathāgata has attained these marks, he is called the Tathāgata.
The sons of the gods said:

"The various marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are profoundly deep; because the wisdom of all Buddhas is unimpeded, they are able to reveal this suchness and also able to explain the characteristics of the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā."
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the sphere of activity of all Buddhas; it likewise reveals the world to all Buddhas.
“Furthermore, Subhūti!”
All Buddhas rely upon the offering of the Dharma, and they revere, respect, and praise the Dharma.
This Dharma is the Prajñāpāramitā; all Buddhas offer, revere, respect, and praise the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all Buddhas, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata is one who knows gratitude and knows how to repay it.
If someone were to ask correctly:
"Who is one who knows gratitude and knows how to repay it? [the answer would be: the Tathāgata.
One should answer:
"The Buddha is one who knows gratitude and knows how to repay it. Subhūti!
In what way is the Buddha one who knows gratitude and repays kindness?

It is because the path practiced by the Tathāgata and the Dharma practiced by him led to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he therefore protects and mindfully attends to that very path and that very Dharma.
For this reason, you should know that the Buddha is one who recognizes kindness and repays kindness.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows that all dharmas are without action; it is also because the Tathāgata knows how to repay kindness.
Subhūti! By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata knows that all dharmas have the characteristic of non-action; he has attained such wisdom.
For this reason, the prajñāpāramitā likewise reveals the world to all Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas have no knower and no seer, how does the Prajñāpāramitā reveal the world to the Buddhas?”
“Subhūti! It is so, it is so!
Of all dharmas, there is no knower and no seer.”
Subhūti! Why is it that all dharmas have no knower?
Because all dharmas are empty.
Why is it that all phenomena have no seer?
Because all phenomena lack a basis.
Therefore, all phenomena have no knower and no seer.
Subhūti! It is by means of the prajñāpāramitā that the Tathāgata has attained such dharmas.
Therefore, the prajñāpāramitā likewise reveals the world to all Buddhas.
Because they do not perceive form, they reveal the world;
because they do not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, they reveal the world.
In this way, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals the world of all Buddhas.
“World-Honored One!
Why is it called ‘revealing the world by not seeing form’?
Why is it called ‘revealing the world by not seeing feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness’?”
“Subhūti! If form does not arise conditioned by form, this is called ‘not seeing form’;
if consciousness does not arise conditioned by feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is called ‘not seeing consciousness.’”
If one does not see the world in this manner, it is called truly seeing the world.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the world is empty;
the *prajñāpāramitā* reveals the emptiness of the world as it truly is.
The world is characterized by detachment; the perfection of wisdom reveals the world as it truly is, as detached.
The world is characterized by purity; the perfection of wisdom reveals the world as it truly is, as pure.
The world is quiescent; the perfection of wisdom reveals the quiescence of the world as it truly is.
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom likewise reveals the world of all Buddhas in this same way.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the sake of a great matter; the Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the sake of an inconceivable matter, an incomparable matter, an immeasurable matter, and a matter equal to the unequaled.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
The perfection of wisdom has emerged for the sake of a great task; it has emerged for the sake of an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an immeasurable task, and a task equal to the unequaled.
Subhūti! How is it that the perfection of wisdom has arisen for the sake of a great task?
Has it arisen for the sake of an inconceivable task, an incomparable task, an immeasurable task, and a task equal to the unequaled?
Subhūti! The Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Buddha-Dharma, the self-existent Dharma, and the Dharma of the Omniscient One are vast and inconceivable, beyond all measure.
Therefore, Subhūti, it is for the sake of a great matter and an inconceivable matter that the Prajñāpāramitā has appeared.
How is it that the Prajñāpāramitā has appeared for the sake of an incomparable matter and an immeasurable matter?
Subhūti! The Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Buddha-Dharma, the Self-Existent Dharma, and the Dharma of the Omniscient One are ineffable and immeasurable. Therefore, Subhūti!
The Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the sake of that which is incalculable and immeasurable.
In what way has the Prajñāpāramitā emerged for the sake of that which is unequaled?
Subhūti! There is no one who is equal to the Tathāgata, let alone anyone who is superior. Therefore, Subhūti!
“The Prajñāpāramitā has emerged for the sake of that which is unequaled.
“World-Honored One!
Only the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Buddha-Dharma, the Self-Existent Dharma, and the Dharma of the Omniscient One are inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable;”
Form is also inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable.
“Subhūti! Form is also inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable.”
All dharmas are likewise inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is no mind and no mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Subhūti, form (*rūpa*) is ineffable; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also ineffable; indeed, all phenomena are ineffable.
Because there is no conceptual differentiation therein, Subhūti, form is immeasurable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also immeasurable; and all dharmas are likewise immeasurable.
Subhūti! Why is this?
Form is immeasurable;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are immeasurable; all dharmas are immeasurable.
Subhūti! The measure of form does not exist and cannot be apprehended;
the measure of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness does not exist and cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, all dharmas are without measure and non-existent;
they cannot be apprehended. Why is this?
The measure of form is non-existent and cannot be apprehended;
the measure of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is non-existent and cannot be apprehended;
the measure of all phenomena is non-existent and cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti! Because form does not exist, because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, and because all phenomena do not exist, no measure can be apprehended.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does space possess mind or mental factors?
"No, World-Honored One."
“Subhūti! For these reasons, all dharmas are inconceivable.
Because they extinguish all calculation and deliberation, they are called inconceivable.”
Because all designations are extinguished, it is called "inexpressible. Subhūti,
what is called a designation is precisely the karma of consciousness.
Subhūti! That which is immeasurable transcends all measures. Subhūti!
Just as space is inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable,
so too are the dharmas of all Tathāgatas, the Buddha-dharmas, the self-existent dharmas, and the dharmas of the Omniscient One— inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable.

When this inconceivable and unequaled Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus and twenty bhikṣuṇīs, through not grasping at any phenomena, exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind;
sixty thousand upāsakas and thirty thousand upāsikās attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena;
and twenty bodhisattvas attained the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and shall all attain Buddhahood within this Bhadrakalpa.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This profound Prajñāpāramitā has appeared for the sake of a great matter, even unto appearing for the sake of the matter of the unequaled.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is! Subhūti!”
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* has emerged for the sake of a great matter, even unto the matter of the peerless and unequaled.
All the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of the Buddhas is contained within the *prajñāpāramitā*;
all the stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are likewise contained within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti! It is just as when a consecrated Kṣatriya king entrusts all matters concerning the cities and all matters concerning the villages to his ministers; the king has no cause for anxiety.
In this way, Subhūti, it is so with all Tathāgatas.

All matters pertaining to śrāvakas, matters pertaining to pratyekabuddhas, and matters pertaining to Buddhas—all are contained within the Prajñāpāramitā; the Prajñāpāramitā is able to accomplish those matters.
Therefore, Subhūti,
you should know that the perfection of wisdom has appeared for the sake of a great task, even unto the task of that which is unequaled.

Subhūti! The *prajñāpāramitā* emerges because it does not accept or cling to form (*rūpa*); it emerges because it does not accept or cling to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*); it emerges because it does not accept or cling to the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha; and it emerges even because it does not accept or cling to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that the Prajñāpāramitā does not receive sarvajñatā and does not cling to sarvajñatā?”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Do you perceive any dharma of an arhat that can be accepted or clung to?
“No, World-Honored One.”
"I do not see any dharma that can give rise to attachment.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! I also do not perceive the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Because I do not perceive it, I neither accept nor cling to it.
"Therefore, Subhūti, omniscience (sarvajñā) cannot be grasped and cannot be clung to.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to understand and difficult to attain. If there are those who can believe in and understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that these persons have already made offerings to various Buddhas in previous lives.”
"Bhagavān!

If all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become practitioners of faith and cultivate the stage of faith for one kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, compared to someone who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* for a single day."
"By deliberating and reflecting, one observes that patience is penetrating and sharp; this merit is supreme.
The Buddha told the devaputras:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they will swiftly attain nirvāṇa. This person cannot be equaled by one who practices within the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) for an eon, or even slightly less than an eon."
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
Not far from there, they suddenly vanished.
The devaputras of the desire realm returned to the heavens of the desire realm, and the devaputras of the form realm returned to the heavens of the form realm.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“If a bodhisattva is able to have faith and resolve in the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, from where did such a person pass away to come and be born here?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, immediately has faith and resolves upon it, without doubt, regret, or difficulty; if they delight in seeing and delight in hearing it, constantly maintain this mindfulness, and do not depart from those who expound the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Subhūti! It is just as, for example, a newborn calf does not leave its mother;

so too is it with a bodhisattva who, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, does not leave the teacher of the Dharma until they have attained the ability to read, recite, and transcribe the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva, having passed away from among humans, will be reborn again among humans.
"World-Honored One!"

Are there any bodhisattvas who, having accomplished such causes and conditions of merit, make offerings to the Buddhas in other worlds and, upon the end of their lives there, come to be born in this realm?
“Subhūti! There are bodhisattvas who, having accomplished such merit, make offerings to the Buddhas in other worlds, and at the end of their lives there, come to be born here in this world.”

Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who, having accomplished such merits, hear the Bodhisattva Maitreya preaching the Prajñāpāramitā in the Tuṣita Heaven and inquire about its matters; they pass away from there and are reborn here in this world.
Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a person in a previous life heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā* but did not inquire about its meaning, such a person, if born among humans, will have a mind characterized by continuous doubt and regret that is difficult to resolve.
Subhūti! You should know that this person failed to inquire about this in previous lives. Why is that?
In this Prajñāpāramitā, because the mind harbors doubts and regrets that are difficult to resolve. Furthermore, Subhūti,

if a person in a previous life heard this profound Prajñāpāramitā for one day, two days, three days, four days, or five days, and inquired about its contents, yet did not act according to what was taught, that person will, upon changing bodies, continue to hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā and inquire about its contents, their faith remaining unimpeded.
If they depart from the Dharma Master and no longer engage in questioning and debate, they will again be dragged away by causes and conditions and lose the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Such is the nature of things.
If a person is able to pose difficult questions regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet is unable to practice in accordance with what has been taught;

if at times they delight in hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and at other times do not, their mind being light and fickle like fine cotton wool—one should know that this bodhisattva has newly set out in the Mahāyāna. Although this bodhisattva’s faith is pure, if they are not protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will fall into one of two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Chapter 14: The Parable of the Ship At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti: "Suppose, for example, a ship in the great ocean were suddenly wrecked.
If the people on board do not grasp onto wood, or a plank, or an air-filled bag, or a corpse, you should know that these people will not reach the other shore, but will drown and die in the water."

Subhūti! If among those people there are some who seize a wooden plank, a life-preserving float, or a corpse, you should know that these people will not drown in the water; they will reach the other shore in safety and without distress.
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva:

if, regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they possess faith, patience, delight, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence, yet do not take up the prajñāpāramitā, you should know that such a person will fall away midway and descend into the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, possesses faith, patience, delight, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, relinquishment, and diligence, they grasp the prajñāpāramitā.

Because they are protected by the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not regress on the middle way; having transcended the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, they shall abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who, carrying an unbaked earthen jar, went to a river, well, pond, or spring to fetch water; you should know that this jar will soon break apart and return to the earth.
Why is this? Because the jar has not yet been fired, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva is also like this: though they have faith in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, have patience, have delight, have a pure mind, have a profound mind, have aspiration, have understanding, have equanimity, and have diligence, because they are not protected by the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that such a person has not yet attained *sarvajñatā* and will regress midway.
Subhūti! What constitutes the regression from the middle way for a bodhisattva?
It refers to falling into the stage of a śrāvaka or falling into the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who, carrying a well-baked jar, went to a river, a well, a pond, or a spring to fetch water; you should know that this jar is firm and indestructible, and he will return carrying the water.
Why is this? Because this jar has been fired, Subhūti!
The Bodhisattva is also like this.

If they possess faith, patience, delight, a pure mind, a profound mind, aspiration, understanding, equanimity, and diligence regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and because they are protected by the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that this Bodhisattva will not regress midway but will reach *sarvajñatā* in safety and security.
“Subhūti! It is as if there were a ship in the great ocean that has not yet been repaired or prepared; it is pushed out onto the water’s edge and loaded with various goods.

You should know that this ship will leak and sink midway, causing the loss of the goods. Because these merchants lack skillful means, they lose much of their wealth and bring suffering and distress upon themselves.”
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva.

Although they possess faith up to diligence regarding anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, because they are not protected by the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, they fail to reach sarvajñatā and fall away midway, losing the great treasure and becoming distressed within themselves.
Those who lose the great precious treasure and perish midway fall into the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
"losing the great precious treasure" means losing the treasure of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

Subhūti! It is like a ship by the side of the great ocean, well-constructed and made sturdy; when it is launched into the water and laden with various goods, you should know that this ship will not sink midway, but will surely reach its destination wherever it goes.
Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva.

If they possess faith up to diligence regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they are protected by the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this bodhisattva will not regress midway from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because such is the nature of dharmas.

If a bodhisattva possesses faith in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, up to and including diligence, because they are protected by the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; rather, through these various merits, they advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! It is as if there were an old man, one hundred and twenty years of age, afflicted by various ailments—wind, cold, and heat. Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Would this person be able to rise from his bed?
"No, World-Honored One!"
“Subhūti! Such a person might at times be able to rise.
“World-Honored One!”
Even if they were able to rise, they would not be able to travel far—whether ten li or twenty li.
Why is this? Because these people have already been overcome by old age and illness; although they can rise, they cannot travel far.
“Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva.
Although they have resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and even possess diligence, [they may still regress].”

Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, although they possess faith up to diligence, because they are not protected by the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not attain *sarvajñatā* and instead regress midway, falling into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! Suppose this man of one hundred and twenty years of age were to suffer from a wind, cold, or heat-related ailment and wished to rise from his bed; and there were two strong men, each supporting one of his armpits, comforting him by saying:
"Go wherever you wish; we shall support you well, so do not fear falling midway."
"Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva.

If they possess faith up to diligence regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, because they are protected by the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, you should know that this bodhisattva will not regress midway and will be able to reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Twenty-five Thousand Lines*, Scroll Five;
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Twenty-five Thousand Lines*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
15. Chapter on the Greatness [of the Perfection of Wisdom], Chapter Fifteen.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“How should a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening train in the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom, they should first draw near to spiritual friends who are able to teach the perfection of wisdom.”
This person instructs them thus: "Good son, come!
All that you have given in alms should be dedicated toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"You, son of good family!
Do not be greedily attached even to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Whether it be form (*rūpa*), or feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
Why is this? Because this sarvajñā (omniscience) is not something to which one can become attached. Good son!
All your observance of the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom should be dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; do not give rise to attachment.
Whether it be form, or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is this? O son of good family!
Since this sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is not something to which one can become attached,
you, son of good family,
should likewise not crave or cling to the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
“Subhūti! In this way, a bodhisattva who has newly resolved his mind should be gradually taught so that he may enter the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“World-Honored One! [Subhūti said.]
When bodhisattvas resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and desire to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, what they undertake is exceedingly difficult.
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! Just as these bodhisattvas have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and desire to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, what they undertake is exceedingly difficult."

This person resolves their mind for the sake of bringing peace to the world, and resolves their mind for the sake of bringing happiness to the world, thinking: "I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
He acts as a savior for the world, a refuge for the world, a shelter for the world, the ultimate path for the world, an island for the world, a guide for the world, and a destination for the world.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva, upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, become a savior for the world?
A bodhisattva preaches the Dharma in order to sever all the sufferings and afflictions within birth and death.
They rescue sentient beings from suffering and affliction. Subhūti,
this is called a bodhisattva acting as a savior for the world when they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
How is it that when a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they become a refuge for the world?
Beings are subject to the nature of birth, the nature of old age, sickness, and death, and the nature of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

This bodhisattva is able to deliver sentient beings from this state of birth, from the states of old age, sickness, and death, and from the states of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Subhūti,
this is called a bodhisattva acting as a refuge for the world when they attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
"How does a bodhisattva, upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, become a shelter for the world? Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he teaches the Dharma because he is without attachment."
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘non-attachment’? “Subhūti!”
If form is neither bound nor liberated, neither arising nor ceasing, this is called non-attachment to form.
If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated, neither arising nor ceasing, this is called non-attachment to consciousness.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Because all dharmas are neither bound nor liberated, they are not clung to.
When a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is able to preach such dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; this is called the bodhisattva acting as a shelter for the world.
"How does a bodhisattva, upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, become the ultimate path for the world?
Subhūti, the ultimate limit of form is not called 'form'; the ultimate limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not called 'consciousness'."
"Just as it is with the ultimate characteristic, so it is with all dharmas.
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are likewise characterized by the ultimate, then all bodhisattvas should have already attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? Because within it there is no conceptual discrimination. "So it is, so it is!"
Subhūti! Within this there is no discrimination.
When bodhisattvas contemplate and understand it in this way, their minds do not sink, and they form this thought:
"When I have attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Subhūti, this is called the Bodhisattva, upon attaining unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, acting as the ultimate path for the world.
How does a bodhisattva, upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, become an island for the world?
It is like a piece of land in the midst of water where the current is cut off; this is called an island.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Form is severed at its prior limit and its posterior limit; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are severed at their prior limits and their posterior limits.
Because they are severed at their prior and posterior limits, all phenomena are entirely severed.
If all dharmas are completely severed, this is called the subtle and wondrous nirvāṇa that is true and non-perverted.
Subhūti, this is what is meant when a bodhisattva, upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, acts as an island for the world.
"How does a bodhisattva, upon attaining unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, act as a guide for the world?

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, he does not teach the Dharma for the sake of the arising and ceasing of form; rather, he teaches the Dharma solely for the sake of the true mark."

He does not preach the Dharma for the sake of the arising and ceasing of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he preaches the Dharma only for the sake of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

He does not preach the Dharma for the sake of the arising and ceasing of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, or omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); he preaches the Dharma only for the sake of the true mark.
Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva acting as a guide for the world when they attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
How does a bodhisattva act as a destination for the world when they attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment?

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they teach sentient beings that form tends toward emptiness; they teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness tend toward emptiness; all dharmas tend toward emptiness, neither coming nor going.
Why is this? Form is empty, neither coming nor going;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, neither coming nor going.
Even unto the emptiness of all dharmas, there is neither coming nor going.
Therefore, all dharmas tend toward emptiness, yet they do not go beyond this tendency;

all dharmas tend toward signlessness, toward wishlessness, toward non-arising, toward non-birth, toward non-existence, toward a dream, toward the immeasurable, toward the boundless, toward selflessness, toward tranquility, toward nirvana, and toward the non-returning, which is non-going.
"All dharmas do not transcend this destination.
"World-Honored One!
Who is able to believe in and understand such a dharma?"
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has long practiced the path under previous Buddhas and has perfected their roots of goodness, they will then be able to have faith and understanding.
“World-Honored One!”
"What are the characteristics of one who is able to have faith and understanding? "Subhūti,
the characteristic of faith and understanding is to be free from the nature of desire, hatred, and delusion."
“Such a person is able to know the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“World-Honored One!

This bodhisattva is able to understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, and likewise proceeds toward it; having attained the characteristics of this course, they are able to serve as a course for immeasurable sentient beings.”
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! This bodhisattva, proceeding in this manner, is able to serve as a refuge for immeasurable sentient beings."
“Subhūti! This is called the bodhisattva’s ability to serve as a refuge for immeasurable sentient beings when he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!”

This bodhisattva performs what is exceedingly difficult; he is able to create such a great adornment for the sake of bringing immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, yet no sentient being can be apprehended.
“Just so, just so, Subhūti! What the bodhisattva undertakes is exceedingly difficult;
for the sake of bringing immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, he puts on the great armor, yet no sentient being can be apprehended.”

Subhūti! This is the great adornment of a bodhisattva: it is not for the sake of form, nor for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is not for the sake of the stage of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, nor for the sake of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) that one undertakes this great adornment; it is not for the sake of adorning all phenomena that a bodhisattva undertakes this great adornment. It is thus that a bodhisattva undertakes the great adornment.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva can practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they will not fall into the two stages—namely, the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.”
“Subhūti! Seeing what meaning do you say such a thing:
that if a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they will not fall into the two stages—the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha?”
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is profound; herein there is no dharma to be cultivated, nothing to be cultivated, and no one who cultivates. Why is this so?”
"Bhagavān!
Within this profound prajñāpāramitā, there is no determinate dharma.
To cultivate emptiness is to cultivate prajñāpāramitā."
"Bhagavān!
Not cultivating any dharmas is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā.
Cultivating the boundless is the cultivation of the prajñāpāramitā."
"To cultivate non-attachment is to cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, one should test an irreversible bodhisattva by means of the profound perfection of wisdom."
If one does not crave or cling to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and does not harbor expectations based on the discourses of others;

and if, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one is not startled, not terrified, does not sink into despondency, and does not retreat, but instead feels joy and delight in the heart—then it should be known that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva who, in previous lives, has already heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because if, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, one is not startled, not terrified, does not sink into despair, and does not retreat, one should know that this is an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva.
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, how should they contemplate it?”
“Subhūti! This bodhisattva should contemplate the perfection of wisdom in accordance with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
“World-Honored One!”
"What is called 'contemplating in accordance with the mind of sarvajñā'? "Subhūti,
contemplating in accordance with empty space is what is called contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā in accordance with the mind of sarvajñā."
Subhūti! To contemplate in accordance with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is itself non-contemplation. Why is this?

The immeasurable is omniscience (*sarvajñā*). The immeasurable is formless; it is without feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it is without knowledge, without wisdom, without the path, without attainment, and without fruit; it is without arising, without cessation, without action, and without an agent; it is without direction, without destination, and without abiding. The immeasurable thus falls within the category of the immeasurable.
Subhūti! Just as space is immeasurable, so too is sarvajñā (all-knowledge) immeasurable.
No dharma can be apprehended, nor is there anyone who apprehends it.

It cannot be attained through form; it cannot be attained through feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; it cannot be attained through the perfection of generosity, nor through the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Form is itself omniscience (sarvajñā);
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves omniscience.
The perfection of giving is itself omniscience;
the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are themselves omniscience.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; it is difficult to understand and difficult to know.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is!
O sons of the gods!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to understand, and difficult to know.
For this reason, I wish to remain silent and not preach the Dharma, thinking thus:
"Regarding the Dharma that I have attained, within this Dharma there is no attainer; there is no Dharma to be attained, nor is there any means by which it could be attained."
"The characteristics of all dharmas are thus profoundly deep; because space is profoundly deep, these dharmas are profoundly deep.
Because I am profoundly deep, all dharmas are profoundly deep."
"Because it is neither coming nor going, it is profound; therefore, all dharmas are profound.
The devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is rare, World-Honored One!"
This Dharma that has been taught is difficult for all the world to believe.
The world practices with craving and attachment, yet this Dharma is taught for the sake of being without craving and attachment.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma accords with all dharmas.”
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
This Dharma has no locus of obstruction and possesses no characteristic of obstruction; it is like empty space.
World-Honored One!
This dharma is unarisen, because all dharmas are unattainable.
World-Honored One!
"This dharma has no location, because it cannot be apprehended in any location.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Elder Subhūti is born after the Buddha; whatever he teaches is for the sake of emptiness.
Subhūti then addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms, saying:
"Regarding what you have said—that the Elder Subhūti is born after the Buddha—"
"Because he arises in accordance with whatever dharma arises, why is he called 'born after the Buddha'?
"The sons of the gods!
Because he accords with suchness (tathatā), Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata."
Just as the Tathāgata’s suchness neither comes nor goes,
Subhūti, so too,
following that suchness, it has from the very beginning neither come nor gone.
Therefore, Subhūti, you are born after the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all dharmas;
the suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The Suchness of the Tathāgata is itself non-Suchness.
Therefore, Subhūti, you are born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Just as the Suchness of the Tathāgata is such, it is everywhere and at all times indestructible and non-conceptual.
Therefore, Subhūti, you are born after the Tathāgata.
Just as the Tathāgata’s suchness neither abides nor does not abide,
so too is Subhūti’s suchness.
Therefore, Subhūti, you are born following the Tathāgata.
Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata has no place of obstruction,
so too the suchness of all dharmas has no place of obstruction.
Therefore, Subhūti, you are born following the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of all dharmas are all a single suchness; they are non-dual and without distinction. This suchness is without action, and there is nothing that is not suchness.
If this suchness is neither suchness nor non-suchness, then for this reason it is suchness, being without duality and without distinction.
For this reason, Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the suchness of the Tathāgata is unimpaired and undifferentiated in all places.
The suchness of all dharmas is likewise neither destroyed nor differentiated.
Because the suchness of the Tathāgata is thus undifferentiable, it is without destruction or distinction.
Therefore, Subhūti is born in accordance with the Tathāgata.

As is the suchness of the Tathāgata, so is it not separate from the suchness of all phenomena; this suchness is not different from all phenomena, and there is no non-suchness within this suchness; at all times, it is eternally suchness.
It is thus, it is thus!
Subhūti, because this suchness is not different from that suchness, one accords with suchness as it truly is, and yet there is no practice of anything to be practiced.
For this reason, Subhūti, you are born after the Tathāgata.
Just as the Suchness of the Tathāgata is neither past, nor future, nor present, so too is the Suchness of all phenomena; it is likewise neither past, nor future, nor present.
Therefore, Subhūti, because he arises in accordance with Suchness, he is said to be "born after the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the Suchness of the Tathāgata;
the Suchness of the Tathāgata is the Suchness of the past.
The suchness of the past is the suchness of the Tathāgata;
the suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the future;
the suchness of the future is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of the present.
The suchness of the present is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The suchness of the past, future, and present is the suchness of the Tathāgata; they are non-dual and without distinction—the suchness of all phenomena.
Subhūti, suchness is neither dual nor differentiated.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva is born following the Tathāgata.

The suchness of a bodhisattva is the very same as the suchness at the time of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; because a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of this suchness, they are called a Tathāgata.
When the Buddha spoke these words on suchness, the earth shook in six ways.
Because of this suchness, Subhūti was born following the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Subhūti was not born following form;

he was not born following feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he was not born following the fruit of stream-entry; he was not born following the fruit of once-returning; he was not born following the fruit of non-returning; he was not born following the fruit of arhatship; and he was not born following the path of a pratyekabuddha.
"Therefore, Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This Suchness is profound.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Śāriputra! This suchness is profoundly deep.
Now, as this suchness is being taught, three thousand bhikṣus, because they do not grasp at any dharmas, have exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind.
Śāriputra! Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, amidst all dharmas, became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Five thousand devas and humans attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Six thousand bodhisattvas, not grasping at any dharmas, had their outflows exhausted and their minds attained liberation. Śāriputra!

These six thousand bodhisattvas had previously made offerings to and attended upon five hundred buddhas; under those buddhas, they practiced giving, morality, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration. Because they were not protected by the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they have now, without grasping at any dharmas, exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind.

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva practices the path of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, because they are not protected by the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, they realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and become followers of the śrāvaka vehicle.
Śāriputra!

Suppose there were a bird whose body was one hundred yojanas long, or perhaps two, three, four, five, or even five hundred yojanas long, yet its wings were not yet fully developed. It wished to come from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven down to Jambudvīpa, and so it threw itself down.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Would this bird, while midway, have this thought:
"I wish to return to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
would it be possible for me to return? "No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
The bird further made this vow:
"When I reach Jambudvīpa, will my body remain unharmed, and will I obtain my wish?
[The Buddha asked. "No, World-Honored One!"
When this bird reaches Jambudvīpa, its body will surely be injured;
it will either die or suffer near-death agony. Why is this?
"World-Honored One!
Such is the nature of things.
For although his body is already large, his wings have not yet been fully developed."
“Śāriputra, it is the same for a bodhisattva.

Although for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges they practice giving, maintain precepts, exercise patience, exert diligence, and cultivate meditative concentration; and although they give rise to the great mind and great vows, undertake immeasurable tasks, and desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—if they are not protected by the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā, they will fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva contemplates the categories of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation practiced by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, their mind still grasps at signs.

Because this bodhisattva grasps at signs and dwells on them, he does not know the various Buddhas' categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because they do not know and do not see, upon hearing the mere names of the emptiness of all dharmas, they grasp at the characteristics of those sounds and dedicate [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
You should know that this bodhisattva has fallen into the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
"It is because a bodhisattva is separated from the perfection of wisdom that such is the nature of things.
"World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva is separated from the perfection of wisdom, they will harbor doubts regarding unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment and will not attain certainty."
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should skillfully practice the skillful means of the prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, and Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain."
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is!
O sons of the gods!”
"The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"As the Buddha has taught, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound and Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain.
Yet, according to my understanding of the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is easy to attain."
Why is this? Because no dharma can be apprehended; within the emptiness of all dharmas, there is no one who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
No dharma can be apprehended, nor can any dharma used for attainment be apprehended, because all dharmas are empty.
"Whatever dharmas are taught for the sake of what is to be abandoned, those dharmas are also empty.
World-Honored One!
