The dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the dharma used by one who attains it, and the dharma used by one who realizes it—all such dharmas are empty."
World-Honored One!
For these reasons, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is easily attained.
All things that can be attained are identical to empty space.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment were easy to attain, then the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not fall back."
"For this reason, you should know that Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is difficult to attain. "Śāriputra,
what do you think?"
“Does form regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “No, Subhūti. “Śāriputra!”
"Do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment? "No, Subhūti."
“Śāriputra, apart from form, is there any dharma that can be found which regresses from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “No, Subhūti.”
“Śāriputra, apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that can be found which regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?”
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, does the suchness of form ever regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, does the suchness (tathatā) of feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness ever regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, apart from the suchness of form,
is there any dharma that can be found which regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, apart from the suchness of feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that can be found which would fall back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, apart from the suchness of all phenomena,
is there any dharma that can be found which regresses from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, since such a thing cannot be found when sought in reality, what dharma could there be that would regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
“Śāriputra!
There is no dharma that regresses from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra said:
"According to the meaning of what Subhūti has said, there would be no bodhisattvas who regress.
If that were so, then the Buddha’s teaching of the three vehicles would have no distinction."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:
"You should ask Subhūti: 'Do you wish for there to be even a single vehicle of the bodhisattvas?'"
Śāriputra then asked Subhūti:
"Do you wish for there to be a single vehicle of the bodhisattvas?
Subhūti replied:
“Could there be three types of persons within this [emptiness], namely:
those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Buddha vehicle? “Subhūti!...”
"Just as there are no distinctions among the three marks within [emptiness], Śāriputra,
is there even one mark?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, within suchness,
do you see even a single person of the One Vehicle?"
"No, Subhūti! Śāriputra, when sought in this way according to reality, this dharma cannot be apprehended."
Why do you entertain such thoughts as:
"This is the Śrāvaka vehicle, this is the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and this is the Buddha vehicle"?
These three vehicles are, in their essence, without distinction.
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing these matters, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, one should know that this bodhisattva is able to accomplish awakening.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
All that you delight in expounding is through the power of the Buddha.
That is to say, within suchness, there is no distinction among those who seek the three vehicles.
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this matter, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, you should know that this bodhisattva is able to accomplish bodhi.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what kind of bodhi does this bodhisattva accomplish?”
“Śāriputra! This bodhisattva accomplishes unsurpassed awakening.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should they practice?
The Buddha said:

"Regarding all sentient beings, one should practice an even mind, a mind of loving-kindness, a non-discriminatory mind, a humble mind, a peaceful mind, a non-angry mind, a non-afflictive mind, a non-mocking mind, a mind like that of a parent, and a mind like that of a brother, and engage in conversation with them."
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva wishes to accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should train in this way and practice in this way.
Chapter 16: The Marks of the Avaivartika. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Sixteen: The Marks of the Avaivartika. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What are the characteristics of an irreversible bodhisattva?
How should I know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"All stages—the stage of ordinary beings, the stage of śrāvakas, the stage of pratyekabuddhas, and the stage of Tathāgatas—these various stages are, within suchness, undifferentiated, non-dual, and not distinct."

The bodhisattva, by means of this suchness, enters into the true reality of all phenomena; yet they do not discriminate, thinking, "This is suchness" or "This is the characteristic of suchness. Following along with this suchness, they enter into the true reality of all phenomena.
Having emerged from this suchness, one hears further teachings;
without doubt or regret, and without declaring them right or wrong, one sees that all dharmas enter into suchness.
Whatever this bodhisattva speaks, it is never for the sake of that which is unbeneficial.
His words are invariably beneficial, and he does not observe the long and short of others. Subhūti!
By these characteristics, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an avaivartika bodhisattva does not rely on the discourses of non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; he knows truly and sees truly.
Furthermore, Subhūti, an avaivartika bodhisattva does not pay homage to other devas, nor does he offer them flowers or incense.
By these characteristics, Subhūti, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
An irreversible bodhisattva never falls into the three evil realms, nor does he receive a female body. Subhūti!"
By these characteristics, one should know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an *avaivartika* bodhisattva does not kill living beings himself, nor does he instruct others to kill; he does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not use double-tongued speech, does not use harsh words, and does not engage in idle chatter; he is not covetous, not malicious, and not held by wrong views; nor does he instruct others to practice wrong views.
Regarding these ten paths of wholesome action, he constantly practices them himself and also teaches others to practice them.
This bodhisattva does not engage in the ten unwholesome paths even in his dreams; indeed, even in his dreams, he constantly practices the ten paths of wholesome action.
Subhūti! By these characteristics, one should know that a bodhisattva is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Regarding the sūtras that one recites and studies, one should form this thought:
"Desiring to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, I shall preach the Dharma for them;
through this gift of Dharma, may their aspirations be fulfilled in accordance with the Dharma."
"By means of this Dharma-gift, one shares it with all sentient beings.
Subhūti! By these characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when an avaivartika bodhisattva hears the profound Dharma, his mind is free from doubt or regret; he is measured in speech and gentle in tone; he sleeps little; whether coming or going, his mind is always undisturbed; his movements are not hurried or rash; he always maintains a single-pointed mind, walking with a calm and steady gait, looking at the ground as he proceeds."
Subhūti! By such characteristics as these, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

The irreversible bodhisattva’s clothing and bedding are free from defilement; they always delight in purity, are fully endowed with dignified deportment, and their body is constantly at ease and secure, with little illness.
Subhūti! Within the body of an ordinary person there are eighty thousand families of worms; within the body of an avaivartika bodhisattva, such worms do not exist.
Why is this? Subhūti,
because these roots of goodness of the bodhisattva transcend the world, and as those roots of goodness increase, they attain purity of mind and purity of body.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what constitutes the purity of a bodhisattva’s mind?"
“Subhūti! As a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness increase, flattery, crookedness, and deceit gradually perish of their own accord; because they have perished, the mind becomes pure.”
Because their minds are pure, they are able to transcend the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; this is called the purity of the bodhisattva’s mind.
Subhūti, by these characteristics, you should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
An avaivartika bodhisattva does not crave gain or offerings and has little stinginess or envy.
When hearing the profound Dharma, his mind does not sink; because his wisdom is deep, he listens to the Dharma with a single-minded focus."
Whatever dharmas they hear, all accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
By means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, all worldly affairs are identical to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); they do not perceive any matter of livelihood that does not accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti! By these characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If an evil Māra comes to the bodhisattva and transforms himself into eight great hells,
and within each hell he transforms himself into hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas, saying these words:
"The Buddha has bestowed upon all these bodhisattvas the prediction of *avaivartika* [irreversibility]."
Now you have fallen into this great hell; if you were to receive the prediction of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), you would simultaneously receive the prediction of hell.
If you can now repent of this mind, you shall not fall into hell, but shall instead be born in the heavens.
If this bodhisattva hears these words, their mind remains unmoved and free from anger, and they think:
"It is impossible for an avaivartika bodhisattva to fall into the evil realms."
"Subhūti! By these signs and characteristics, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a wicked Māra transforms himself into a śramaṇa and approaches the bodhisattva, saying these words:
"That which you have previously heard, recited, and studied, you ought to repent and abandon."
If you abandon [this teaching] and no longer listen or accept it, I shall constantly come to your presence;
what you have heard was not spoken by the Buddha, but is all merely words of ornamental embellishment.
"The sūtras I have spoken are truly the words of the Buddha.

If, upon hearing these words, their mind is moved by anger or resentment, you should know that this bodhisattva has not yet received a prediction from the Buddhas; they are not a bodhisattva of fixed destiny, nor do they abide within the nature of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva.

Subhūti! Upon hearing these matters, one’s mind remains unmoved and free from anger; rather, relying solely on the characteristics of all phenomena—which are without birth, without action, and without arising—one does not follow the words of others.

Subhūti, just as an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted directly realizes the characteristics of all phenomena, and because these phenomena are unarisen and non-originated, he cannot be obstructed by Māra. Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva is likewise; that which cannot be broken by those seeking the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, he does not regress from, but will certainly reach *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), abiding within the nature of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and no longer following the words of others.
Subhūti! By these characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
If an evil Māra comes to where the bodhisattva is and says this:
"What you are practicing is the practice of birth and death, not the practice of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
You should now, within this very body, bring an end to suffering and attain *nirvāṇa*."

"If one can act in this way, then one will no longer undergo the various sufferings of birth and death; since even the arising of this present body cannot be found, how much less could one desire to receive a future body?
When a bodhisattva hears these words, their mind remains unmoved and free from anger.
The evil Māra spoke again, saying:

"You now wish to see all these bodhisattvas making offerings—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; and you wish to see them practicing the holy life under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, drawing near to them to seek instruction."
For the sake of those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, he raised many questions and inquiries:
"How should a bodhisattva dwell?
How should a bodhisattva practice?"
These bodhisattvas, in the presence of the Buddhas, were able to practice all matters according to what they heard.

Even though they taught in this way, studied in this way, and practiced in this way, they were still unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and did not abide in *sarvajñā*. How much less could you possibly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
If this bodhisattva hears these words, their mind remains unmoved and free from anger.
At that moment, Māra the Evil One again transforms himself into various bhikṣus and says:

"These bhikṣus have all exhausted their outflows and are arhats. Previously, they all resolved their minds on seeking the Buddha-way, yet now they all abide in the stage of an arhat; how much less, then, can you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
If a bodhisattva thinks:
"I have heard this from another; thus I shall not lose anything," and if his mind does not waver and no contrary thoughts arise, such is the work of Māra.
If a bodhisattva practices the perfections in this way and trains in the perfections in this way, it is impossible that they should not attain sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, as the Buddhas have taught, trains according to what they have heard and practices according to what they have heard, and does not depart from this path nor depart from the mindfulness of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), it is impossible that they should not attain *sarvajñā*."
Subhūti! By these characteristics, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If an evil Māra comes to an avaivartika bodhisattva and says:
"All-knowledge (sarvajñatā) is identical to empty space; these dharmas do not exist, and there is no person who attains the Way by means of these dharmas."

Why is this? If one attains the Way, one attains the Dharma of the Way; all dharmas employed for attainment are like empty space. The knower knows the Dharma, and the dharmas employed for knowing are non-existent and identical to empty space. You have suffered in vain.
If it is said that attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is itself the work of Māra and not what was taught by the Buddha,
then a bodhisattva should reflect upon this as follows:
"If anyone reviles me and seeks to cause me to depart from *sarvajñatā*, that is the work of Māra."
"In these matters, one should give rise to a firm mind, an unshakable mind, and an irreversible mind. Subhūti,
by these characteristics, you should know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
if an avaivartika bodhisattva wishes to enter the first dhyāna, the second, the third, or the fourth dhyāna, his mind becomes increasingly trained and disciplined."
Although this bodhisattva enters the various dhyānas, he returns to take up the dharmas of the desire realm and is not reborn according to those dhyānas.
Subhūti, by these signs,
one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, the mind of an avaivartika bodhisattva does not crave fame or praise; toward all sentient beings, his mind is free from anger and obstruction, and he constantly gives rise to a mind of peace, security, and benefit."
In their coming and going, they remain undistracted, always maintaining a single-pointed mind and never losing their dignified deportment.
Subhūti, if such a bodhisattva lives as a householder, they do not become stained by or attached to various sensual desires.
Regarding all the sensual desires they experience, their minds give rise to weary detachment and they constantly harbor fear.
It is like a perilous road filled with many bandits and dangers;
although there is food to eat, they feel weary detachment and fear, their minds find no peace, and they think only of when they will pass through this dangerous path.

Although an avaivartika bodhisattva may live as a householder, they perceive all the various sensual desires as faults and evils; their minds do not crave or cherish them, nor do they sustain themselves through wrong livelihood or unrighteous means.
One would rather lose one's own body and life than encroach upon others.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva dwelling at home should bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; even while remaining a householder, they are able to accomplish such meritorious virtues.
Why is this? Because they have attained the power of the Prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti!
By these signs, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Vajrapāṇi spirit constantly follows and attends upon the avaivartika bodhisattva, not allowing non-human beings to approach him.
This bodhisattva’s mind is free from derangement; his faculties are complete and without deficiency; he cultivates noble and virtuous conduct, never failing in such virtue.
He does not use incantations or medicinal herbs to entice women.
He does not act for his own sake, nor does he instruct others to do so.
This bodhisattva constantly cultivates a pure livelihood; he does not practice divination for good or bad fortune, nor does he predict for others whether they will give birth to a son or a daughter.
All such matters as these he does not engage in.
Subhūti, by these characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!
There are further characteristics of an irreversible bodhisattva which I shall now explain. Subhūti!"

An avaivartika bodhisattva does not delight in speaking of miscellaneous worldly matters, matters of government, matters of warfare, matters of bandits, matters of cities and villages, or matters concerning elephants, horses, chariots, clothing, food and drink, and bedding; he does not delight in speaking of flowers, perfumes, women, or courtesans; he does not delight in speaking of tortoises, nor of the great ocean, nor of matters that cause affliction to others.
They do not delight in discoursing on various worldly matters, but delight only in discoursing on the *prajñāpāramitā*.
They are never separated from the mind that corresponds to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and they do not delight in strife or litigation;
their minds always delight in the Dharma and do not delight in what is contrary to the Dharma.
One should delight in spiritual friends and not delight in enemies;
one should delight in reconciling disputes and not delight in slandering others;
one should delight in the Buddha-dharma and leave the household life.
They always delight in being born in other pure Buddha-lands, with mastery according to their will.
In whatever place they are born, they constantly obtain offerings to all Buddhas. Subhūti!

An avaivartika bodhisattva, having frequently passed away from the desire realm or the form realm, is reborn in a central land; they are skilled in the arts and proficient in understanding the scriptures.
He fully understands all incantations and physiognomy.
He may be born in a remote region;
yet even if born in a remote region, he will surely be in a great kingdom.
If one possesses such qualities and characteristics, it should be known that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
an *avaivartika* bodhisattva does not form such thoughts:"
"I am an avaivartika, yet I am not an avaivartika"—
Subhūti, such a doubt does not arise.
One who has personally realized the stage of *avaivartika* will never again harbor doubt.
Just as one who has realized the Dharma of a *srotāpanna* has no doubt in their mind regarding that realization and is able to perceive all manner of demonic activities, so it is here.
Having awakened, one does not follow [delusion].
The Bodhisattva is also like this:
within the stage of *avaivartika*, their mind has no doubt.
They are able to awaken to all manner of demonic activities.
Having awakened to them, they do not follow them. Subhūti!
For example, suppose a person has committed a heinous crime; their mind is constantly filled with remorse and fear, which they do not abandon until death.
Being unable to distance themselves from such a sinful mind, it constantly follows that mind until the end of life.
Subhūti! It is the same for an avaivartika bodhisattva.

The mind of an avaivartika bodhisattva always dwells securely within the stage of avaivartika, remaining immovable; they are able to recognize all the various demonic activities that might be attempted to destroy them by the devas, humans, and asuras of all worlds.
Having awakened, he does not follow [dualistic views].
Within the Dharma he has realized, his mind is resolute and free from all doubt.
Even when changing bodies, he does not give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; nor, upon changing bodies, does he doubt that he will not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Within the Dharma realized through one's own self-attestation, one does not follow others.
Abiding in the stage of self-realization, it cannot be destroyed. Why is this?
Because they have accomplished indestructible wisdom, they abide in the nature of *avaivartika*. Subhūti!
If a wicked Māra were to manifest in the form of a Buddha and approach an *avaivartika* bodhisattva, saying these words:
"Good son! Within this very body, you may realize arhatship; what need is there for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Why is this?"
"A Bodhisattva has achieved the marks for attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereas you do not possess these marks.
Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva hears these words, their mind remains unmoved and unaltered, and they immediately form this thought:
"If this is an evil Māra, or one sent by Māra, it was not spoken by the Buddha.
If it were spoken by the Buddha, it could not be otherwise.
If a bodhisattva can reflect in this way:
"This is Māra who has transformed his body into that of a Buddha, wishing to cause me to distance myself from the Prajñāpāramitā.

If Māra then withdraws and disappears, one should know that this bodhisattva has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from previous Buddhas and dwells securely within the stage of *avaivartika*.
Why is this? Because such a person possesses the marks of an *avaivartika*. Subhūti!
By these signs, one should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, an avaivartika bodhisattva,
for the sake of protecting the Dharma, does not spare his own body or life."
For the sake of the true Dharma, they practice diligence with this thought:
"I shall not only protect the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the past and present, but I shall also protect the true Dharma of the Buddhas in future ages."
"I too shall be included among those in the future who receive the prediction [of enlightenment], and I shall personally protect the Dharma.
Because this bodhisattva perceives such benefits, he protects the True Dharma, even at the cost of his own body and life; his mind does not sink nor does it feel regret.
Subhūti! By these characteristics, you should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
"When an avaivartika bodhisattva hears the Dharma being taught by the Tathāgata, their mind has no doubt.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When this bodhisattva hears the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, does his mind have no doubts?
Or does it likewise have no doubts when he hears śrāvakas preaching the Dharma? "Subhūti! [The Buddha said:]
When this bodhisattva hears the Dharma from śrāvakas, he likewise has no doubts.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has attained the forbearance of the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva has accomplished such marks and characteristics of merit, you should know that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
— *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in Twenty-five Thousand Lines*, Scroll Six.
The Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom in Small Sections, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Seventeen: On Profound Merit. Chapter Seventeen: On Profound Merit.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
This non-retrogressive bodhisattva has accomplished great merit.”
The World-Honored One is able to explain the characteristics of irreversible bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To explain these characteristics is to explain the characteristics of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"You are able to demonstrate to the bodhisattvas the mark of profundity. Subhūti!

That which is the mark of profundity is the meaning of emptiness; it is the signless, the unconditioned, the unarisen, the unborn, the undestroyed, the non-existent, the unstained, the quiescent, and the meaning of nirvāṇa as far removed [from all phenomena]."
“World-Honored One!
Is it only the meaning of emptiness, up to and including the meaning of nirvāṇa, that is not the meaning of all dharmas? “Subhūti!
All dharmas are also of profound meaning. Why is this? Subhūti!
Form is profound; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are profound.
In what way is form profound? It is profound in the same way that suchness is profound.
In what way are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness profound? They are profound in the same way that suchness is profound.
Subhūti! That form is non-existent is the profound depth of form;
that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent is the profound depth of consciousness.
Subhūti said: “It is rare, World-Honored One!
By means of subtle and wondrous skillful means, you conceal form to reveal nirvāṇa; you conceal feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to reveal nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva can contemplate and examine this profound prajñāpāramitā, thinking:
'In accordance with the teaching of the prajñāpāramitā, I should train in this way;'"
As it is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā, "I should practice in this manner.
When a bodhisattva contemplates and cultivates in this way for even a single day, the merit they produce is immeasurable.
Subhūti! It is, for example, like a person of great desire who has many sensual thoughts and makes an appointment with a beautiful woman.
Because this woman is detained by an obstacle, she misses the appointment and does not arrive.
Subhūti, what do you think?
With what phenomena is this person of great desire associated when they experience thoughts of desire?
“World-Honored One!

This person of great desire merely gives rise to thoughts associated with sensual desire, recollecting and imagining this woman, thinking: ‘It will not be long before I shall sit, lie down, and play with her in laughter.’”
“Subhūti, what do you think?
How many thoughts of desire does such a person give rise to in one day and one night?”
“World-Honored One!
This person gives rise to thoughts very many times in one day and one night. “Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva contemplates and studies according to the teachings of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will be free from the faults and evils of regression and abandon the hardships of birth and death throughout many kalpas.

The merit produced by this bodhisattva in a single day through practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* surpasses the merit of a bodhisattva who, having distanced themselves from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practices giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were apart from the perfection of wisdom and were to make offerings for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas—what do you think? Would their merit be great?
Subhūti said: "Very many, World-Honored One!
They are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable."
The Buddha said:
“It is not as great as the merit of a bodhisattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as taught, even for a single day; that merit is exceedingly vast.”

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to transcend the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, enter the rank of a bodhisattva, and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practices giving, upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom while separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, what do you think? Would their merit be great?
Subhūti said, “Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious as when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* according to its teaching for even a single day, practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; the latter's merit is far greater."
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva,

for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were to practice the gift of Dharma to sentient beings while remaining apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, what do you think— would their merit be great?
Subhūti said: “Very much, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as a bodhisattva who, regarding the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, practices according to the teaching for even a single day, bestowing the gift of Dharma upon sentient beings; the merit of this is exceedingly great."
Why is this? If a bodhisattva does not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not depart from *sarvajñatā*.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while separated from the perfection of wisdom, what do you think—would their merit be great?
Subhūti said, “Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as a bodhisattva dwelling according to the teachings of the Prajñāpāramitā for even a single day, practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the merit of the latter is far greater."
Why is this? It is impossible for a bodhisattva who does not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā* to fall away from *sarvajñatā*.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, were apart from the prajñāpāramitā and dedicated to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment the merit of such material gifts, Dharma gifts, and meditative concentrations—what do you think? Would that merit be great?
Subhūti said: “It is very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as meritorious as when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as it has been taught, even for a single day; by dedicating the merit of their material gifts, Dharma gifts, and meditative concentration toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their merit is exceedingly great."
"Why is this? Because this is the foremost dedication, namely, not being separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, all phenomena that arise through action are merely conceptualizations and discriminations.
How then can it be said that a bodhisattva acquires a vast amount of merit?”
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they are also able to observe that these produced merits are empty and non-existent, deceptive and unreal, and lack any mark of solidity.”
If a bodhisattva contemplates according to their capacity, they will not be separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
By not being separated from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately attain immeasurable, incalculable merit.
“World-Honored One!
What is the distinction between ‘immeasurable’ (apramāṇa) and ‘incalculable’ (asaṃkhyeya)? “Subhūti!”
" 'Asaṃkhyeya' means that which cannot be fully enumerated.
'Immeasurable' means exceeding all measures and numbers.
"World-Honored One!"
“Is there any cause or condition by which form is also immeasurable, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also immeasurable?
The Buddha said, “There is.”
“Subhūti, form is also immeasurable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also immeasurable.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
"What is the meaning of 'immeasurable'?
"Subhūti, 'immeasurable' means emptiness; it means signlessness and wishlessness."
“World-Honored One!
Is ‘immeasurable’ merely a synonym for emptiness, and not any other meaning? “Subhūti!
"What do you think? Do I not say that all dharmas are empty?
"The World-Honored One has said so. "Subhūti!"
If emptiness is itself inexhaustible, and if emptiness is itself immeasurable,
then within the meaning of this Dharma there is no distinction. Subhūti!

That which the Tathāgata has taught—the inexhaustible and the immeasurable, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-origination, non-extinction, non-existence, and the undefiled nirvāṇa—is spoken of only by means of names and skillful expedients.
Subhūti said: “It is rare, World-Honored One!
The true mark of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words, yet now it is being explained.”
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are ineffable. “So it is, so it is!”
Subhūti! All dharmas are ineffable. Subhūti!
"All dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness; they cannot be spoken of.
"World-Honored One!
This meaning that cannot be spoken of neither increases nor decreases."
If that were so, then the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) would likewise have neither increase nor decrease;

the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) would also have neither increase nor decrease.

If these perfections neither increase nor decrease, how can a bodhisattva, by means of these perfections that neither increase nor decrease, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva increases or decreases the various pāramitās, they will not be able to draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. “It is so, it is so!”
Subhūti! The meaning that is ineffable neither increases nor decreases.
When a bodhisattva who skillfully understands expedient means practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such a thought:
"Whether the dānapāramitā increases or decreases," he reflects:
"This dānapāramitā exists as a mere name."
"When this bodhisattva practices giving, they dedicate this mindfulness, this mind, and all roots of goodness in accordance with the characteristics of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva who is well-versed in skillful means practices and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such thoughts as:
"The perfection of ethical discipline is increasing or decreasing."
"...the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation, whether they increase or decrease. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva who is well-versed in skillful means practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, he does not form such a thought:
"If the Prajñāpāramitā increases or decreases," he thinks,
"the Prajñāpāramitā exists as nothing more than a name."
"When cultivating wisdom, one should dedicate this mindfulness, this mind, and these roots of goodness in accordance with the characteristics of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is this 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'?
"Subhūti, anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is precisely suchness (tathatā), which neither increases nor decreases."
If a bodhisattva constantly practices in accordance with such mindfulness, they will draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus, Subhūti, although the ineffable meaning neither increases nor decreases, one does not retreat from these various thoughts, nor does one retreat from the various pāramitās.
When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and do not regress from the bodhisattva practice.
One who forms such a thought draws near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Honored One!
The preceding mind of a bodhisattva is close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the subsequent mind is also close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
World-Honored One!
The preceding mind and the succeeding mind do not coexist with one another;
likewise, the succeeding mind and the preceding mind also do not coexist with one another.
“World-Honored One!
If the preceding mind and the succeeding mind do not coexist, how can the bodhisattva’s various roots of goodness increase? “Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
When a lamp is lit, is it the initial flame that burns the wick, or is it the final flame?
"World-Honored One!"
"It is not burned by the first flame, yet it is not apart from the first flame;
it is not burned by the last flame, yet it is not apart from the last flame. "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Does this wick burn?
"World-Honored One!"
"This wick is indeed burning.
"Subhūti, it is the same with the bodhisattva."
One does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial mind, yet it is not apart from the initial mind;
one does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the final mind, yet it is not apart from the final mind that it is attained.
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma of causes and conditions is profound.
A bodhisattva does not attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment by means of the initial mind, nor do they attain it apart from the initial mind.”
One does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the final thought-moment, nor is one detached from the final thought-moment when attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Subhūti, what do you think?
If a mind has already ceased, does that mind arise again?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti,
what do you think?"
“Is the arising of the mind a characteristic of cessation?
“World-Honored One,
it is a characteristic of cessation.”
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Is this mark of cessation a dharma that should cease?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti,
what do you think?"
"Does it likewise abide thus, abiding in suchness?
"World-Honored One,
it likewise abides thus, abiding in suchness."
“Subhūti! If one abides in this way, abiding in suchness (tathatā), is that then permanence?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Is this Suchness profound?”
“World-Honored One!
This Suchness is profound. “Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Is this suchness the mind?
"No, World-Honored One."
“Subhūti, are you free from such a mind?
“No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti, do you perceive suchness? “No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti, what do you think?
If a person practices in this way, is it a profound practice?”
“World-Honored One!
If a person practices in this way, it is practicing without a locus. Why is this? Because...”
"This person does not engage in any conditioned activities. "Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, in what does he practice?"
“World-Honored One!
One practices within the ultimate truth. “Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
If a bodhisattva practices within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), does that person practice with signs (nimitta)?
"No, World-Honored One!"
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Does this bodhisattva destroy all marks?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti,
what do you think?"
"How does a bodhisattva destroy all marks?
"World-Honored One, this bodhisattva does not train in this way: 'I am practicing the bodhisattva path; within this body, I shall sever all marks.'"
If one were to sever these marks but had not yet fulfilled the path to Buddhahood, one would become a śrāvaka.
World-Honored One!
This is the power of the bodhisattva’s great skillful means: knowing the faults of these marks, they do not grasp at the markless.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva practices the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—in a dream, does this increase the perfection of wisdom?"
If there is an increase during the daytime, there should likewise be an increase within dreams. Why?
Because the Buddha has taught that day and night, as well as dreams, are equal and without distinction.
“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva cultivates the perfection of wisdom, then the perfection of wisdom truly exists.
For this reason, even within a dream, one should increase the perfection of wisdom.”
Śāriputra! If a person performs an action within a dream, does that action have a karmic retribution?
The Buddha has taught that all phenomena are like dreams; therefore, there should be no karmic retribution.
If there were retribution for conceptualizing after awakening,
Śāriputra, then if a person were to kill a living being in a dream and, upon waking, were to conceptualize, "It was a pleasure that I killed," [they would incur retribution].
"What is this karma? "Subhūti! Where there are no conditions, there is no karma;
where there are no conditions, volition does not arise."
“In this way, Śāriputra, when there is no object-condition, there is no karma; when there is no object-condition, volition does not arise.
When there is an object-condition, there is karma; when there is an object-condition, volition arises.”
If the mind operates within the phenomena of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, there are instances where the mind undergoes defilement and instances where it undergoes purification.
Therefore, Śāriputra, karma arises from causes and conditions; it does not arise without causes and conditions.
“Thought arises from causes and conditions; it does not arise without causes and conditions.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti, “If a bodhisattva, while dreaming, practices giving and dedicates it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, is that giving called a dedication?”
“Śāriputra! The Bodhisattva Maitreya is currently seated here; the Buddha has granted him the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You may question him, and Maitreya shall answer.”
Śāriputra then asked Maitreya Bodhisattva:
“Subhūti has said:
‘Maitreya, you should answer this matter.’”
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:
"Regarding what was said— that Maitreya should answer— Śāriputra!"
Now, do you answer by means of the name "Maitreya"?
Or do you answer by means of form?
Or do you answer by means of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness?
If you answer by means of the emptiness of form?
Or the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
This emptiness of form cannot answer; this emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness cannot answer.

Śāriputra! I do not perceive any dharma that is able to provide an answer; nor do I perceive an answerer, the person being answered, the means by which one answers, or the dharma that is to be answered.
"I also do not see any dharma that receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Regarding the dharma as it has been taught, have you realized this dharma?"
Maitreya said,
"I have not realized anything by following the teachings as they were spoken.
Śāriputra then had this thought:
“Maitreya Bodhisattva’s wisdom is profoundly deep, for he has practiced the Prajñāpāramitā throughout the long night.
At that time, the Buddha, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, said to Śāriputra:
“What do you think?”
"Do you see this dharma by which you have attained arhatship?
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
The Bodhisattva likewise practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this way; because he possesses skillful means, he does not form the thought:
"This dharma receives the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Those who have already received the prediction, those who are receiving it now, and those who will receive it in the future—
if a bodhisattva practices in this way, he is practicing the perfection of wisdom and has no fear that he will not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"I shall practice with diligent perseverance and will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva should always be neither startled nor terrified."
If one finds oneself among fierce beasts, one should not be terrified. Why is this?
A bodhisattva should form this thought:
"If I am now devoured by these evil beasts, I shall give myself as an offering.
By means of this perfection of dāna-pāramitā, may I draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
I shall thus practice with diligent perseverance and attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
at that time, within that world, there will be no realm of animals whatsoever.
"If a bodhisattva finds himself among enemies and bandits, he should not be terrified. Why is this?
Because it is not the dharma of a bodhisattva to cherish his own body or life; he should form this thought:"
“If there should be one who takes my life, I should not give rise to anger toward them.
By means of fulfilling the pāramitā of kṣānti, I shall draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"I should thus practice with diligent vigor so as to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, within the world, there shall be no enemies, bandits, or any malevolent thieves."
"If a bodhisattva finds himself in a place without water, he should not be alarmed or terrified, but should instead think:
'I ought to preach the Dharma for all sentient beings to eliminate their thirst.'"
"If I should die from thirst and exhaustion, I should think:
'It is because these sentient beings lack merit that they are in this place where there is no water.
I must thus practice with diligent vigor so as to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
At that time, in places within the world where there was no water, he also caused sentient beings to practice with diligent vigor and cultivate various merits;
then, within the world, the water of eight virtues appeared spontaneously.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva finds himself in the midst of a famine, he should not be alarmed or terrified, but should form this thought:
'I must practice with such diligent vigor that I may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

At that time, within that world, there was no such affliction as famine; it was fully endowed with happiness, and whatever was required according to one's wishes would arrive the very moment it was thought of.
"Just as in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whatever one thinks of is obtained.
If a bodhisattva is thus neither startled nor terrified, it should be known that this bodhisattva is able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva finds himself in a place of pestilence,
he should not be terrified. Why is that?
Because there is no dharma herein that can be afflicted by illness, I should thus practice with diligent vigor to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, among all sentient beings in the world, there shall be no threefold illnesses; I shall practice with diligent vigor, following the conduct of all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva reflects that anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi will only be attained after a long time, they should not be terrified."

Why is this? Since the prior limit of the world has been as brief as a single moment of thought, one should not conceive the notion of long duration, nor should one consider the prior limit to be something remote.
Although the past limit is exceedingly remote, it is nonetheless identical with a single thought-moment. Thus, Śāriputra,
even if a bodhisattva takes a long time to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should not be startled, terrified, or fall back.

Chapter 18: Gaṅgadevā The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, Chapter Eighteen: Gaṅgadevā. At that time, there was a woman in the assembly named Gaṅgadevā who rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Regarding this matter, I am neither startled nor terrified.
In future ages as well, I shall expound this essential teaching for the sake of sentient beings.
He then took golden flowers and scattered them over the Buddha; they remained suspended in mid-air above the Buddha’s crown.
At that time, the Buddha smiled.
Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what cause and for what reason do you smile?
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that they do not smile without a cause or condition.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This woman Gaṅgadevā shall, in a future age during the Constellation Kalpa, attain Buddhahood under the name Suvarṇapuṣpa.
Now she shall transform her female body to become a man and be born in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhya."
In the presence of those Buddhas, he constantly practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
After his life ended, he went from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field, constantly practicing the holy life until he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never being separated from the Buddhas.
Just as a wheel-turning sage king, from one palace to another, from birth until the end of his life, never sets foot upon the ground; Ānanda,
this woman is also like this.
From one buddha-field to another buddha-field, they constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never being separated from a Buddha.
Ānanda had this thought:
"At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas was like the assemblies of the Buddhas.
The Buddha, knowing the thought in Ānanda’s mind, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"So it is, so it is! You should know that at that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas was like the assemblies of all the Buddhas. Ānanda!"
In this world of the Buddha Golden Flower, the śrāvakas who have entered nirvāṇa are immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation.
Within that world, there are no calamities from wild beasts or hostile bandits, nor are there the afflictions of famine or disease.
"Ānanda!
When that Buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there shall be no such calamities of fear.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where did this woman first plant the roots of goodness for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
“Ānanda! [the Buddha replied.]
This woman first planted roots of goodness in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
by means of these roots of goodness, she dedicated them toward anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I also took golden flowers and scattered them over Dīpaṃkara Buddha, seeking anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Ānanda!
At that time, I scattered five stalks of flowers over Dīpaṃkara Buddha, seeking anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Dīpaṃkara Buddha, knowing that my roots of goodness were pure and mature, immediately bestowed upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, when this woman heard that I had received the prediction, she made a vow, saying:
"May I also be like this, and in a future age, receive such a prediction."
"Now this person has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Ānanda!
This person first planted roots of goodness and gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Has this person long practiced the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said: "So it is, Ānanda!"
"This person has long practiced the conduct of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“If a bodhisattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, how should they cultivate emptiness?
How should they enter the samādhi of emptiness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate that form is empty; they should contemplate that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.
With an undistracted mind, they should contemplate all phenomena as being without anything to be seen and without anything to be realized.”
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, a bodhisattva should not realize emptiness."
"How does a bodhisattva enter the samādhi of emptiness without realizing emptiness?

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva fully contemplates emptiness, having already generated the mind [for awakening], yet merely contemplates emptiness without realizing it, thinking: 'I shall study emptiness.'"
Now is the time for study, not the time for realization; one does not yet deeply collect the mind and bind it to the object of focus.
At that time, the bodhisattva does not regress from the factors conducive to enlightenment, nor do they exhaust the outflows.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva possesses great wisdom and deep roots of goodness, they are able to form this thought:
"Now is the time for study, not the time for realization, as I am seeking to attain the prajñāpāramitā."
“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person who was brave, robust, and possessed great strength, such that he was difficult to shake;
his appearance was upright and handsome, and he was loved and respected by others.”
He was well-versed in the art of war, possessed sharp and精良 weapons, and was fully endowed with all sixty-four skills;
he was thoroughly practiced in all other arts and crafts and was beloved by people.
Whatever they undertake shall all be successfully accomplished.
Because of these benefits, they bring great advantage to many; all people revere and honor them, and their joy increases manifold.

This person, for some minor reason, accompanied by his parents whom he supports and leading his wife and children, passes through dangerous and difficult places; he comforts and encourages his parents and children, ensuring they are free from fear.
He spoke these words:
"Although this road is perilous and filled with many hostile bandits, you shall surely attain safety and peace, without further misfortune or exhaustion.

Because that man was accomplished in wisdom and strength and had no rival before him, he was able to ensure that his parents, wife, and children avoided these many hardships and reached the cities, towns, villages, and hamlets unharmed and without loss, their hearts filled with great joy.
Toward all enemies and bandits, they do not give rise to malicious thoughts.
Why is this? Because there is no craft or skill among all such arts that this person has not mastered through refinement and understanding.
Within that perilous path, he manifested a multitude of people, more numerous than the hostile bandits.
Furthermore, the weapons they wielded were sharp and formidable.
Consequently, all those hostile bandits retreated and dispersed on their own.
Therefore, this person is able to be confident that they will be secure and free from affliction.
It is so, it is so! Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva takes all sentient beings as his object, binding his mind in the samādhi of loving-kindness; he transcends all fetters and the factors that assist the fetters, transcends all Māras and those who assist Māra, and transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, abiding in the samādhi of emptiness yet without exhausting his outflows.
“Subhūti! At that time, the bodhisattva practices the gate of liberation of emptiness, yet does not realize the signless, nor does he fall into the realm of signs.
It is like a bird flying through the void, which does not fall.”
They move through space, yet do not dwell in space.
Subhūti, it is the same for the bodhisattva.
If one practices emptiness and studies emptiness, practices signlessness and studies signlessness,
and practices wishlessness and studies wishlessness,
yet without having fully perfected the Buddha-dharmas, one does not fall into [the mere state of] emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

For example, it is like a skilled archer who is well-versed in the art of shooting; he shoots arrows into the air, each arrow meeting the next, so that by his own will and for as long or as short a duration as he desires, they do not fall.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, because they are protected by skillful means, they do not realize the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi). This is for the sake of accomplishing the roots of goodness for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; only when they have accomplished unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment do they then realize the ultimate reality.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate the true reality of all phenomena in this way,
yet not realize it as a final attainment.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What the bodhisattvas undertake is exceedingly difficult and most rare.”
"One who trains in this manner does not, however, realize [the fruit of] attainment.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because these bodhisattvas do not abandon any sentient beings, they give rise to such great vows."
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva gives rise to such a thought:
"I should not abandon any sentient being; I must deliver them all."
He immediately enters the liberation door of the emptiness samādhi, as well as the liberation doors of the signless and wishless samādhis.
At that time, the bodhisattva does not realize the limit of reality midway.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva is protected by skillful means.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva wishes to enter such profound meditative absorptions—namely, the liberation door of the emptiness samādhi, and the liberation doors of the signless and wishless samādhis—this bodhisattva should first form this thought:

"Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to the mark of a sentient being and attached to the notion of attainment. Once I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall sever all these views and preach the Dharma for them."
He immediately enters the liberation gate of the emptiness samādhi.

By means of this mind and the power of his prior skillful means, this bodhisattva does not realize the limit of reality midway, nor does he lose the samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva has accomplished the power of skillful means, his wholesome dharmas increase all the more, his faculties become sharp and penetrating, and he also attains further growth in the various powers and factors of awakening of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva forms this thought:
'Sentient beings have for a long night wandered in the mark of self; once I have attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, I shall sever this mark and preach the Dharma for them.'"
He immediately enters the liberation door of the signless samādhi.

By means of this mind and the power of his prior skillful means, this bodhisattva does not realize the limit of reality midway, nor does he lose the samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have accomplished the power of skillful means, they further increase all wholesome dharmas; their roots of goodness become penetrating and sharp, and they also attain the increase of the various powers and factors of awakening of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva forms this thought:
'Beings have for a long night practiced the perception of permanence, the perception of pleasure, the perception of purity, and the perception of self.'"

Based on these perceptions, one acts with the thought, "I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. To sever these perceptions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self, I preach the Dharma for them, saying:
"This dharma is impermanent and not permanent; it is suffering and not pleasure; it is impure and not pure; it is non-self and not self."

By means of this mind and the power of prior skillful means, although he has not yet attained the samādhis of a Buddha, has not yet perfected the Buddha-dharmas, and has not yet realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is nevertheless able to enter the gate of liberation of the unconditioned samādhi (anabhisaṃskāra-samādhi), without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva forms this thought:
'Sentient beings have for a long night practiced with the notion of attainment; even now they practice with the notion of attainment.'
Previously one practiced with signs, now one likewise practices with signs;
previously one practiced in inversion, now one likewise practices in inversion;
previously one practiced with the characteristic of conjunction, now one likewise practices with the characteristic of conjunction.
"In the past I practiced false appearances, and now I still practice false appearances;
in the past I practiced wrong views, and now I still practice wrong views.

I shall now exert myself with diligence to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, so that for the sake of severing such appearances in sentient beings, I may preach the Dharma to eliminate these various faults."

"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva contemplates all sentient beings in this way, by means of that mind and the power of prior skillful means, they contemplate the characteristics of profound dharmas—whether as empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unborn, or non-existent."
Subhūti! It is impossible that a bodhisattva who has accomplished such wisdom would abide in the three realms or fall into the production of conditioned phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should ask other bodhisattvas: 'How should one train in these dharmas?'"
How does one give rise to it?
The mind enters emptiness, yet does not realize emptiness;
it enters signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, and non-existence, yet does not realize non-existence, and is thus able to cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If a bodhisattva answers in this way, they should simply contemplate emptiness, contemplate signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, non-birth, and non-existence.

They do not instruct regarding the prior mind, nor do they speak of the prior mind; it should be known that such a bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from past Buddhas, and has not yet abided in the stage of *avaivartika*.
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva is unable to explain the unique characteristics of an irreversible bodhisattva, nor can they correctly demonstrate or answer them.
One should know that this bodhisattva has not yet reached the stage of irreversibility.
“World-Honored One!
How is one to know that this is an avaivartika [bodhisattva]? “Subhūti!
“Whether they have heard it or not, if a bodhisattva can answer correctly in this way, you should know that they are an avaivartika.
“World-Honored One! [the bodhisattva said.]
"For this reason, although many sentient beings practice for bodhi, few are able to provide such a correct answer.
Subhūti, there are few bodhisattvas who are able to receive the prediction of non-retrogression (avaivartika)."
If one has received the prediction of enlightenment, one is able to answer correctly in this manner.
You should know that such a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness are bright and pure;
you should know that such a bodhisattva cannot be surpassed by anyone in all the worlds, including gods, humans, and asuras.
Chapter 19: The Bodhisattva-Avyavartin’s Awakening to Māra The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Nineteen: The Bodhisattva-Avyavartin’s Awakening to Māra. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, does not become attached to the three realms, nor to the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; and if he contemplates all dharmas as being like a dream and does not realize [nirvāṇa] therein."
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If, while dreaming, a bodhisattva sees the Buddha seated upon a high throne amidst a great assembly, surrounded with reverence by countless hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus and countless hundreds of thousands of billions of multitudes, as he preaches the Dharma for them.
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
In a dream, the bodhisattva sees himself in the midst of space, preaching the Dharma to a great assembly.
He perceives his own body emitting a great radiance and awakens.
Having awakened, he reflects thus:
"I know that the three realms are like a dream; I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
“Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!”
How should one know that when a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, in that world there will be no names for the three evil realms at all?
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, while dreaming, sees animals and makes this vow:

"I shall practice with diligent vigor so that when I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, in that world there will not even be the name of the three evil realms for all beings," [he increases his roots of goodness].
"Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva sees a city or town on fire, they should immediately form this thought:
"This is just like the appearance I saw in my dream.
When a bodhisattva achieves such an appearance, one should know that they are an avaivartika bodhisattva."
"If I possess these marks and am an avaivartika [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva, by the power of this word of truth, may the fires of this city and its walls now be extinguished."
"If the fire is extinguished, you should know that this bodhisattva has already received the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from a previous Buddha.
If the fire is not extinguished, you should know that this bodhisattva has not yet received the prediction."
Subhūti, if a fire were to burn down one household, he would leave another household;
if it were to burn down one village, he would leave another village. Subhūti!
You should know that these sentient beings have committed the grave offense of destroying the Dharma.
They now experience in this present life the remaining karmic retribution for that destruction of the Dharma. Subhūti!
By these causes and conditions, you should know that these are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti, I shall now further explain the characteristics of an irreversible bodhisattva.
Subhūti! If a man or a woman is possessed by a ghost, the bodhisattva should form this thought:
"If I have already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from previous Buddhas, and my profound mind desires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

If my practice is pure and free from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, I shall certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is not that I should not attain it now in the presence of the infinite asaṃkhyeya Buddhas of the ten directions.
These Buddhas know all things, see all things, attain all things, and realize all things.
If these Buddhas were to know my profound mind, I would certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
"By the power of these words of truth, may the non-human being who possesses this man or woman depart quickly.

If, when the Bodhisattva speaks these words, the non-human being does not depart, it should be known that this Bodhisattva has not yet been granted the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by a previous Buddha.
Subhūti! If, when a bodhisattva speaks these words, non-humans depart, you should know that this bodhisattva has already received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from previous Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
there may be a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment], yet makes this vow:
'If I have already received a prediction from previous Buddhas, then non-human beings shall now depart from this person.'"
The evil Māra immediately came to that place and caused the non-human beings to depart.
Why was this? Because the power of the evil Māra surpasses that of the non-human beings, the non-human beings departed at once.
At this, the bodhisattva thinks to himself:
"It is by my power that the non-human being has departed far away," yet he does not realize it is the power of Māra.

For this reason, they despise and treat with contempt all other bodhisattvas, thinking: "I have already received my prediction from previous Buddhas, whereas these people have not yet received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from those previous Buddhas."
By these causes and conditions, pride increases.
Because of the causes and conditions of pride, one becomes distant from *sarvajñā*, the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.

One should know that such a bodhisattva, having given rise to pride through minor causes and conditions, lacks skillful means and will inevitably fall into one of the two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Through the causal conditions of such vows, the works of Māra arise.
If a bodhisattva does not rely upon spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) in this regard, they will be bound by Māra, and that bondage will become even more firm.
Subhūti! You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
The evil Māra, wishing to corrupt and disturb the bodhisattva by means of names and causes, assumes various forms and approaches the bodhisattva’s dwelling, saying these words:
"O son of good family!..."
The Buddhas have already bestowed upon you the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Your present name is such-and-such; your parents' names are such-and-such; the names of your brothers, sisters, and kinsmen are such-and-such; and even the names of your ancestors for seven generations have all been spoken.
"You were born in such-and-such a country, such-and-such a city, such-and-such a village, and such-and-such a family.
If that person’s nature and conduct are gentle and mild, he speaks of their gentle and mild nature and conduct in previous lives;
if their nature is impetuous, he likewise speaks of their impetuous nature in previous lives.

If such a person practices the dharma of *āraṇyaka*—whether by begging for alms, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*), not drinking beverages after midday, eating in a single sitting, restricting the quantity of food, dwelling among corpses, sitting in an open space, sitting at the foot of a tree, remaining constantly seated without lying down, sitting wherever a seat is laid out, having few desires and being content, practicing seclusion, or refusing oil for anointing the feet—and delights in speaking little and engaging in little discourse, even Māra the Evil One will claim that they practiced these dharmas of *āraṇyaka*, up to and including delighting in speaking little and engaging in little discourse, in their past lives.
"You possess the merit of dhūta practices in this present life, and you possessed the merit of dhūta practices in previous lives as well.
Because of these causes and conditions—namely, hearing such names mentioned and being told of these dhūta merits—a mind of arrogance arises in this bodhisattva."
Immediately, the Evil Māra spoke these words again:
"You have already received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the past.
For what reason?"
"You now possess the marks and characteristics of the merit of an avaivartika [non-regressive] bodhisattva. "Subhūti!
The true marks of an avaivartika bodhisattva as described by me do not exist in this person."
Subhūti! You should know that such a bodhisattva is possessed by Māra. Why is this?
Such a person lacks the characteristics of an avaivartika bodhisattva; merely hearing the names spoken by an evil Māra, they then treat other bodhisattvas with contempt.
Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva gives rise to the works of Māra because of names.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, because of names, give rise to demonic activities.
That is to say, a Māra comes to their place and says:
"You received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* from a previous Buddha; when you become a Buddha, your name shall be such-and-such."
The name by which this bodhisattva originally aspired was identical to what the Māra had spoken; because he lacked wisdom and skillful means, he then thought:
"When I attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the name by which I aspire shall be exactly as this bhikṣu has spoken—it accords with my own original vow."
Thus, following what the evil Māra has instilled, that bhikṣu accepts his words and, on account of mere names and causal conditions, comes to despise all other bodhisattvas.
Subhūti! The characteristics of a truly non-retrogressive bodhisattva that I have described do not exist in this person.
Because of the causes and conditions of their contemptuousness, they have distanced themselves from *sarvajñā*, the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.

If this bodhisattva is separated from skillful means and good spiritual friends, and encounters evil associates, they will fall into one of two stages: either the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, within this very body, regrets their previous states of mind and distances themselves from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they shall remain for a long time in saṃsāra before returning once more to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because these mental offenses are grave.
For example, if a bhikṣu violates one or two of the four pārājika rules, he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya.
Because this bodhisattva treats other bodhisattvas with contempt on account of their names, the transgression he incurs is heavier than the four grave prohibitions.
Subhūti! Setting aside these four prohibitions, such a transgression is even heavier than the five heinous crimes.
That is to say, because of names, they give rise to a mind of conceit.
Subhūti! Due to these causes and conditions of names, such subtle demonic activities arise; a bodhisattva should be aware of them.
Having awakened, he remains detached. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
when Māra the Evil One sees that a bodhisattva is practicing detachment, he approaches him and speaks these words:"
"Good son! The Tathāgata always praises those who practice detachment. Subhūti!
“I do not say that a bodhisattva is practicing detachment by staying in forest hermitages, secluded places, among the trees of the mountains, or in remote wildernesses.
“World-Honored One! [The interlocutor replied.]
If dwelling in an araṇya, a secluded place, among the mountains, beneath a tree, or in a remote wilderness were not called "seclusion," what else could be considered seclusion?
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva distances himself from the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, such distancing is called ‘seclusion’ whether he is near a village;
it is also called ‘seclusion’ whether he is in an araṇya, a quiet and secluded place, among the mountains beneath trees, or in a remote and desolate location.”
Subhūti! Such seclusion is what I authorize.
If a bodhisattva practices day and night in this manner of seclusion;
If one is near a village, this is also called "seclusion";
if one is in an araṇya, a quiet and secluded place, among the mountains, beneath a tree, or in a remote and desolate location, this is also called "seclusion."

Subhūti! If there is that which Māra praises as "seclusion"—namely, dwelling in forest hermitages, empty and quiet places, among the trees of the mountains, or in remote and desolate regions—and although a bodhisattva possesses such seclusion, they do not distance themselves from the mindsets of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they do not cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they act for the sake of fulfilling all-encompassing wisdom, then this is called a practitioner of a muddled and mixed path.
If this bodhisattva practices such seclusion, it is not yet pure, for he looks down upon other bodhisattvas who dwell near villages.

One whose mind is pure, who has distanced himself from the minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who is unmixed with evil and unwholesome dharmas, attains the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and supernormal powers.
One who has attained mastery of the *prajñāpāramitā* lacks skillful means.

Although a bodhisattva may dwell for hundreds of *yojanas* in a desolate wilderness—a place frequented only by birds, beasts, bandits, and malevolent spirits—for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, or even longer than that number, they cannot know the characteristic of true seclusion. Being far removed from true seclusion, they do not understand how to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a profound resolve.
Such a bodhisattva is also called one who practices amidst turmoil.
If they are greedily attached to their reliance [on others], such a form of seclusion cannot bring joy to my heart.
Why is this? Among those whom I have authorized to practice seclusion, I do not see such a person; such a person does not exist who practices seclusion in this manner. "Subhūti!..."
Furthermore, an evil Māra may come to where the bodhisattva is dwelling, stay suspended in mid-air, and say these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
That which you practice is true seclusion, as praised by the Buddha."
