"By means of this seclusion, you shall swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Yet, when that bodhisattva comes from his place of seclusion to a village and sees other bhikṣus seeking the Buddha-way who are gentle and mild by nature, he conceives thoughts of contempt, thinking: "You are practitioners of the clamorous life."

Subhūti! These bodhisattvas take bustling crowds to be true seclusion and take true seclusion to be bustling crowds. Thus they speak of their faults and fail to give rise to a mind of reverence; they treat those who deserve reverence with contempt, and treat those who deserve contempt with reverence.
He formed this thought: "Non-human beings see me;

they come to mind me and come to assist me. I shall practice that which the Buddha has authorized as true solitary conduct. You, however, dwell near a village; who would mind you? Who would assist you?"
Having formed this thought, they look down upon other bodhisattvas who practice pure conduct. Subhūti,
you should know that such a person is a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas.
One should know that such a person defiles other bodhisattvas with foulness and impurity;
one should know that such a person is a counterfeit bodhisattva;
one should know that such a person is a great thief among all the devas and humans of the world, a thief in the form of a śramaṇa.
Subhūti! Those who seek the path of the Buddha should not associate with such persons. Why is this?
People such as these are called those who possess overweening pride. "Subhūti!

If a bodhisattva cherishes all-knowledge (sarvajñā), cherishes unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and with a profound mind desires to attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment and wishes to benefit all sentient beings, they should not associate with such people."

Those who seek the Buddha-way should always seek their own benefit, constantly cultivate weary detachment and dread toward the triple world, and give rise to the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward these people.
I shall thus practice with diligent vigor.
When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may such evils not exist; should they arise, I shall swiftly eliminate them.
Subhūti! Practicing in this manner is what constitutes the power of a bodhisattva’s wisdom.

Chapter Twenty: Seeking Bodhi with a Profound Mind. Chapter Twenty: Seeking Bodhi with a Profound Mind.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
who are the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are the good spiritual friends of these bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because they are able to instruct bodhisattvas so that they may enter the *prajñāpāramitā*,
Subhūti, these are called the good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
the six pāramitās are the good spiritual friends of a bodhisattva;
the six pāramitās are the great teachers of a bodhisattva.
The six pāramitās are the path of the bodhisattva;
the six pāramitās are the light of the bodhisattva;
the six pāramitās are the torch of the bodhisattva.
Subhūti! All Buddhas of the past were born from the six pāramitās;
all Buddhas of the future will likewise be born from the six pāramitās.
All the Buddhas of the present in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are born from the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, the sarvajñā (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is born from the six pāramitās.
Why is this? All Buddhas practice the six pāramitās and gather in sentient beings through the four means of integration—
namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation— and thereby attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that the six pāramitās are the Great Teacher, they are the father and the mother, they are the home and the refuge, they are the island and the rescue, and they are the ultimate path.
The six pāramitās benefit all sentient beings.
For this reason, a bodhisattva who wishes for their own profound wisdom to be clear and lucid does not follow the words of others nor place faith in the teachings of others.
"If one wishes to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, one should study this Prajñāpāramitā.
"World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of this Prajñāpāramitā?"
“Subhūti! The characteristic of non-obstruction is this Prajñāpāramitā.
“World-Honored One!”
"Is there any causal basis by which, just as the *prajñāpāramitā* has the characteristic of non-obstruction, all phenomena (*dharma*) likewise have the characteristic of non-obstruction?
"There is, Subhūti."
Just as the perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of non-obstruction, so too do all phenomena have the characteristic of non-obstruction.
Why is this, Subhūti?
All dharmas are devoid of marks; all dharmas have the mark of emptiness.
Therefore, Subhūti, you should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is also devoid of marks and has the mark of emptiness, and that all dharmas are likewise devoid of marks and have the mark of emptiness.
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are devoid of marks and have the mark of emptiness, how can sentient beings have defilement and purity?
For what reason?”
Dharmas characterized by detachment are neither defiled nor pure; dharmas characterized by emptiness are neither defiled nor pure.
Dharmas characterized by detachment and dharmas characterized by emptiness cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Apart from the characteristic of detachment and apart from the characteristic of emptiness, there is no further dharma that can attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One,
how should I now understand this meaning?
“Subhūti! I shall question you in return; answer me as you see fit. Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Do sentient beings, throughout the long night, cling to 'I' and 'mine'? "It is so, it is so!"
"Bhagavān!
Sentient beings have for a long night been attached to 'self' and 'what belongs to self. " "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Are 'self' and 'what belongs to self' empty?
"World-Honored One, they are."
“Self and what belongs to self are empty. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”
"Do sentient beings, by means of 'I' and 'mine,' come and go within birth and death? "It is so, it is so!
World-Honored One!"
“Sentient beings wander through birth and death because of the notions of ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self. Subhūti,
such sentient beings are said to be defiled, for they follow after what they receive and to which they are attached.”
Within this, there is truly no defilement, nor is there anyone who receives defilement. Subhūti!
If one does not grasp at any phenomena, then there is no self and no "mine"; this is called purity.
"In this, there is truly no purity, nor is there anyone who attains purity.
When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it is called practicing the perfection of wisdom.
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva practices in this way, they do not practice with regard to form, nor do they practice with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
If a bodhisattva practices in this way, they cannot be overcome by any in the world, whether gods, humans, or asuras.
World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva who practices in this manner surpasses all that is practiced by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, abiding in a state that is unsurpassed.
World-Honored One!

The Bodhisattva Anabhibhū, practicing day and night with this mindfulness that accords with the perfection of wisdom, draws near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think?
Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were simultaneously to obtain human bodies and give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having generated the mind [of enlightenment], they practice giving for as long as their life lasts.
By means of this giving, they dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Would that person, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit? Subhūti said:
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“If a bodhisattva, for even a single day, practices the mindfulness that accords with the *prajñāpāramitā*, their merit will surpass that [of the former].”
Rejoicing in the bodhisattva’s practice and maintaining mindfulness in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*, one can serve as a field of merit for all sentient beings. Why is this?
With the exception of the Buddhas, no other sentient beings possess such profound compassion as that of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, all bodhisattvas are able to give rise to such wisdom.

Through this wisdom, they see all sentient beings undergoing various sufferings and afflictions as if being executed; thus, the bodhisattva immediately attains the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Having attained great compassion, he observes all sentient beings with his divine eye; seeing immeasurable sentient beings who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution and fallen into the various states of misery, he immediately gives rise to a heart of pity.
They do not dwell in these marks, nor do they dwell in other marks. Subhūti,
this is called the great light of wisdom of all bodhisattvas.
One who practices this path becomes a field of merit for all sentient beings and does not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the offerings they receive—clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessary requisites—because they practice the *prajñāpāramitā* with single-minded devotion, they are able to purify the repayment of the donors' kindness and draw near to *sarvajñatā*.

Therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes not to consume in vain the offerings of the land, if they wish to benefit all sentient beings, if they wish to show the right path to all sentient beings, if they wish to release all sentient beings from the bonds of prison, and if they wish to bestow the eye of wisdom upon all sentient beings, they should constantly practice and maintain mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one practices with mindfulness corresponding to the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), whatever this bodhisattva speaks will also be in accord with the perfection of wisdom. Why is this?
Whatever this bodhisattva speaks, it all accords with the mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
whatever they contemplate, that too accords with their speech.
A bodhisattva should constantly maintain such mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā* day and night.
Subhūti! It is as if a person were to obtain a hitherto unknown treasure.
Having obtained it, he rejoices greatly, yet then loses it again.
For these reasons, he was filled with sorrow and distress.
His mind constantly thought:
"How have I now lost this great treasure?"
"Subhūti! It is the same for a bodhisattva.
The great treasure is this prajñāpāramitā."
"Once a bodhisattva has attained this, they should always, with a mind corresponding to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), keep the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in mind.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
If all thoughts have, from the very beginning, been by nature eternally detached, why do you say that one should not abandon this mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva can understand in this way, they do not depart from the prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?
“The perfection of wisdom is empty; within it, there is no falling away or loss.
“World-Honored One, if the perfection of wisdom is empty, how does a bodhisattva achieve growth through the perfection of wisdom?”
"How does one also draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is neither increase nor decrease."

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink into despondency, and does not retreat, you should know that this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
“World-Honored One!
Is the mark of emptiness of the prajñāpāramitā itself the practice of the prajñāpāramitā? “No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Is there any other dharma apart from the perfection of wisdom that practices the perfection of wisdom? “No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Can emptiness practice emptiness? “No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Can one practice emptiness apart from emptiness? “No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
Is the practice of form the practice of the perfection of wisdom? “No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Is the practice of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the practice of the perfection of wisdom? “No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Is there any dharma apart from form that can practice the prajñāpāramitā? “No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
Apart from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, is there any dharma that can practice the perfection of wisdom? “No, Subhūti!”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva practice so that it is called ‘practicing the perfection of wisdom’? “Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Do you perceive any dharma that practices the perfection of wisdom?
"No, World-Honored One."
“Subhūti! Do you see the dharma of the prajñāpāramitā as the sphere of practice for a bodhisattva?
“No, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, what do you think?
Regarding that dharma which you do not perceive, does it have any arising?”
"No, World-Honored One! Subhūti,
this is called the 'patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas' (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) of all Buddhas."
A bodhisattva who can accomplish such patience shall receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, this is called the path of fearlessness of all Buddhas.

If a bodhisattva practices this path, cultivating and drawing near to it, it is impossible that they should not attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom, great wisdom, self-existent wisdom, all-encompassing wisdom, and Tathāgata wisdom.
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas are unarisen, can one receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* on that basis? “No, Subhūti.”
“World-Honored One!
How is it now that one is said to have received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? “Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Do you see any dharma that has received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"No, World-Honored One!"
I do not perceive any dharma that receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor do I perceive the dharma by which it is received, nor do I perceive the dharma that is attained.
“Subhūti! Just as all these dharmas are unattainable,
one should not speak in this way:”
"This dharma can be attained; this dharma that is employed can be attained.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, within the great assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand, because it is ultimately detached.
If anyone hears this Prajñāpāramitā, writes it down, receives and maintains it, or recites it, you should know that this person’s merit is not small.
“Kauśika! What do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action; the merit they would obtain would not equal that of a person who hears this Prajñāpāramitā, writes it down, receives and upholds it, and recites it. It would not reach even a hundredth part of it, nor a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part, nor could it even be approached by calculation or analogy.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
“Kauśika! Such sons and daughters of good family are superior to you.”
Śakra Devānām Indra said:

"This person, by the mere moment of first generating the thought [of awakening], already surpasses me; how much more so when they hear the Prajñāpāramitā, write it down, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to what is taught."
Such a person is the most preeminent among all those in the world—among gods, humans, and asuras.

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they not only surpass all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—but also surpass the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha; this is the bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Not only does it surpass the srotāpanna, but it even surpasses the pratyekabuddha, as well as the bodhisattva who, being devoid of the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfection of dāna without skillful means.

Not only does one who practices the perfection of giving without skillful means and apart from the perfection of wisdom surpass [others], but one who practices the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditation without skillful means and apart from the perfection of wisdom also surpasses them.
In this way, such a bodhisattva is most preeminent.
If a bodhisattva practices in accordance with what is taught in the Prajñāpāramitā, they surpass all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.
All those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—should all pay homage and make offerings to them.

If a bodhisattva practices in accordance with what is taught in the *prajñāpāramitā*, that bodhisattva does not sever the knowledge of all modes; that bodhisattva draws near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that bodhisattva will certainly sit at the site of enlightenment; and that bodhisattva rescues sentient beings who are drowning in birth and death.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, it is called training in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Training in this way is called not training in the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
If a bodhisattva trains in this way, the Four Heavenly Kings will bring four alms bowls to his dwelling and say to him:
"O son of good family!
May you swiftly train and attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment."
"When you sit at the site of enlightenment, we shall offer these four bowls.
"World-Honored One!
I myself shall go to inquire after your well-being, let alone the other devaputras."
Bodhisattvas who study the Prajñāpāramitā are always protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
As for the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings in the world, because these bodhisattvas are able to practice the Prajñāpāramitā accordingly, they are free from such sufferings.
“World-Honored One!
These are the merits of this bodhisattva in the present life.
At that time, Ānanda had this thought:
"Does Śakra Devānām Indra speak thus by the power of his own wisdom,
or is it through the Buddha's spiritual power?
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what Ānanda was thinking, said to him:
"All this is through the Buddha's supernatural power.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is!"
Ānanda! All that Śakra Devānām Indra has spoken is due to the Buddha’s spiritual power. Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva studies the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, all the māras in the trichiliocosm give rise to doubt and confusion.

Will this bodhisattva realize the limit of reality by way of the middle path and thereby fall into the stage of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, or will he proceed directly to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
**Chapter 21: Reverence for the Bodhisattva** The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one: Reverence for the Bodhisattva. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“If a bodhisattva does not depart from the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, at that time Māra the Evil One will be filled with grief and distress as if an arrow had pierced his heart. He will unleash great rains and hail, along with thunder and lightning bolts, desiring to cause the bodhisattva to be terrified and his hair to stand on end, so that his mind may retreat and sink back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, even for a single thought-moment.”
"Ānanda! It is not necessarily the case that Māra wishes to trouble and disturb all bodhisattvas.
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of bodhisattva is confused by Māra?
"Ānanda, there are bodhisattvas who,
in previous lives, heard the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet were unable to believe and accept it."
Such a person will be troubled and disturbed by Māra, who will find an opportunity to exploit them.
"Furthermore, Ānanda,
if when a bodhisattva hears the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, doubt arises in their mind as to whether this profound *prajñāpāramitā* actually exists..."
Is it not so, Ānanda? In this way,
such a bodhisattva also provides an opportunity for Māra, the Evil One, to gain the upper hand.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
There are bodhisattvas who are separated from virtuous friends and fall under the influence of evil associates; such persons do not hear the meaning within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
Because they have not heard it, they do not know it and do not see it; how then should they practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, and how should they cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*?
"Ānanda! Such a person also provides an opportunity for Māra, the Evil One.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
If a bodhisattva upholds false teachings, this person also provides an opportunity for Māra.
Māra thinks to himself:
"This person assists me; he will also cause others to assist me, and he will be able to fulfill my wishes."
"Ānanda! Such a person also provides an opportunity for Māra, the Evil One.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
How does a bodhisattva provide an opportunity for Māra?
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, says to other bodhisattvas:
"This *prajñāpāramitā* is so profound that even we cannot fathom its depths; what use is it for you to hear it?"
"Such a person also gives the evil Māra an opportunity.
Ānanda! If a bodhisattva treats another bodhisattva with contempt, saying:"
"I am a practitioner who dwells in seclusion, whereas you possess none of these virtues.
At that time, the evil Māra was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness. Ānanda!

If there are certain bodhisattvas who, when an evil Māra utters their names, become conceited because they have received those names; these individuals lack the marks and characteristics of the qualities of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva, yet they falsely claim the qualities of an *avaivartika*. They increase their afflictions, exalting themselves and disparaging others, saying:
"I possess such meritorious qualities, whereas you do not."
At that time, Māra the Evil One was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"My palace is no longer empty; it increases the number of those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals."
Because the evil Māra exerts his supernatural power upon them, all people believe and accept what these individuals say.
Having accepted it, they learn according to what they see and act according to what they are told.
Having studied according to what they see and practiced according to what they say, they further increase their afflictions.

Because such people possess perverted minds, the karmic retributions of the actions of body, speech, and mind they initiate are all suffering; by these causes and conditions, they increase the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Ānanda! When Māra the Evil One sees this benefit, he too is greatly delighted. Ānanda!
If one who seeks the Buddha-way disputes with śrāvakas,
the evil Māra further thinks:
"Although this person is far removed from sarvajñatā, they are not yet very far."
“Ānanda! If a bodhisattva quarrels with another bodhisattva, Māra the Evil One will be greatly delighted and think:
‘These two persons have both moved far away from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).’”

"Ānanda! If a bodhisattva who has not received a prediction of enlightenment becomes resentful toward one who has received such a prediction, and they engage in mutual contention, using harsh words and abuse—if such a person cherishes *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), then for every single thought that arises, one kalpa is subtracted from their time; only then shall they again be able to give rise to the great adornments."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Can such a transgressor repent for their offense?”
"One must complete the full number of kalpas associated with mindfulness before one can again give rise to the great adornment.
The Buddha said,
"There is an escape."
I say that both bodhisattvas and śrāvakas possess the dharma for emerging from transgressions;
I do not say there is no such emergence. Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva quarrels with another bodhisattva, using harsh words and insults, and does not repent or apologize, harboring resentment in his heart,
I do not say that such a person has a method for the removal of their offense.
If such a person cherishes *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), they will complete their cycle through the kalpas of mindfulness and shall once again give rise to the great adornment.
Ānanda! If a bodhisattva quarrels with another bodhisattva, using harsh words and insults, they should immediately repent and apologize, and never do so again.
He forms this thought:
"I should humble myself before all sentient beings.
If I were to respond with anger or contention toward others, it would be a great loss."
"I ought to act as a bridge for all sentient beings.
I should not even slight others such as you, much less retaliate against them!
I should remain like one who is deaf and mute, and must not destroy my own profound resolve."
"When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall deliver these very beings.
Why then do you add further anger and give rise to resentment and obstruction yourself? Ānanda!
"One who seeks the bodhisattva path should not give rise to even the slightest anger or obstruction toward śrāvakas.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a bodhisattva dwell together with other bodhisattvas? What is their method?
The Buddha said, "One should regard each other as one would the Buddha, thinking: 'He is my Great Teacher; we are carried together on the same vehicle and travel together upon the same path.'"
"As they have trained, so shall I also train.
If their practice is mixed, it is not that which I should learn.
If their training is pure and accords with the mindfulness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), then I too should train."
"If a bodhisattva trains in this way, this is called 'training together.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
If a bodhisattva trains for the sake of exhaustion, they train in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
if they train for the sake of non-arising, for the sake of detachment, or for the sake of cessation, they train in omniscience.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"As you have said, when a bodhisattva trains for the sake of exhaustion, they train in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
when they train for the sake of non-arising, training for the sake of detachment, and training for the sake of cessation, they train in omniscience."
Subhūti, what do you think?
It is by means of suchness that the Tathāgata is named "Tathāgata."
“Is this Suchness not exhausted, not departed, and not extinguished?
“It is so, World-Honored One. “Subhūti!”
One who trains in this manner is said to train in *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Training in *sarvajñatā* is training in the *prajñāpāramitā*, and training in the Buddha-ground, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this manner reaches the further shore of all training.
One who trains in this manner cannot be overcome by Māra or the followers of Māra.
One who trains in this way will swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
One who trains in this way will swiftly sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
One who trains in this way trains in the sphere of one's own practice.
One who trains in this way trains in the Dharma of rescue and protection.
One who trains in this way trains in great loving-kindness and great compassion.
One who trains in this way trains in the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects.
One who trains in this way trains to deliver sentient beings.
One who trains in this way trains to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
One who trains in this way trains to open the gate of the ambrosia of immortality.
Subhūti! Ordinary persons of inferior capacity cannot train in this way.
Only those who wish to discipline all sentient beings can train in this way.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this manner does not fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor is he born in a border region.
Training in this manner, he is not born into the families of caṇḍālas, nor into families of bamboo and grass workers, nor into families of scavengers, nor into any other poor or lowly families.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this manner will not be blind, nor sightless, nor squint-eyed; he will not be stunted, nor deaf-mute, nor dull-witted, nor physically deformed; his physical faculties will be complete.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this way does not take the lives of others, does not steal the property of others, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not use divisive speech, does not use harsh speech, does not engage in idle chatter, is not covetous, is not malicious, does not hold wrong views, does not live by wrong livelihood, does not keep a retinue of those with wrong views, and does not keep a retinue of those who break the precepts.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this manner is not reborn in the long-lived heavens. Why is that?
Because Bodhisattvas have accomplished skillful means (*upāya*).
What are these skillful means?
They are said to arise from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); thus, although they are able to enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), they are not reborn according to that absorption.
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this way attains the pure power of a Buddha and the purity of fearlessness.
“World-Honored One!”
"If all dharmas are by nature pure in their characteristics, what further pure dharma does a bodhisattva obtain?
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"

Subhūti! All dharmas have the characteristic of primordial purity. When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā within these dharmas that possess the characteristic of primordial purity, they are not startled, not terrified, do not sink, and do not retreat; this is called the pure prajñāpāramitā.

Subhūti! Ordinary beings do not know and do not see that all dharmas are by nature pure; for this reason, bodhisattvas arouse diligent vigor, train therein, and attain the pure powers and fearlessnesses.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this manner is able to thoroughly penetrate the minds and mental activities of all sentient beings. Subhūti!
Just as there is very little land where Jāmbūnada gold is produced, so too among the masses of sentient beings, few are able to study the Prajñāpāramitā in this way.
Just as among sentient beings, few are able to generate the karma for a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), while many are able to generate the karma for various minor kings.
Thus it is, Subhūti!
Few are the sentient beings who are able to practice the path of the prajñāpāramitā; many are those who set out in the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti! There are few sentient beings who are able to train in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Among those who train in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there are even fewer who are able to practice according to what they have taught.
Among those who practice according to what has been taught, few are able to study the Prajñāpāramitā accordingly.
Among those who study it accordingly, few are able to attain the state of *avaivartika*.
Therefore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva who wishes to be among the least of the few should study the *prajñāpāramitā* and cultivate the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Chapter 22: On the Absence of the Affliction of Avarice. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Two: On the Absence of the Affliction of Avarice. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, then the mind of affliction does not arise; the mind of avarice does not arise; the mind of breaking the precepts does not arise; the mind of anger and resentment does not arise; the mind of indolence does not arise; the mind of distraction does not arise; and the mind of delusion does not arise.”
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they encompass all the pāramitās. Subhūti!
Subhūti, just as the sixty-two views are all subsumed within the view of a self,
so too when a bodhisattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, they subsume all the perfections.
For example, Subhūti, when a person dies, because the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has ceased, all the faculties (indriya) cease as well.
In the same way, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva studies the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they encompass all the perfections.
Therefore, Subhūti,
[this is] the most supreme among all. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Are the sentient beings in a trichiliocosm many?
"World-Honored One, they are."
"The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are already many; how much more so those in the trichiliocosm?
Subhūti, all these sentient beings are bodhisattvas."
Suppose, Subhūti, there were a person who for as long as their life lasted provided offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicines.
What do you think?
Would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit?
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One! “Subhūti!
If there were a bodhisattva who, for as long as a finger-snap, practiced the prajñāpāramitā, their merit would surpass that [of the former].
Thus it is, Subhūti!
The prajñāpāramitā brings great benefit to all bodhisattvas and is able to assist them in attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; wishes to be the unsurpassed one among all sentient beings; wishes to act as a protector for all sentient beings; wishes to become fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma; wishes to attain the sphere of action of the Buddhas; wishes to attain the playful mastery of the Buddhas; wishes to attain the lion’s roar of the Buddhas; and wishes to attain the great assemblies for preaching the Dharma throughout the trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Subhūti! I do not see a bodhisattva training in the prajñāpāramitā who does not obtain such fully perfected benefits.
[Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!"
"Does this bodhisattva also attain the fulfillment of the benefits of a śrāvaka?

"Subhūti, the bodhisattva also trains in the fulfillment of the benefits of a śrāvaka, yet does not wish to abide within the dharma of a śrāvaka. Desiring to fulfill all merits, he must certainly be able to know them all, yet he does not abide therein, forming this thought:"
"I, too, shall speak of these merits of the śrāvakas to transform and guide sentient beings.

If a bodhisattva trains in this way, they can serve as a field of merit for all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—and will be the most preeminent among the fields of merit of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
A bodhisattva who trains in this manner draws near to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); they do not abandon the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and do not depart from the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom in this way is said to be non-retrogressive regarding omniscience; they remain far from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and draw near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
If this bodhisattva should have such a thought as:
"This is the perfection of wisdom; this is that perfection of wisdom; through it, I shall attain sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
To discriminate in this way is likewise not to practice the perfection of wisdom.

If a bodhisattva does not discriminate the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, and does not say, "This is the perfection of wisdom," or "This is such-and-such a perfection of wisdom," [thinking] "I shall attain *sarvajñā*," [then they practice it].
"In this way, neither seeing nor hearing, neither perceiving nor cognizing, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra had this thought:
"This bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* already surpasses all sentient beings; how much more so when they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*!"

If a person delights in hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, that person has attained a great benefit, the most supreme within their lifespan; how much more so for one who is able to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"This person shall be one whom the world covets and admires; this person shall be able to discipline and guide sentient beings.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a handful of māndārava flowers, scattered them over the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!

If there are those who resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may they be endowed with the Buddha-dharmas, endowed with sarvajñā (all-knowledge), endowed with the self-arisen dharma, and endowed with the untainted dharma.
World-Honored One!
I shall not give rise to even a single thought that would cause anyone who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to fall back.
“World-Honored One!

Although I see the various sufferings and afflictions within birth and death, I do not give rise to even a single thought of wishing to cause a Bodhisattva to regress; for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I too shall practice with diligent vigor.”
Why is this? Because such people as these, being able to give rise to such a mind, bring great benefit to the entire world.
Having attained deliverance myself, I shall deliver those who have not yet been delivered.
Having attained liberation myself, I shall liberate those not yet liberated.
Having attained peace myself, I shall bring peace to those not yet at peace.
Having attained nirvāṇa myself, I shall lead across to nirvāṇa those not yet crossed over.
"Bhagavān!

If a person rejoices in a bodhisattva who has first resolved for awakening, or rejoices in one who practices the six pāramitās, or rejoices in one who is irreversible (avaivartika), or rejoices in one who is in his final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), how much merit will that person obtain?"
“Kauśika! Even Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, can be weighed; but the merit of this person’s sympathetic joy cannot be measured. Kauśika!”
"The three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system may still be weighed and measured, but the merit of this person’s sympathetic joy cannot be weighed or measured.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If a person is unable to rejoice in these various states of mind, they are possessed by Māra; one should know that such a person belongs to the retinue of Māra.
One should know that a person who cannot rejoice in these various states of mind has passed away from the realm of Māra and been reborn here in this world.
Why is this? Because all these states of mind are capable of destroying all demonic activities.
This person’s merit from sympathetic joy should be dedicated toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If a person gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they do not abandon the Buddha, they do not abandon the Dharma, and they do not abandon the Saṅgha.
For this reason, one should give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) toward all such minds.
"So it is, so it is, Kauśika! If a person rejoices in these various states of mind, you should know that this person will swiftly encounter a Buddha."

By virtue of these roots of goodness from this merit of sympathetic joy, wherever such a person is born, they will always receive offerings, respect, reverence, and praise; they shall never hear evil sounds, nor fall into the various evil realms, but will always be reborn in the heavens.
Why is this? Because this person rejoices for the sake of benefiting immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
This mind of sympathetic joy gradually increases until it can reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When this person attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa. Kausika!
For this reason, you should know that when this person rejoices in these various states of mind, they rejoice for the sake of the roots of goodness of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This mind is like an illusion; how can it attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Do you perceive the minds of these people as being like an illusion?”
"No, World-Honored One!
I do not perceive this mind as being like an illusion.
"What do you think?"
If one does not see this illusion, nor see that which is like an illusion,
and the mind is detached from illusion and detached from the mind that is like an illusion— would one further see any dharma that can be attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"No, World-Honored One!
Apart from illusion and apart from the mind that is like an illusion, one does not perceive any further dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
World-Honored One!
If I do not perceive any distinct dharma, what dharma could I possibly speak of as either existing or non-existing?
World-Honored One!
If a phenomenon is ultimately detached, it does not exist within the categories of being or non-being;
if a phenomenon is ultimately detached, that phenomenon cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
World-Honored One!
Since non-existent dharmas cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
for this reason, the prajñā-pāramitā is ultimately detached.
If a dharma is ultimately detached, it cannot be cultivated.
Such a dharma cannot give rise to other dharmas, because the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately detached.
World-Honored One!
Since the *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimately detached, how can it attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is also ultimately detached; how can that which is detached attain that which is detached?
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"

The perfection of wisdom is ultimately detached, and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is also ultimately detached; for this reason, one is able to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Subhūti! If the perfection of wisdom were not ultimately detached, it would not be the perfection of wisdom.
It is thus, Subhūti!
Nor does one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* apart from the *prajñāpāramitā*; nor is it attained by means of separation, through that which is separated.
— *The Minor Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Three: Praising the Bodhisattvas. Chapter Twenty-Three: Praising the Bodhisattvas.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are practicing its most profound meaning.”
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are practicing the profoundly deep meaning."

Subhūti! What the bodhisattva undertakes is exceedingly difficult: he practices the most profound meaning yet does not realize that meaning—namely, the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the conduct of a bodhisattva is not difficult.
Why is this? Because—”
The one who attains realization cannot be apprehended; the means by which realization is attained cannot be apprehended; nor can the dharma that is realized be apprehended.

If a bodhisattva, upon hearing such a teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink into despondency, and does not retreat, you should know that this bodhisattva is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet they do not perceive themselves as practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If they likewise do not engage in such discrimination,
you should know that this bodhisattva is close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and has distanced themselves from the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha.
“World-Honored One!
It is like space, which does not form the thought:
‘This is distant; this is near.’”
Why is this? Because space is without discrimination,
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is also like this; it does not form the thought:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me;
anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is without discrimination.
“World-Honored One!...”
For example, a person conjured by illusion does not form this thought:
"The illusionist is near to me; the spectators are far from me. Why is that?
World-Honored One!
Because a person conjured by illusion is without discrimination.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is also like this; it does not form such a thought as:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me;
unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is without discrimination.
“World-Honored One!...”
For example, a reflection does not think:
"That which is its cause is near to me; other things are far from me. Why is this?
"Because a reflection is without discrimination,
O Bhagavan,
the perfection of wisdom is also like this; it does not form such a thought:"
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me;
anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me. Why is this?
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is without discrimination.
"World-Honored One!
Just as the Tathāgata has neither hatred nor affection, so too the Prajñāpāramitā has neither hatred nor affection."
“World-Honored One!
Just as the Tathāgata is free from all conceptual discrimination, so too is the prajñāpāramitā free from all conceptual discrimination.
World-Honored One!”
Just as a person conjured by the Tathāgata does not form this thought:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me;
anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is near to me."
Why is this? Because the person emanated by the Tathāgata is without discrimination.
World-Honored One!
The perfection of wisdom is also like this; it does not form such a thought as:
"The stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha are far from me;
unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment is near to me."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is without discrimination.
"World-Honored One!..."
"Just as a person created by the Tathāgata can perform various tasks according to their function yet remains without conceptual discrimination,
so too, World-Honored One,
is the Prajñāpāramitā: according to what is practiced, it accomplishes everything, yet remains without any conceptual discrimination."
World-Honored One!
It is like a craftsman who, by means of a mechanical wooden figure—whether male or female—can accomplish whatever task it is assigned to perform, yet without any conceptual discrimination.
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: according to what is practiced and cultivated, it can accomplish everything, yet it remains without discrimination.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are practicing the meaning of firmness.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, this is precisely practicing the meaning of firmness.
At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm had this thought:

"If a person who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* can practice such profound *prajñāpāramitā* without realizing the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet does not fall into the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha, one should know that what this bodhisattva accomplishes is exceedingly difficult, and they are worthy of the veneration of all the world."
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"It is not difficult for a bodhisattva practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā not to realize [the fruit] prematurely."

If a bodhisattva, for the sake of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, gives rise to the great adornment, yet ultimately sentient beings cannot be apprehended and those who might be delivered cannot be apprehended, and yet he is able to resolve:
"I shall deliver them."
That would indeed be difficult,
O sons of the gods!
Such a person, wishing to deliver sentient beings, is wishing to deliver empty space.
Why is this? Because space is detached, sentient beings are also detached.
Therefore, one should know that what these bodhisattvas do is exceedingly difficult: though there are no sentient beings, they act for the sake of sentient beings, giving rise to great adornment.
It is like a person fighting against space.
The Buddha has taught that sentient beings cannot be apprehended; because sentient beings are detached, those who can be delivered are also detached;
because sentient beings are detached, form is also detached.
Because sentient beings are detached, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also detached;
because sentient beings are detached, all dharmas are also detached.
If a bodhisattva, hearing such a teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, one should know that this is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha asked Subhūti:
"For what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva not become startled, not become terrified, not sink down, and not retreat?
[Subhūti replied: "World-Honored One!"
Because it is empty, it does not sink;
because it is non-existent, it does not sink. Why is this?
That which perishes cannot be apprehended;
the phenomenon of perishing cannot be apprehended;
nor can the locus of perishing be apprehended.
"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing such a teaching, is not startled, not terrified, does not sink, and does not retreat, you should know that this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. "Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, Īśvara the lord of beings, and all the sons of gods together pay him homage.

Subhūti! Not only do Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, the Lord of Beings Īśvara, and the various sons of gods pay homage to this bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom; all the gods of the Brahma world—the Brahmapurohita, the Brahmakāyika, the Mahābrahmā, the Ābhāsvara, the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, the Ābhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Anabhraka, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, the Avṛha, the Atapa, the Sudṛśa, the Sudarśana, and the Akaniṣṭha gods—all of them pay homage to this bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti! All the Buddhas currently residing in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds are mindful of this bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!
If, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are brought to mind by all the Buddhas, one should know that this bodhisattva is indeed an avaivartika.
“Subhūti! Suppose all the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to become evil Māras, and each one were to manifest as that many evil Māras.
None of these evil Māras can destroy a bodhisattva who practices this perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva accomplishes two dharmas, the evil Māras cannot destroy them.
What are these two?
First, contemplating that all phenomena are empty;
second, not abandoning any sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these two dharmas, Māra the evil one cannot destroy them.
"Subhūti! Furthermore, there are two other dharmas that Māra the evil one cannot destroy."
What are these two?
First, being able to practice according to what one preaches;
second, being held in the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these two dharmas, all the devas come to offer them sustenance and respect, and inquire after them with words of consolation, saying:
"O son of good family!
By practicing this conduct, you shall swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood."
As you practice this conduct, for those sentient beings who have no refuge, you shall become their refuge;
for those sentient beings who have no shelter, you shall become their shelter;
for those sentient beings who have no reliance, you shall become their reliance.
For sentient beings who have no island, I shall become their island;
for sentient beings who have no ultimate path, I shall become their ultimate path;
for sentient beings who have no refuge, I shall become their refuge.
"I shall provide light for sentient beings who are in ignorance;
I shall provide a destination for sentient beings who have no destination. Why is this?
When this bodhisattva practices the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* and accomplishes these four merits,

all the Buddhas currently residing in the immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable worlds of the ten directions, surrounded by their assemblies of bhikṣus, proclaim and praise them, uttering their names as they teach the Dharma.

Subhūti! For example, it is as if I were now extolling and praising the Bodhisattva Real-Characteristic (Dharmalakṣaṇa), proclaiming his name, as well as other bodhisattvas who, in the presence of Akṣobhya Buddha, have practiced the holy life without ever departing from this practice of the Prajñāpāramitā.
In this way, Subhūti!

All the Buddhas of the ten directions who currently exist likewise extol and praise them, proclaiming the names of the bodhisattvas within my land who practice the holy life and do not depart from the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when all Buddhas preach the Dharma, do they universally extol and praise all bodhisattvas?”
"No, Subhūti! When the Buddhas teach the Dharma, there are those who offer praise and those who do not. Subhūti!"
"When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they extol and praise those bodhisattvas who are *avaivartika*.
World-Honored One,
when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, do they also extol and praise those who have not yet attained the state of *avaivartika*?"
“Subhūti! There are also Buddhas who praise and extol those who have not yet attained the stage of *avaivartika*. Who are they?
These are those who can follow and learn the path practiced by Akṣobhya Buddha when he was a bodhisattva.
Such bodhisattvas, although they have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), are likewise praised and extolled by all Buddhas.

Subhūti! If there are those who can follow and learn the path practiced by a bodhisattva of true reality, such bodhisattvas, even though they have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), are still praised and extolled by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*,
who believe in and understand that all phenomena are unarisen, yet have not yet attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
they believe in and understand that all phenomena are empty, yet within the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), they have not yet attained mastery.
They are able to practice the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas, yet they have not yet entered the stage of *avaivartika*. Subhūti,
when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they likewise praise and extol bodhisattvas who practice in this manner.

Those who, before attaining the stage of *avaivartika*, are praised and extolled by the Buddhas when they preach the Dharma, will leave behind the stages of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*, draw near to the stage of a Buddha, and will certainly receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom and is praised and extolled by the Buddhas when they preach the Dharma, you should know that this bodhisattva will certainly reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Chapter 24: Entrustment. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-four: Entrustment. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, believes and understands it without doubt, without regret, and without difficulty, that bodhisattva shall likewise believe and understand the profound prajñāpāramitā when hearing it from the presence of the Buddha Akṣobhya and his various bodhisattvas."
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva can believe and understand the Prajñāpāramitā as taught by the Buddha, this person will certainly reach the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika). Subhūti!
If a person merely hears the Prajñāpāramitā, they still obtain great benefit; how much more so for one who believes, understands, and practices according to what is taught!
Such a person shall abide in sarvajñatā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Apart from suchness (tathatā), no other dharma can be apprehended."
Who will abide in omniscience?
Who will attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment?
Who will preach the Dharma?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Regarding what you have asked—since apart from suchness (tathatā) no other dharma can be apprehended—who would abide in omniscience (sarvajñatā)? Who would attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)? And who would be the one to preach the Dharma?”
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti, there is no dharma apart from suchness; one abides within suchness."
Since even suchness itself cannot be apprehended, how much less so one who dwells in suchness?
Suchness cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
yet apart from suchness, one also cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“In suchness, there is no one who teaches the Dharma;
apart from suchness, there is likewise no one who teaches the Dharma.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! Since there is no such thing as abiding in suchness, no one who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and no one who preaches the Dharma,
yet a bodhisattva, upon hearing this profound Dharma, does not doubt, does not regret, and does not find it difficult, but desires to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi— this is truly most difficult.”
Subhūti said to Śakra-devānām-indra: “Kauśika!

As you have said, for a bodhisattva to hear this profound Dharma and neither doubt, nor regret, nor find it difficult, desiring to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—this is what is truly most difficult.”
"Kauśika! All dharmas are empty; who, then, could have doubts, regrets, or objections regarding this?
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"As it has been said, all things arise from emptiness and are without obstruction.
It is like shooting an arrow upward into the void; once released, the arrow travels without hindrance. Subhūti!"
"What has been spoken regarding unimpededness is also like this.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If I speak in this way and answer in this way, am I speaking in accordance with what the Tathāgata has said, and am I answering in accordance with the Dharma?
"Kauśika! Your speaking in this way and your answering in this way are indeed in accordance with what the Tathāgata has said; they are in accordance with the Dharma; they are all correct answers."
Kauśika! All that Subhūti has spoken is based upon emptiness.
Subhūti himself cannot even apprehend the prajñāpāramitā, let alone one who practices the prajñāpāramitā.
One does not even attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, much less one who has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
one does not even attain *sarvajñā*, much less one who has attained *sarvajñā*;
one does not even attain *tathatā*, much less one who has attained *tathatā*.
One cannot even apprehend non-arising, much less one who has attained non-arising;
one cannot even apprehend the powers, much less one who has attained the powers;
one cannot even apprehend the fearlessnesses, much less one who has attained the fearlessnesses.
Since even the Dharma cannot be apprehended, how much less so the one who preaches the Dharma? Kauśika!
Subhūti always delights in seclusion and delights in the practice of non-apprehension.

Kauśika! The practice of this Subhūti does not equal even one hundredth part of the practice of a bodhisattva; it does not equal even one part in a hundred thousand million billion, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

Kauśika! Excluding only that which is practiced by the Tathāgata, the bodhisattva’s practice of the prajñāpāramitā is the greatest, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among all other practices.
The conduct of a bodhisattva is also the greatest, the most excellent, the highest, and the most sublime among the conduct of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Therefore, Kauśika!
"If anyone wishes to be the most supreme among all sentient beings, they should practice the Prajñāpāramitā as practiced by Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the sons of the gods from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven in the assembly scattered celestial māndārava flowers over the Buddha.
Six hundred bhikṣus rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and joined their palms toward the Buddha.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, their cupped hands were completely filled with flowers; they then scattered these flowers over the Buddha.
Having scattered [the flowers], they spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
We shall all practice this supreme conduct."
The Buddha then smiled.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, immeasurable rays of light in blue, yellow, red, and white issue forth from their mouths.

These rays of light shone everywhere throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds, reaching upward as far as the Brahma Heaven; they then circled the body three times and entered through the crown of the head.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"For what reason and by what cause do you smile?
The Buddhas do not smile without a cause.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These six hundred bhikṣus shall attain buddhahood during the Nakṣatra Kalpa, all bearing the same name, Saṃpuṣpita. Ānanda!
The number of bhikṣu-saṃghas for these Tathāgatas will all be equal, as will their lifespans, which shall each be twenty thousand kalpas."
From that time forth, those bhikṣus will always attain renunciation in whatever place they are born; in that world, five-colored, exquisite flowers will constantly rain down.
Therefore, Ānanda!
If a person wishes to practice the supreme practice, they should practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva wishes to practice the practice of a Tathāgata, they should practice the Prajñāpāramitā.

Ānanda! If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, you should know that this person, having passed away from the human realm, or having passed away from the Tuṣita heaven, has come to be born among humans.
Why is this? Because it is easy to practice the perfection of wisdom among humans and in the Tuṣita heaven. Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, having faith in it, delighting in it, receiving and upholding it, reading and reciting it, and copying it;
and having copied it, uses this perfection of wisdom to instruct, admonish, benefit, and gladden all other bodhisattvas.

One should know that such a person is seen by the Tathāgata; one should know that such a person has planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas, and not planted roots of goodness in the presence of the disciples.

Ānanda! If a bodhisattva studies the Prajñāpāramitā without being startled or afraid, and with faith and joy accepts, upholds, reads, and recites it, practicing according to what is taught, you should know that this person has come into the presence of the Buddhas of the present.
If there are those who have faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither slandering nor opposing it, you should know that such persons have already made offerings to all Buddhas. Ānanda!
If a person plants roots of goodness under a Buddha seeking arhatship or pratyekabuddhahood, these roots of goodness are not in vain, and they likewise do not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Therefore, Ānanda,
I now entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to you. Ānanda!"
Regarding the Dharma I have taught, with the sole exception of the Prajñāpāramitā,
if one forgets or loses what has been received and upheld, the fault is still slight.
But if you receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā and even forget a single phrase, the fault is exceedingly grave.
Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this Prajñāpāramitā to you.
All that you have heard and received should be recited and chanted; you must master it thoroughly, keep it well in mind, and ensure that every phrase and sentence is clearly understood.
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
"Ānanda!..."

If there is anyone who, in the present, wishes to honor and make offerings to me with a mind of loving-kindness, that person should, with such a mind, make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice according to what is taught; this is the very way to make offerings to me.
Ānanda! This person not only makes offerings to me, but also reverently makes offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Ānanda!

If you cherish and hold me dear and do not abandon me, you should likewise cherish and hold the Prajñāpāramitā dear and not abandon it, even for a single phrase; be careful never to forget or lose it.

“Ānanda! For the sake of entrusting the Prajñāpāramitā, even if I were to speak for one eon, a hundred eons, ten million, a billion, or ten trillion nayutas of eons, or even for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, I could never finish.
Ānanda! For now, I shall speak only briefly.
Just as I am currently the Great Teacher, so too have all the Buddhas of the past and present throughout the ten directions been the Great Teachers among all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras.
The Prajñāpāramitā also acts as the Great Teacher among all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras.
For such immeasurable reasons as these, I entrust the Prajñāpāramitā to you among all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If a person cherishes and honors the Buddha, cherishes and honors the Dharma, cherishes and honors the Saṃgha, and cherishes and honors the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, they should, by means of that same cherishing and honoring, cherish and honor the Prajñāpāramitā."
This is precisely the means by which I perform my teaching and transformation. Ānanda!

If there is anyone who receives, maintains, reads, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, you should know that such a person is receiving and maintaining the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

“Ānanda! When the Prajñāpāramitā is about to be severed, whoever wishes to protect and assist it is, in fact, protecting and assisting the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”
Why is this? Ānanda!
The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas arises entirely from the prajñā-pāramitā.
Ānanda! The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all past Buddhas arose from the *prajñāpāramitā*;
the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all future Buddhas will likewise arise from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all the Buddhas in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds in the present also arises from the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should skillfully train in the six pāramitās. Why is this?
Ānanda! These perfections are the mothers of all bodhisattvas, for they are able to give birth to all buddhas.
If a bodhisattva studies these six perfections, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, Ānanda,
I entrust these six pāramitās to you with special care. Why is this?
"These six pāramitās are the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. Ānanda!

If you were to teach the Dharma of the Hīnayāna for the sake of those of the Hīnayāna, and all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to realize arhatship through this teaching; [the merit would still not equal that of one who teaches the Mahāyāna]."
"As your disciple, your merit is so slight as to be hardly worth mentioning;
however, if you were to explain the six pāramitās for the sake of a bodhisattva, then as my disciple, your merit would be complete, and I would be truly delighted."

Ānanda! If a person were to teach the sentient beings of a trichiliocosm this Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle, causing them to attain the realization of Arhatship—would the merit of these acts of giving, maintaining the precepts, and cultivating goodness not be great?
Ānanda replied,
“Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Although this merit is great, it does not equal the merit of a śrāvaka who explains the Prajñāpāramitā to a bodhisattva for even a single day; the latter's merit is far greater."

Ānanda! Setting aside this single day, suppose one were to preach the Dharma to a bodhisattva from dawn until the time for the midday meal; setting aside that period from dawn until the meal, suppose it were even for the duration of a single *le-ke* (a short measure of time); setting aside even that single *le-ke*, suppose it were for even a brief moment (*muhūrta*). The roots of goodness and merit of such a person cannot be compared with those of all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
If a bodhisattva practices in this way and maintains mindfulness in this way, it is impossible that they would ever regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Chapter 25: Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya, from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Chapter Twenty-Five: Seeing the Buddha Akṣobhya. At that time, as the Buddha was teaching the Prajñāpāramitā, the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, beheld the Buddha Akṣobhya in a great assembly, surrounded by those who paid him respectful homage, as he taught the Dharma.
Like the waters of the great ocean, they were immovable.

At that time, all the bhikṣus were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, and had attained mastery over their minds; there were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, their number being immeasurable.

The Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and the fourfold assembly in the great gathering no longer saw the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, nor the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, nor the magnificent adornments of that buddha-field.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"All dharmas are likewise; they do not confront the eye.
Just as the present Buddha Akṣobhya, along with the arhats and the assembly of bodhisattvas, no longer appear."
Why is this? A dharma does not see a dharma; a dharma does not know a dharma. Ānanda!
"All dharmas are neither knowers nor seers; they have no agent, no attachment, and are non-conceptual.
Ānanda! All dharmas are inconceivable, just like an illusory person."
All phenomena have no experiencer, because they are not solid.
A bodhisattva who practices in this manner is said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom, and remains without attachment even toward phenomena.
A bodhisattva who trains in this manner is said to be training in the *prajñāpāramitā*. Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva wishes to reach the further shore of all dharmas, they should train in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Among all trainings, the training in the *prajñāpāramitā* is the foremost, because it brings peace, happiness, and benefit to all the world.
“Ānanda! One who trains in this way provides a refuge for those who have no refuge.
One who trains in this way is approved by all Buddhas and praised by all Buddhas.”
Having trained in this manner, the Buddhas are able to shake the trichiliocosm with a single toe. Ānanda!
By training in this Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddhas attain unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena of the past, future, and present.
Ānanda! For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme and most wonderful.
"Ānanda! [he said].
If one wishes to measure the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), it is as if measuring empty space. Why is this?
Because this perfection of wisdom is immeasurable.
Ānanda! I do not say that the prajñāpāramitā has limits or measure. Ānanda!
“Names, phrases, and language are finite, whereas the Prajñāpāramitā is infinite.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is the Prajñāpāramitā infinite?”
“Ānanda! Because the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible, it is immeasurable;
because the perfection of wisdom is detached, it is immeasurable.”
Ānanda! All Buddhas of the past emerged from the Prajñāpāramitā, yet the Prajñāpāramitā is not exhausted;
all Buddhas of the future will emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā, yet the Prajñāpāramitā is not exhausted.
All the Buddhas of the immeasurable worlds in the present emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā, yet the Prajñāpāramitā is not exhausted.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā has not been exhausted, is not now exhausted, and shall never be exhausted.
"Ānanda!
If a person wishes to exhaust the perfection of wisdom, they wish to exhaust space.
At that time, Subhūti had this thought:
"This matter is extremely profound; I shall question the Buddha about it.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
“Is the perfection of wisdom inexhaustible? “Subhūti,
the perfection of wisdom is inexhaustible.”
“Because space is inexhaustible, the Prajñāpāramitā is inexhaustible.
“World-Honored One,
how should one give rise to the Prajñāpāramitā?”
“Subhūti! Because form is inexhaustible, this gives rise to the perfection of wisdom;
because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible, this gives rise to the perfection of wisdom.”

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination in this manner, remaining free from the two extremes; this is the unique quality of a bodhisattva.

If a bodhisattva contemplates the dharma of dependent origination in this way, they will not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they will swiftly draw near to sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and will certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Subhūti! If there are bodhisattvas who regress, they do not conceive such thoughts, nor do they know how a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, or how one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination by means of the inexhaustible dharma.”
Subhūti! If there are bodhisattvas who regress, they do not possess such power of skillful means. Subhūti!

If there are bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive, they all attain such power of skillful means; that is to say, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination by means of these inexhaustible dharmas.
When a bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, they do not perceive any phenomena as arising without causes and conditions;
nor do they perceive any phenomena as having an agent or an experiencer. They never perceive such things.
Subhūti! This is called a bodhisattva’s contemplation of the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination when practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they do not perceive this buddha-world, nor do they perceive that buddha-world, nor do they perceive any dharma, yet they see this buddha-world and that buddha-world.
Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who can practice the prajñāpāramitā in this way, at that time Māra, the Evil One, will be filled with grief, as if an arrow has pierced his heart.
For example, when someone has recently lost their parents, they suffer from great grief and anguish;
likewise, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, Māra the Evil One suffers from great grief and anguish.
“World-Honored One!
Is it only one evil Māra who is afflicted with grief and poison, or are all the evil Māras of the trichiliocosm likewise afflicted with grief and poison? “Subhūti!”
All these evil Māras will be filled with grief and distress, each unable to remain at ease in their own seats. Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā in this manner, none among the devas, humans, or asuras in all the worlds can find an opportunity to harm them, nor do they see any dharma that could cause them to regress.
Therefore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice the prajñāpāramitā in this manner.

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, they then fulfill the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, and the perfection of meditative concentration.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they fulfill all the perfections and are also able to fulfill the power of skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
As this bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they are able to know everything that is done as soon as it arises.
Therefore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the power of skillful means should study the Prajñāpāramitā and should cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom and gives rise to the perfection of wisdom, they should bring to mind the Buddhas of the present in immeasurable and boundless worlds, and the *sarvajñā* (all-knowing) wisdom of those Buddhas—all of which arise from the perfection of wisdom.”
When a bodhisattva reflects in this way, they should contemplate thus:
"Just as the Buddhas of the ten directions have attained the characteristics of all dharmas, so too shall I attain them."
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should give rise to such a thought. Subhūti!"

If a bodhisattva can give rise to such a thought for even as long as a finger-snap, it surpasses the merit of giving practiced for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges; how much more so for a day or half a day! One should know that this bodhisattva will certainly reach the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika);
one should know that this bodhisattva is held in the mindful care of all Buddhas.
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who is held in the mindfulness of the Buddhas will not be reborn in other realms; they shall certainly be established in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
